bathos.c: Bathos Ba"thos (bā"thŏs), n. [Gr. ba`qos depth, fr. baqy`s deep.] (Rhet.) A ludicrous descent from the elevated to the low, in writing or speech; anticlimax.

bathybius.c: Bathybius ‖Ba*thyb"i*us (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. baqy`s deep + bi`os life] (Zool.) A name given by Prof. Huxley to a gelatinous substance found in mud dredged from the Atlantic and preserved in alcohol. He supposed that it was free living protoplasm, covering a large part of the ocean bed. It is now known that the substance is of chemical, not of organic, origin.

bathygraphic.c: Bathygraphic Bath`y*graph"ic (?), a. [Gr. baqy`s deep + graphic.] Descriptive of the ocean depth; as, a bathygraphic chart.

bathymetrical.c: Bathymetrical Bathymetric { Bath`y*met"ric (?), Bath`y*met"ric*al (?), } a. Pertaining to bathymetry; relating to the measurement of depths, especially of depths in the sea. -- Bath`y*met"ric*al*ly, adv.

bathymetry.c: Bathymetry Ba*thym"e*try (?), n. [Gr. ba`qos depth + -metry.] The art or science of sounding, or measuring depths in the sea.

bating.c: Bating Bat"ing (?), prep. [Strictly p. pr. of Bate to abate.] With the exception of; excepting.

batiste.c: Batiste Ba*tiste" (?), n. [F. batiste, from the name of the alleged first maker, Baptiste of Cambrai. Littré.] Originally, cambric or lawn of fine linen; now applied also to cloth of similar texture made of cotton.

batlet.c: Batlet Bat"let (?), n. [Bat stick + -let.] A short bat for beating clothes in washing them; -- called also batler, batling staff, batting staff. Shak.

batman.c: Batman ‖Bat"man (băt"măn), n. [Turk. baṭman.] A weight used in the East, varying according to the locality; in Turkey, the greater batman is about 157 pounds, the lesser only a fourth of this; at Aleppo and Smyrna, the batman is 17 pounds. Simmonds.
Batman Bat"man (bä"main or băt"main), n.; pl. Batmen (băt"mein). [F. bât packsaddle + E. man. Cf. Bathorse.] A man who has charge of a bathorse and his load. Macaulay.

batoidei.c: Batoidei ‖Ba*toi"de*i (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. ba`tos a kind of ray + -oid.] (Zool.) The division of fishes which includes the rays and skates.

baton.c: Baton Bat"on (băt"ŭn, F. bä`tôN"; 277), n. [F. bâton. See Baston.] 1. A staff or truncheon, used for various purposes; as, the baton of a field marshal; the baton of a conductor in musical performances.

batoon.c: Batoon Ba*toon" (?), n. See Baton, and Baston.

batrachia.c: Batrachia ‖Ba*tra"chi*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. batra`cheios belonging to a frog, fr. ba`trachos frog.] (Zool.) The order of amphibians which includes the frogs and toads; the Anura. Sometimes the word is used in a wider sense as equivalent to Amphibia.

batrachian.c: Batrachian Ba*tra"chi*an (?), a. (Zool.) Pertaining to the Batrachia. -- n. One of the Batrachia.

batrachoid.c: Batrachoid Bat"ra*choid (?), a. [Batrachia + -oid.] (Zool.) Froglike. Specifically: Of or pertaining to the Batrachidæ, a family of marine fishes, including the toadfish. Some have poisonous dorsal spines.

batrachomyomachy.c: Batrachomyomachy Bat`ra*cho*my*om"a*chy (?), n. [Gr. batrachomyomachi`a; ba`trachos frog + my^s mouse + ma`chh battle.] The battle between the frogs and mice; -- a Greek parody on the Iliad, of uncertain authorship.

batrachophagous.c: Batrachophagous Bat`ra*choph"a*gous (?), a. [Gr. ba`trachos frog + fagei^n to eat.] Feeding on frogs. Quart. Rev.

batsman.c: Batsman Bats"man (?), n.; pl. Batsmen (?). The one who wields the bat in cricket, baseball, etc.; in baseball, the batsman is usually called the batter.

batwing.c: Batwing Bat's-wing {Bat's"-wing" (?) or Bat"wing }, a. Shaped like a bat's wing; as, a bat's-wing burner.

batta.c: Batta ‖Bat"ta (băt"tȧ), n. [Prob. through Pg. for Canarese bhatta rice in the husk.] Extra pay; esp. an extra allowance to an English officer serving in India. Whitworth.
Batta ‖Bat"ta (băt"tȧ), n. [Hind. baṭṭa.] Rate of exchange; also, the discount on uncurrent coins. [India]

battable.c: Battable Bat"ta*ble (?), a. [See Batful.] Capable of cultivation; fertile; productive; fattening. [Obs.] Burton.

battailant.c: Battailant Bat"tail*ant (?), a. [F. bataillant, p. pr. See Battle, v. i. ] [Obs.] Prepared for battle; combatant; warlike. Spenser. -- n. A combatant. Shelton.

battailous.c: Battailous Bat"tail*ous (?), a. [OF. bataillos, fr. bataille. See Battle, n.] Arrayed for battle; fit or eager for battle; warlike. [Obs.] “In battailous aspect.” Milton.

battalia.c: Battalia Bat*tal"ia (băt*tāl"yȧ; 106), n. [LL. battalia battle, a body of troops. See Battle, n.] 1. Order of battle; disposition or arrangement of troops (brigades, regiments, battalions, etc.), or of a naval force, for action.

battalion.c: Battalion Bat*tal"ion (băt*tăl"yŭn; 106), n. [F. bataillon, fr. It. battaglione. See Battalia.] 1. A body of troops; esp. a body of troops or an army in battle array. [archaic] “The whole battalion views.” Milton.
Battalion Bat*tal"ion (?), v. t. To form into battalions. [R.]

battel.c: Battel Bat"tel (?), n. [Obs. form. of Battle.] (Old Eng. Law) A single combat; as, trial by battel. See Wager of battel, under Wager.
Battel Bat"tel, n. [Of uncertain etymology.] Provisions ordered from the buttery; also, the charges for them; -- only in the pl., except when used adjectively. [Univ. of Oxford, Eng.]
Battel Bat"tel, v. i. To be supplied with provisions from the buttery. [Univ. of Oxford, Eng.]
Battel Bat"tel, v. t. [Cf. Batful, Batten, v. i.] To make fertile. [Obs.] “To battel barren land.” Ray.

battler.c: Battler Batteler { Bat"tel*er (?), Bat"tler } (?), n. [See 2d Battel, n.] A student at Oxford who is supplied with provisions from the buttery; formerly, one who paid for nothing but what he called for, answering nearly to a sizar at Cambridge. Wright.

batten.c: Batten Bat"ten (băt"t'n), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Battened (băt"t'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Battening.] [See Batful.] 1. To make fat by plenteous feeding; to fatten. “Battening our flocks.” Milton.
Batten Bat"ten, v. i. To grow fat; to grow fat in ease and luxury; to glut one's self. Dryden.

Batten Bat"ten, n. [F. bâton stick, staff. See Baton.] A strip of sawed stuff, or a scantling; as, (a) pl. (Com. & Arch.) Sawed timbers about 7 by 2 1/2 inches and not less than 6 feet long. Brande & C. (b) (Naut.) A strip of wood used in fastening the edges of a tarpaulin to the deck, also around masts to prevent chafing. (c) A long, thin strip used to strengthen a part, to cover a crack, etc.
Batten Bat"ten, v. t. To furnish or fasten with battens.
Batten Bat"ten, n. [F. battant. See Batter, v. t.] The movable bar of a loom, which strikes home or closes the threads of a woof.

battening.c: Battening Bat"ten*ing (?), n. (Arch.) Furring done with small pieces nailed directly upon the wall.

batter.c: Batter Bat"ter (băt"tẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Battered (băt"tẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Battering.] [OE. bateren, OF. batre, F. battre, fr. LL. battere, for L. batuere to strike, beat; of unknown origin. Cf. Abate, Bate to abate.]

Batter Bat"ter, n. [OE. batere, batire; cf. OF. bateure, bature, a beating. See Batter, v. t.] 1. A semi-liquid mixture of several ingredients, as, flour, eggs, milk, etc., beaten together and used in cookery. King.
Batter Bat"ter, n. A backward slope in the face of a wall or of a bank; receding slope.
Batter Bat"ter, v. i. (Arch.) To slope gently backward.
Batter Bat"ter (băt"tẽr), n. The one who wields the bat in baseball; the one whose turn it is at bat; formerly called the batsman.

batterer.c: Batterer Bat"ter*er (băt"tẽr*ẽr), n. One who, or that which, batters.

batteringram.c: Battering-ram Bat"ter*ing-ram` (?), n. 1. (Mil.) An engine used in ancient times to beat down the walls of besieged places.

battering.c: Battering train Bat"ter*ing train` (?). (Mil.) A train of artillery for siege operations.

battery.c: Battery Bat"ter*y (?), n.; pl. Batteries (?). [F. batterie, fr. battre. See Batter, v. t.] 1. The act of battering or beating.

batting.c: Batting Bat"ting (?), n. 1. The act of one who bats; the management of a bat in playing games of ball. Mason.

battle.c: Battle Bat"tle (?), a. Fertile. See Battel, a. [Obs.]

Battle Bat"tle, n. [OE. bataille, bataile, F. bataille battle, OF., battle, battalion, fr. L. battalia, battualia, the fighting and fencing exercises of soldiers and gladiators, fr. batuere to strike, beat. Cf. Battalia, 1st Battel, and see Batter, v. t. ] 1. A general action, fight, or encounter, in which all the divisions of an army are or may be engaged; an engagement; a combat.

Battle Bat"tle (băt"t'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Battled (-tl'd); p. pr. & vb. n. Battling.] [F. batailler, fr. bataille. See Battle, n.] To join in battle; to contend in fight; as, to battle over theories.
Battle Bat"tle, v. t. To assail in battle; to fight.
Battle range Bat"tle range`. (Mil.) The range within which the fire of small arms is very destructive. With the magazine rifle, this is six hundred yards.

battleaxe.c: Battle-axe Battle-ax { Bat"tle-ax` Bat"tle-axe` } (-ăks`), n. (Mil.) A kind of broadax formerly used as an offensive weapon.

battledoor.c: battledoor bat"tle*door` (?), n. [OE. batyldour. A corrupted form of uncertain origin; cf. Sp. batallador a great combatant, he who has fought many battles, Pg. batalhador, Pr. batalhador, warrior, soldier, fr. L. battalia; or cf. Pr. batedor batlet, fr. batre to beat, fr. L. batuere. See Battle, n.] 1. An instrument, with a handle and a flat part covered with parchment or crossed with catgut, used to strike a shuttlecock in play; also, the play of battledoor and shuttlecock. [Also spelled battledore.]

battlement.c: Battlement Bat"tle*ment (-meint), n. [OE. batelment; cf. OF. bataillement combat, fr. batailler, also OF. bastillier, bateillier, to fortify. Cf. Battle, n., Bastile, Bastion.] (Arch.) (a) One of the solid upright parts of a parapet in ancient fortifications. (b) pl. The whole parapet, consisting of alternate solids and open spaces. At first purely a military feature, afterwards copied on a smaller scale with decorative features, as for churches.

battleship.c: battleship bat"tle*ship`. (Nav.) [shortened from line-of-battle ship, i.e. the most heavily armored ship suited to be in the front line of a naval battle.] An armor-plated warship built of steel and heavily armed, generally having over ten thousand tons displacement, and intended to be fit to combat the heaviest enemy ships in line of battle; the most heavily armed and armored class of warship at any given time.

battologize.c: Battologize Bat*tol"o*gize (băt*tŏl"lo*jīz), v. t. To keep repeating needlessly; to iterate. Sir T. Herbert.

battology.c: Battology Bat*tol"o*gy (băt*tŏl"lo*jy̆), n. [F. battologie, fr. Gr. battologi`a; ba`ttos; a stammerer + lo`gos speech.] A needless repetition of words in speaking or writing. Milton.

batton.c: Batton Bat"ton (?), n. See Batten, and Baton.

battue.c: Battue ‖Bat"tue` (?), n. [F. battue, fr. battre to beat. See Batter, v. t., and cf. Battuta.] (Hunting) (a) The act of beating the woods, bushes, etc., for game. (b) The game itself. (c) The wanton slaughter of game. Howitt.

batture.c: Batture ‖Bat`ture" (?), n. [F., fr. battre to beat.] An elevated river bed or sea bed.

battuta.c: Battuta ‖Bat*tu"ta (?), n. [It. battuta, fr. battere to beat.] (Mus.) The measuring of time by beating.

batty.c: Batty Bat"ty (băt"ty̆), a. 1. Belonging to, or resembling, a bat. “Batty wings.” Shak.

batule.c: Batule Bat"ule (băt"ūl or bȧ*tōol"), n. A springboard in a circus or gymnasium; -- called also batule board.

batz.c: Batz ‖Batz (bäts), n.; pl. Batzen (?). [Ger. batz, batze, batzen, a coin bearing the image of a bear, Ger. bätz, betz, bear.] A small copper coin, with a mixture of silver, formerly current in some parts of Germany and Switzerland. It was worth about four cents.

bauble.c: Bauble Bau"ble (bä"b'l), n. [Cf. OF. baubel a child's plaything, F. babiole, It. babbola, LL. baubellum gem, jewel, L. babulus, a baburrus, foolish.] 1. A trifling piece of finery; a gewgaw; that which is gay and showy without real value; a cheap, showy plaything.

baudekin.c: Baudekin Bau"de*kin (?), n. [OE. bawdekin rich silk stuff, OF. baudequin. See Baldachin.] The richest kind of stuff used in garments in the Middle Ages, the web being gold, and the woof silk, with embroidery; -- made originally at Baghdad. [Spelt also baudkin, baudkyn, bawdekin, and baldakin.] Nares.

baudrick.c: Baudrick Bau"drick (?), n. A belt. See Baldric.

baulk.c: Baulk Bauk { Bauk, Baulk } (?), n. & v. See Balk.

baume.c: Baume Bau`mé" (?), a. Designating or conforming to either of the scales used by the French chemist Antoine Baumé in the graduation of his hydrometers; of or relating to Baumé's scales or hydrometers. There are two Baumé hydrometers. One, which is used with liquids heavier than water, sinks to 0° in pure water, and to 15° in a 15 per cent salt solution; the other, for liquids lighter than water, sinks to 0° in a 10 per cent salt solution and to 10° in pure water. In both cases the graduation, based on the distance between these fundamental points, is continued along the stem as far as desired.

baunscheidtism.c: Baunscheidtism Baun"scheidt*ism (?), n. [From the introducer, a German named Baunscheidt.] (Med.) A form of acupuncture, followed by the rubbing of the part with a stimulating fluid.

beauxite.c: Beauxite Bauxite { Baux"ite, Beaux"ite } (?),n. [F., fr. Baux or Beaux, near Arles.] (Min.) A ferruginous hydrate of alumina. It is the most commonly used ore for the preparation of aluminum and alumina. It is also used for the lining of furnaces which are exposed to intense heat.

bavardage.c: Bavardage ‖Ba`var`dage" (?), n. [F.] Much talking; prattle; chatter. Byron.

bavarian.c: Bavarian Ba*va"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Bavaria. -- n. A native or an inhabitant of Bavaria.

bavaroy.c: Bavaroy Bav"a*roy (?), n. [F. Bavarois Bavarian.] A kind of cloak or surtout. [Obs.] Johnson.

bavin.c: Bavin Bav"in (băv"ĭn), n. [Cf. Gael. & Ir. baban tuft, tassel.] 1. A fagot of brushwood, or other light combustible matter, for kindling fires; refuse of brushwood. [Obs. or Dial. Eng.]

bawbee.c: Bawbee Baw*bee" (?), n. [Perh. corrupt. fr. halfpenny.] A halfpenny. [Spelt also baubee.] [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]

bawble.c: Bawble Baw"ble (?), n. A trinket. See Bauble.

bawcock.c: Bawcock Baw"cock (?), n. [From F. beau fine + E. cock (the bird); or more prob. fr. OF. baud bold, gay + E. cock. Cf. Bawd.] A fine fellow; -- a term of endearment. [Obs.] “How now, my bawcock?” Shak.

bawd.c: Bawd Bawd (?), n. [OE. baude, OF. balt, baut, baude, bold, merry, perh. fr. OHG. bald bold; or fr. Celtic, cf. W. baw dirt. Cf. Bold, Bawdry.] A person who keeps a house of prostitution, or procures women for a lewd purpose; a procurer or procuress; a lewd person; -- usually applied to a woman.
Bawd Bawd, v. i. To procure women for lewd purposes.

bawdrick.c: Bawdrick Bawd"rick (?), n. A belt. See Baldric.

bawdry.c: Bawdry Bawd"ry (?), n. [OE. baudery, OF. bauderie, balderie, boldness, joy. See Bawd.] 1. The practice of procuring women for the gratification of lust.

bawdy.c: Bawdy Bawd"y, a. 1. Dirty; foul; -- said of clothes. [Obs.]

bawdyhouse.c: Bawdyhouse Baw"dy*house` (?), n. A house of prostitution; a house of ill fame; a brothel.

bawl.c: Bawl Bawl (bäl), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bawled (bäld); p. pr. & vb. n. Bawling.] [Icel. baula to low, bellow, as a cow; akin to Sw. böla; cf. AS bellan, G. bellen to bark, E. bellow, bull.] 1. To cry out with a loud, full sound; to cry with vehemence, as in calling or exultation; to shout; to vociferate.
Bawl Bawl, v. t. To proclaim with a loud voice, or by outcry, as a hawker or town-crier does. Swift.
Bawl Bawl, n. A loud, prolonged cry; an outcry.

bawn.c: Bawn Bawn (?), n. [Ir. & Gael. babhun inclosure, bulwark.] 1. An inclosure with mud or stone walls, for keeping cattle; a fortified inclosure. [Obs.] Spenser.

bawrel.c: Bawrel Baw"rel (?), n. [Cf. It. barletta a tree falcon, or hobby.] A kind of hawk. [Obs.] Halliwell.

bawson.c: Bawson Bawsin { Baw"sin (?), Baw"son (?), } n. [OE. bawson, baucyne, badger (named from its color), OF. bauzan, bauçant, bauchant, spotted with white, pied; cf. It. balzano, F. balzan, a white-footed horse, It. balza border, trimming, fr. L. balteus belt, border, edge. Cf. Belt.] 1. A badger. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

baxter.c: Baxter Bax"ter (?), n. [OE. bakestre, bakistre, AS. bæcestre, prop. fem. of bæcere baker. See Baker.] A baker; originally, a female baker. [Old Eng. & Scotch]

bay.c: Bay Bay (bā), a. [F. bai, fr. L. badius brown, chestnut-colored; -- used only of horses.] Reddish brown; of the color of a chestnut; -- applied to the color of horses.

Bay Bay, n. [F. baie, fr. LL. baia. Of uncertain origin: cf. Ir. & Gael. badh or bagh bay, harbor, creek; Bisc. baia, baiya, harbor, and F. bayer to gape, open the mouth.] 1. (Geog.) An inlet of the sea, usually smaller than a gulf, but of the same general character.

Bay Bay, n. [F. baie a berry, the fruit of the laurel and other trees, fr. L. baca, bacca, a small round fruit, a berry, akin to Lith. bapka laurel berry.] 1. A berry, particularly of the laurel. [Obs.]
Bay Bay, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bayed (bād); p. pr. & vb. n. Baying.] [OE. bayen, abayen, OF. abaier, F. aboyer, to bark; of uncertain origin.] To bark, as a dog with a deep voice does, at his game.
Bay Bay (?), v. t. To bark at; hence, to follow with barking; to bring or drive to bay; as, to bay the bear. Shak.
Bay Bay (?), n. [See Bay, v. i.] 1. Deep-toned, prolonged barking. “The bay of curs.” Cowper.
Bay Bay, v. t. [Cf. OE. bæwen to bathe, and G. bähen to foment.] To bathe. [Obs.] Spenser.
Bay Bay, n. A bank or dam to keep back water.
Bay Bay, v. t. To dam, as water; -- with up or back.
Bay ice Bay" ice` (?). See under Ice.
Bay leaf Bay" leaf` (?). See under 3d Bay.
Bay rum Bay" rum" (?). A fragrant liquid, used for cosmetic and medicinal purposes.
Bay salt Bay" salt` (?). Salt which has been obtained from sea water, by evaporation in shallow pits or basins, by the heat of the sun; the large crystalline salt of commerce. Bacon. Ure.
Bay State Bay State. Massachusetts, which had been called the Colony of Massachusetts Bay; -- a nickname.
Bay tree Bay" tree`. A species of laurel. (Laurus nobilis).

Bay window Bay" win"dow (?). 1. (Arch.) A window forming a bay or recess in a room, and projecting outward from the wall, either in a rectangular, polygonal, or semicircular form; -- often corruptly called a bow window.
Bay yarn Bay" yarn` (?). Woolen yarn. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

baya.c: Baya ‖Ba"ya (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) The East Indian weaver bird (Ploceus Philippinus).

bayatte.c: Bayatte Bayad { ‖Ba*yad" (?), Ba*yatte" } (?), n. [Ar. bayad.] (Zool.) A large, edible, siluroid fish of the Nile, of two species (Bagrina bayad and Bagrina docmac).

bayadere.c: Bayadere Ba`ya*dere" (?), n. [F., from Pg. bailadeira a female dancer, bailar to dance.] A female dancer in the East Indies. [Written also bajadere.]

bayamo.c: Bayamo Ba*ya"mo (?), n. (Meteor.) A violent thunder squall occurring on the south coast of Cuba, esp. near Bayamo. The gusts, called bayamo winds, are modified foehn winds.

bayantler.c: Bay-antler Bay"-ant`ler (?), n. [See Bez-Antler.] (Zool.) The second tine of a stag's horn. See under Antler.

bayard.c: Bayard Bay"ard (?), n. 1. [OF. bayard, baiart, bay horse; bai bay + -ard. See Bay, a., and -ard.] Properly, a bay horse, but often any horse. Commonly in the phrase blind bayard, an old blind horse.

bayardly.c: Bayardly Bay"ard*ly, a. Blind; stupid. [Obs.] “A formal and bayardly round of duties.” Goodman.

bayberry.c: Bayberry Bay"ber*ry (?), n. (Bot.) (a) The fruit of the bay tree or Laurus nobilis. (b) A tree of the West Indies related to the myrtle (Pimenta acris). (c) The fruit of Myrica cerifera (wax myrtle); the shrub itself; -- called also candleberry tree.

baybolt.c: Baybolt Bay"bolt` (?), n. A bolt with a barbed shank.

bayed.c: Bayed Bayed (?), a. Having a bay or bays. “The large bayed barn.” Drayton.

bayeux.c: Bayeux tapestry Ba`yeux" tap"es*try (?). A piece of linen about 1 ft. 8 in. wide by 213 ft. long, covered with embroidery representing the incidents of William the Conqueror's expedition to England, preserved in the town museum of Bayeux in Normandy. It is probably of the 11th century, and is attributed by tradition to Matilda, the Conqueror's wife.

bayman.c: Bayman Bay"man (?), n. (Nav.) In the United States navy, a sick-bay nurse; -- now officially designated as hospital apprentice.

bayonet.c: Bayonet Bay"o*net (?), n. [F. bayonnette, baïonnette; -- so called, it is said, because the first bayonets were made at Bayonne.]
Bayonet Bay"o*net, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bayoneted; p. pr. & vb. n. Bayoneting.] 1. To stab with a bayonet.

bayou.c: Bayou Bay"ou (?), n.; pl. Bayous (?). [North Am. Indian bayuk, in F. spelling bayouc, bayouque.] An inlet from the Gulf of Mexico, from a lake, or from a large river, sometimes sluggish, sometimes without perceptible movement except from tide and wind. [Southern U. S.]
Bayou State Bay"ou State` (?). Mississippi; -- a nickname, from its numerous bayous.

bayze.c: Bayze Bays { Bays, Bayze } (?), n. See Baize. [Obs.]

bazar.c: Bazar Bazaar { Ba*zaar" Ba*zar" } (bȧ*zär"), n. [Per. bāzar market.] 1. In the East, an exchange, marketplace, or assemblage of shops where goods are exposed for sale.

bdellium.c: bdellium bdel"lium (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. bde`llion; cf. Heb. b'dolakh bdellium (in sense 1).] 1. An unidentified substance mentioned in the Bible (Gen. ii. 12, and Num. xi. 7), variously taken to be a gum, a precious stone, or pearls, or perhaps a kind of amber found in Arabia.

bdelloidea.c: Bdelloidea ‖Bdel*loi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. bde`lla leech + -oid.] (Zool.) The order of Annulata which includes the leeches. See Hirudinea.

bdellometer.c: Bdellometer Bdel*lom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. bde`lla leech + -meter.] (Med.) A cupping glass to which are attached a scarificator and an exhausting syringe. Dunglison.

bdellomorpha.c: Bdellomorpha ‖Bdel`lo*mor"pha (?),n. [NL., fr. Gr. bde`lla leech + morfh` form.] (Zool.) An order of Nemertina, including the large leechlike worms (Malacobdella) often parasitic in clams.

be.c: Be Be (bē), v. i. [imp. Was (wŏz); p. p. Been (bĭn); p. pr. & vb. n. Being.] [OE. been, beon, AS. beón to be, beóm I am; akin to OHG. bim, pim, G. bin, I am, Gael. & Ir. bu was, W. bod to be, Lith. bu-ti, O. Slav. by-ti, to be, L. fu-i I have been, fu-turus about to be, fo-re to be about to be, and perh. to fieri to become, Gr. fy^nai to be born, to be, Skr. bhū to be. This verb is defective, and the parts lacking are supplied by verbs from other roots, is, was, which have no radical connection with be. The various forms, am, are, is, was, were, etc., are considered grammatically as parts of the verb “to be”, which, with its conjugational forms, is often called the substantive verb. √97. Cf. Future, Physic.] 1. To exist actually, or in the world of fact; to have existence.

Be- Be-. [AS. be, and in accented form bī, akin to OS. be and bī, OHG. bi, pi, and pī, MHG. be and bī, G. be and bei, Goth. bi, and perh. Gr. 'amfi` about (cf. AS. beseón to look about). √203. Cf. By, Amb-.] A prefix, originally the same word as by; joined with verbs, it serves: (a) To intensify the meaning; as, bespatter, bestir. (b) To render an intransitive verb transitive; as, befall (to fall upon); bespeak (to speak for). (c) To make the action of a verb particular or definite; as, beget (to get as offspring); beset (to set around).

beach.c: Beach Beach (bēch), n.; pl. Beaches (-ĕz). [Cf. Sw. backe hill, Dan. bakke, Icel. bakki hill, bank. Cf. Bank.] 1. Pebbles, collectively; shingle.
Beach Beach, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beached (bēcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Beaching.] To run or drive (as a vessel or a boat) upon a beach; to strand; as, to beach a ship.
Beach comber Beach" comb`er (?). A long, curling wave rolling in from the ocean. See Comber. [Amer., archaic]

beachcomber.c: beachcomber beachcomber. [Written also beach-comber or beach comber.] (Naut.) 1. A vagrant seaman, usually of low character, who loiters about seaports, particularly on the shores and islands of the Pacific Ocean.

beached.c: Beached Beached (bēcht), p. p. & a. 1. Bordered by a beach.

beachy.c: Beachy Beach"y (?), a. Having a beach or beaches; formed by a beach or beaches; shingly.

beacon.c: Beacon Bea"con (bē"k'n), n. [OE. bekene, AS. beácen, bēcen; akin to OS. bōkan, Fries. baken, beken, sign, signal, D. baak, OHG. bouhhan, G. bake; of unknown origin. Cf. Beckon.] 1. A signal fire to notify of the approach of an enemy, or to give any notice, commonly of warning.
Beacon Bea"con, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beaconed (bē"k'nd); p. pr. & vb. n. Beaconing.] 1. To give light to, as a beacon; to light up; to illumine.

beaconage.c: Beaconage Bea"con*age (?), n. Money paid for the maintenance of a beacon; also, beacons, collectively.

bead.c: Bead Bead (bēd), n. [OE. bede prayer, prayer bead, AS. bed, gebed, prayer; akin to D. bede, G. bitte, AS. biddan, to ask, bid, G. bitten to ask, and perh. to Gr. pei`qein to persuade, L. fidere to trust. Beads are used by the Roman Catholics to count their prayers, one bead being dropped down a string every time a prayer is said. Cf. Sp. cuenta bead, fr. contar to count. See Bid, in to bid beads, and Bide.] 1. A prayer. [Obs.]
Bead Bead, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Beading.] To ornament with beads or beading.
Bead Bead, v. i. To form beadlike bubbles.

Bead proof Bead" proof` (?). 1. Among distillers, a certain degree of strength in alcoholic liquor, as formerly ascertained by the floating or sinking of glass globules of different specific gravities thrown into it; now ascertained by more accurate meters.

bedehouse.c: Bedehouse Beadhouse { Bead"house`, Bede"house` } (?), n. [OE. bede prayer + E. house. See Bead, n.] An almshouse for poor people who pray daily for their benefactors.

beading.c: Beading Bead"ing, n. 1. (Arch.) Molding in imitation of beads.

beadle.c: Beadle Bea"dle (?), n. [OE. bedel, bidel, budel, OF. bedel, F. bedeau, fr. OHG. butil, putil, G. büttel, fr. OHG. biotan, G. bieten, to bid, confused with AS. bydel, the same word as OHG. butil. See. Bid, v.] 1. A messenger or crier of a court; a servitor; one who cites or bids persons to appear and answer; -- called also an apparitor or summoner.

beadlery.c: Beadlery Bea"dle*ry (?), n. Office or jurisdiction of a beadle.

beadleship.c: Beadleship Bea"dle*ship, n. The state of being, or the personality of, a beadle. A. Wood.

beadroll.c: Beadroll Bead"roll` (?), n. (R. C. Ch.) A catalogue of persons, for the rest of whose souls a certain number of prayers are to be said or counted off on the beads of a chaplet; hence, a catalogue in general.

bedesman.c: Bedesman Beadsman { Beads"man, Bedes"man } (?), n.; pl. -men (?). A poor man, supported in a beadhouse, and required to pray for the soul of its founder; an almsman.

beadsnake.c: Beadsnake Bead"snake` (?), n. (Zool.) A small poisonous snake of North America (Elaps fulvius), banded with yellow, red, and black.

bedeswoman.c: Bedeswoman Beadswoman { Beads"wom`an, Bedes"wom`an } (?), n.; pl. -women (?). Fem. of Beadsman.

beadwork.c: Beadwork Bead"work` (?), n. Ornamental work in beads.

beady.c: Beady Bead"y (?), a. 1. Resembling beads; small, round, and glistening. “Beady eyes.” Thackeray.

beagle.c: Beagle Bea"gle (?), n. [OE. begele; perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. beag small, little, W. bach. F. bigle is from English.] 1. A small hound, or hunting dog, twelve to fifteen inches high, used in hunting hares and other small game. See Illustration in Appendix.

beak.c: Beak Beak (bēk), n. [OE. bek, F. bec, fr. Celtic; cf. Gael. & Ir. bac, bacc, hook, W. bach.] 1. (Zool.) (a) The bill or nib of a bird, consisting of a horny sheath, covering the jaws. The form varies much according to the food and habits of the bird, and is largely used in the classification of birds. (b) A similar bill in other animals, as the turtles. (c) The long projecting sucking mouth of some insects, and other invertebrates, as in the Hemiptera. (d) The upper or projecting part of the shell, near the hinge of a bivalve. (e) The prolongation of certain univalve shells containing the canal.

beaked.c: Beaked Beaked (bēkt), a. 1. Having a beak or a beaklike point; beak-shaped. “Each beaked promontory.” Milton.

beaker.c: Beaker Beak"er (bēk"ẽr), n. [OE. biker; akin to Icel. bikarr, Sw. bägare, Dan. baeger, G. becher, It. bicchiere; -- all fr. LL. bicarium, prob. fr. Gr. bi^kos wine jar, or perh. L. bacar wine vessel. Cf. Pitcher a jug.] 1. A large drinking cup, with a wide mouth, supported on a foot or standard.

beakhead.c: Beakhead Beak"head` (?), n. 1. (Arch.) An ornament used in rich Norman doorways, resembling a head with a beak. Parker.

beakiron.c: Beakiron Beak"i*ron (?), n. [From Bickern.] A bickern; a bench anvil with a long beak, adapted to reach the interior surfaces of sheet metal ware; the horn of an anvil.

beal.c: Beal Beal (bēl), n. [See Boil a tumor.] (Med.) A small inflammatory tumor; a pustule. [Prov. Eng.]
Beal Beal, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bealed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bealing.] To gather matter; to swell and come to a head, as a pimple. [Prov. Eng.]

beall.c: Be-all Be"-all` (?), n. The whole; all that is to be. [Poetic] Shak.

beam.c: Beam Beam (bēm), n. [AS. beám beam, post, tree, ray of light; akin to OFries. bām tree, OS. bōm, D. boom, OHG. boum, poum, G. baum, Icel. baðmr, Goth. bagms and Gr. fy^ma a growth, fy^nai to become, to be. Cf. L. radius staff, rod, spoke of a wheel, beam or ray, and G. strahl arrow, spoke of a wheel, ray or beam, flash of lightning. √97. See Be; cf. Boom a spar.] 1. Any large piece of timber or iron long in proportion to its thickness, and prepared for use.
Beam Beam, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beamed (bēmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Beaming.] To send forth; to emit; -- followed ordinarily by forth; as, to beam forth light.
Beam Beam, v. i. To emit beams of light.
Beam tree Beam" tree` (?). [AS. beám a tree. See Beam.] (Bot.) A tree (Pyrus aria) related to the apple.

beambird.c: Beambird Beam"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) A small European flycatcher (Muscicapa grisola), so called because it often nests on a beam in a building.

beamed.c: Beamed Beamed (?), a. Furnished with beams, as the head of a stag.

beamily.c: Beamily Beam"i*ly (?), adv. In a beaming manner.

beaminess.c: Beaminess Beam"i*ness, n. The state of being beamy.

beamingly.c: Beamingly Beam"ing*ly, adv. In a beaming manner; radiantly.

beamless.c: Beamless Beam"less, a. 1. Not having a beam.

beamlet.c: Beamlet Beam"let (?), n. A small beam of light.

beamy.c: Beamy Beam"y (?), a. 1. Emitting beams of light; radiant; shining. “Beamy gold.” Tickell.

bean.c: Bean Bean (bēn), n. [OE. bene, AS. beán; akin to D. boon, G. bohne, OHG. pōna, Icel. baun, Dan. bönne, Sw. böna, and perh. to Russ. bob, L. faba.] 1. (Bot.) A name given to the seed of certain leguminous herbs, chiefly of the genera Faba, Phaseolus, and Dolichos; also, to the herbs.
Bean caper Bean" ca`per. (Bot.) A deciduous plant of warm climates, generally with fleshy leaves and flowers of a yellow or whitish yellow color, of the genus Zygophyllum.
Bean trefoil Bean" tre"foil. (Bot.) A leguminous shrub of southern Europe, with trifoliate leaves (Anagyris foetida).

bear.c: Bear Bear (bâr), v. t. [imp. Bore (bōr) (formerly Bare (bâr)); p. p. Born (bôrn), Borne (bōrn); p. pr. & vb. n. Bearing.] [OE. beren, AS. beran, beoran, to bear, carry, produce; akin to D. baren to bring forth, G. gebären, Goth. baíran to bear or carry, Icel. bera, Sw. bära, Dan. bære, OHG. beran, peran, L. ferre to bear, carry, produce, Gr. fe`rein, OSlav. brati to take, carry, OIr. berim I bear, Skr. bhṛ to bear. √92. Cf. Fertile.] 1. To support or sustain; to hold up.
Bear Bear (bâr), v. i. 1. To produce, as fruit; to be fruitful, in opposition to barrenness.
Bear Bear (bâr), n. [OE. bere, AS. bera; akin to D. beer, OHG. bero, pero, G. bär, Icel. & Sw. björn, and possibly to L. fera wild beast, Gr. fh`r beast, Skr. bhalla bear.]
Bear Bear, v. t. (Stock Exchange) To endeavor to depress the price of, or prices in; as, to bear a railroad stock; to bear the market.
Bear State Bear State. Arkansas; -- a nickname, from the many bears once inhabiting its forests.

bere.c: Bere Bear { Bear, Bere } (bēr), n. [AS. bere. See Barley.] (Bot.) Barley; the six-rowed barley or the four-rowed barley, commonly the former (Hordeum hexastichon or Hordeum vulgare). [Obs. except in North of Eng. and Scot.]
Bere Bere (bēr), v. t. [Cf. OIcel. berja to strike.] To pierce. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bearable.c: Bearable Bear"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being borne or endured; tolerable. -- Bear"a*bly, adv.

bearberry.c: Bearberry Bear"ber*ry (?), n. (Bot.) A trailing plant of the heath family (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi), having leaves which are tonic and astringent, and glossy red berries of which bears are said to be fond.

beard.c: Beard Beard (bērd), n. [OE. berd, AS. beard; akin to Fries. berd, D. baard, G. bart, Lith. barzda, OSlav. brada, Pol. broda, Russ. boroda, L. barba, W. barf. Cf. 1st Barb.]
Beard Beard (bērd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bearded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bearding.] 1. To take by the beard; to seize, pluck, or pull the beard of (a man), in anger or contempt.

bearded.c: Bearded Beard"ed, a. Having a beard. “Bearded fellow.” Shak. “Bearded grain.” Dryden.

beardie.c: Beardie Beard"ie (bērd"y̆), n. [From Beard, n.] (Zool.) The bearded loach (Nemachilus barbatus) of Europe. [Scot.]

beardless.c: Beardless Beard"less, a. 1. Without a beard. Hence: Not having arrived at puberty or manhood; youthful.

beardlessness.c: Beardlessness Beard"less*ness, n. The state or quality of being destitute of beard.

bearer.c: Bearer Bear"er (bâr"ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, bears, sustains, or carries. “Bearers of burdens.” 2 Chron. ii. 18. “The bearer of unhappy news.” Dryden.

bearherd.c: Bearherd Bear"herd` (?), n. A man who tends a bear.

bearhound.c: Bearhound Bear"hound` (?), n. A hound for baiting or hunting bears. Carlyle.

bearing.c: Bearing Bear"ing (bâr"ĭng), n. 1. The manner in which one bears or conducts one's self; mien; behavior; carriage.
Bearing cloth Bear"ing cloth` (bâr"ĭng klŏth`; 115). A cloth with which a child is covered when carried to be baptized. Shak.
Bearing rein Bear"ing rein` (?). A short rein looped over the check hook or the hames to keep the horse's head up; -- called in the United States a checkrein.
Bearing ring Bear"ing ring`. In a balloon, the braced wooden ring attached to the suspension ropes at the bottom, functionally analogous to the keel of a ship.

bearish.c: Bearish Bear"ish, a. 1. Partaking of the qualities of a bear; resembling a bear in temper or manners. Harris.

bearishness.c: Bearishness Bear"ish*ness, n. Behavior like that of a bear.

bearsbreeches.c: bear's-breeches Bear's-breech Bear's"-breech`, bear's"-breech`es (?), n. 1. (Bot.) The English cow parsnip (Heracleum sphondylium) Dr. Prior.

bearsear.c: Bear's-ear Bear's-ear` (bârz"ēr`), n. (Bot.) A kind of primrose (Primula auricula), so called from the shape of the leaf.

bearsfoot.c: Bear's-foot Bear's"-foot` (-fŏot`), n. (Bot.) A species of hellebore (Helleborus fœtidus), with digitate leaves. It has an offensive smell and acrid taste, and is a powerful emetic, cathartic, and anthelmintic.

bearskin.c: Bearskin Bear"skin` (?), n. 1. The skin of a bear.

bearspaw.c: Bear's-paw Bear's"-paw` (?), n. (Zool.) A large bivalve shell of the East Indies (Hippopus maculatus), often used as an ornament.

beartrap.c: Bear-trap dam Bear"-trap` dam. (Engin.) A kind of movable dam, in one form consisting of two leaves resting against each other at the top when raised and folding down one over the other when lowered, for deepening shallow parts in a river.

bearward.c: Bearward Bear"ward` (?), n. [Bear + ward a keeper.] A keeper of bears. See Bearherd. [R.] Shak.

beast.c: Beast Beast (bēst), n. [OE. best, beste, OF. beste, F. bête, fr. L. bestia.] 1. Any living creature; an animal; -- including man, insects, etc. [Obs.] Chaucer.

beasthood.c: Beasthood Beast"hood (?), n. State or nature of a beast.

beastliness.c: Beastliness Beast"li*ness, n. The state or quality of being beastly.

beastly.c: Beastly Beast"ly (bēst"ly̆), a. 1. Pertaining to, or having the form, nature, or habits of, a beast.

beat.c: Beat Beat (bēt), v. t. [imp. Beat; p. p. Beat, Beaten (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beating.] [OE. beaten, beten, AS. beátan; akin to Icel. bauta, OHG. bōzan. Cf. 1st Butt, Button.] 1. To strike repeatedly; to lay repeated blows upon; as, to beat one's breast; to beat iron so as to shape it; to beat grain, in order to force out the seeds; to beat eggs and sugar; to beat a drum.
Beat Beat, v. i. 1. To strike repeatedly; to inflict repeated blows; to knock vigorously or loudly.
Beat Beat (?), n. 1. A stroke; a blow.
Beat Beat, a. Weary; tired; fatigued; exhausted. [Colloq.]
Beat Beat, n. 1. One that beats, or surpasses, another or others; as, the beat of him. [Colloq.]

beaten.c: Beaten Beat"en (bēt"'n; 95), a. 1. Made smooth by beating or treading; worn by use. “A broad and beaten way.” Milton. “Beaten gold.” Shak. “off the beaten track.”

beater.c: Beater Beat"er (bēt"ẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, beats.

beath.c: Beath Beath (bēth), v. t. [AS. beðian to foment.] To bathe; also, to dry or heat, as unseasoned wood. [Obs.] Spenser.

beatifical.c: Beatifical Beatific { Be`a*tif"ic (?), Be`a*tif"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. béatifique, L. beatificus. See Beatify.] Having the power to impart or complete blissful enjoyment; blissful. “The beatific vision.” South. -- Be`a*tif"ic*al*ly, adv.

beatificate.c: Beatificate Be`a*tif"i*cate (?), v. t. To beatify. [Obs.] Fuller.

beatification.c: Beatification Be*at`i*fi*ca"tion (be*ăt`ĭ*fĭ*kā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. béatification.] The act of beatifying, or the state of being beatified; esp., in the R. C. Church, the act or process of ascertaining and declaring that a deceased person is one of “the blessed,” or has attained the second degree of sanctity, -- usually a stage in the process of canonization. “The beatification of his spirit.” Jer. Taylor.

beatify.c: Beatify Be*at"i*fy (be*ăt"ĭ*fī), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beatified (be*ăt"ĭ*fīd); p. pr. & vb. n. Beatifying.] [L. beatificare; beatus happy (fr. beare to bless, akin to bonus good) + facere to make: cf. F. béatifier. See Bounty.] 1. To pronounce or regard as happy, or supremely blessed, or as conferring happiness.

beating.c: Beating Beat"ing (?), n. 1. The act of striking or giving blows; punishment or chastisement by blows.

beatitude.c: Beatitude Be*at"i*tude (?), n. [L. beatitudo: cf. F. béatitude. See Beatify.] 1. Felicity of the highest kind; consummate bliss.

beau.c: Beau Beau (bō), n.; pl. F. Beaux (E. pron. bōz), E. Beaus (bōz). [F., a fop, fr. beau fine, beautiful, fr. L. bellus pretty, fine, for bonulus, dim. of bonus good. See Bounty, and cf. Belle, Beauty.] 1. A man who takes great care to dress in the latest fashion; a dandy.

Beau ideal Beau" i*de"al (bō" i*dē"ail; 277). [F. beau beautiful + idéal ideal.] A conception or image of consummate beauty, moral or physical, formed in the mind, free from all the deformities, defects, and blemishes seen in actual existence; an ideal or faultless standard or model.
Beau monde ‖Beau` monde" (?). [F. beau fine + monde world.] The fashionable world; people of fashion and gayety. Prior.

beaucatcher.c: Beaucatcher Beau"catch`er (?), n. A small flat curl worn on the temple by women. [Humorous]

beaufet.c: Beaufet Beau"fet (?), n. [See Buffet.] A niche, cupboard, or sideboard for plate, china, glass, etc.; a buffet.

beauforts.c: Beaufort's scale Beau"fort's scale` (?). (Meteor.) A scale of wind force devised by Sir F. Beaufort, R. N., in 1805, in which the force is indicated by numbers from 0 to 12.

beauish.c: Beauish Beau"ish (?), a. Like a beau; characteristic of a beau; foppish; fine. “A beauish young spark.” Byrom.

beaumontague.c: Beaumontague Beau`mon"ta*gue (?), n. A cement used in making joints, filling cracks, etc. For iron, the principal constituents are iron borings and sal ammoniac; for wood, white lead or litharge, whiting, and linseed oil.

beaupere.c: Beaupere Beau"pere` (?), n. [F. beau pére; beau fair + pére father.] 1. A father. [Obs.] Wyclif.

beauseant.c: Beauseant ‖Beau`se`ant" (?), n. [F. beaucéant.] The black and white standard of the Knights Templars.

beauship.c: Beauship Beau"ship (?), n. The state of being a beau; the personality of a beau. [Jocular] Dryden.

beauteous.c: Beauteous Beau"te*ous (bū"te*ŭs), a. Full of beauty; beautiful; very handsome. [Mostly poetic] -- Beau"te*ous*ly, adv. -- Beau"te*ous*ness, n.

beautied.c: Beautied Beau"tied (bū"tĭd), p. a. Beautiful; embellished. [Poetic] Shak.

beautifier.c: Beautifier Beau"ti*fi`er (?), n. One who, or that which, beautifies or makes beautiful.

beautiful.c: Beautiful Beau"ti*ful (bū"tĭ*fụl), a. Having the qualities which constitute beauty; pleasing to the sight or the mind.

beautify.c: Beautify Beau"ti*fy (bū"tĭ*fī), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beautified (bū"tĭ*fī); p. pr. & vb. n. Beautifying.] [Beauty + -fy.] To make or render beautiful; to add beauty to; to adorn; to deck; to grace; to embellish.
Beautify Beau"ti*fy, v. i. To become beautiful; to advance in beauty. Addison.

beautiless.c: Beautiless Beau"ti*less, a. Destitute of beauty. Hammond.

beauty.c: Beauty Beau"ty (bū"ty̆), n.; pl. Beauties (bū"tĭz). [OE. beaute, beute, OF. beauté, biauté, Pr. beltat, F. beauté, fr. an assumed LL. bellitas, from L. bellus pretty. See Beau.]

beaver.c: Beaver Bea"ver (?), n. [OE. bever, AS. beofer, befer; akin to D. bever, OHG. bibar, G. biber, Sw. bäfver, Dan. bæver, Lith. bebru, Russ. bobr', Gael. beabhar, Corn. befer, L. fiber, and Skr. babhrus large ichneumon; also as an adj., brown, the animal being probably named from its color. √253. See Brown.]

Beaver Bea"ver, n. [OE. baviere, bauier, beavoir, bever; fr. F. bavière, fr. bave slaver, drivel, foam, OF., prattle, drivel, perh. orig. an imitative word. Bavière, according to Cotgrave, is the bib put before a (slavering) child.] That piece of armor which protected the lower part of the face, whether forming a part of the helmet or fixed to the breastplate. It was so constructed (with joints or otherwise) that the wearer could raise or lower it to eat and drink.
Beaver State Bea"ver State. Oregon; -- a nickname.

beavered.c: Beavered Bea"vered (?), a. Covered with, or wearing, a beaver or hat. “His beavered brow.” Pope.

beaverteen.c: Beaverteen Bea"ver*teen (?), n. A kind of fustian made of coarse twilled cotton, shorn after dyeing. Simmonds.

bebirine.c: Bebirine Bebeerine { Be*bee"rine, or Be*bi"rine } (be*bē"rĭn or -rēn), n. (Chem.) An alkaloid got from the bark of the bebeeru, or green heart of Guiana (Nectandra Rodiœi). It is a tonic, antiperiodic, and febrifuge, and is used in medicine as a substitute for quinine. [Written also bibirine.]

bebeeru.c: bebeeru be*bee"ru (be*bē"rü), n. [Written also bibiru.] [Native name.] (Bot.) A tropical South American tree (Nectandra Rodiœi), the bark of which yields the alkaloid bebeerine, and the wood of which is known as green heart.

bebleed.c: Bebleed Be*bleed" (?), v. t. To make bloody; to stain with blood. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bebloody.c: Bebloody Beblood { Be*blood" (?), Be*blood"y } (?), v. t. To make bloody; to stain with blood. [Obs.] Sheldon.

beblot.c: Beblot Be*blot" (?), v. t. To blot; to stain. Chaucer.

beblubber.c: Beblubber Be*blub"ber (?), v. t. To make swollen and disfigured or sullied by weeping; as, her eyes or cheeks were beblubbered.

bebung.c: Bebung ‖Be"bung (?), n. [G., lit., a trembling.] (Music) A tremolo effect, such as that produced on the piano by vibratory repetition of a note with sustained use of the pedal.

becalm.c: Becalm Be*calm" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Becalmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Becalming.] 1. To render calm or quiet; to calm; to still; to appease.

becard.c: Becard ‖Bec"ard (?), n. (Zool.) A South American bird of the flycatcher family. (Tityra inquisetor).

because.c: Because Be*cause" (?), conj. [OE. bycause; by + cause.] 1. By or for the cause that; on this account that; for the reason that. Milton.

beccabunga.c: Beccabunga ‖Bec`ca*bun"ga (?), n. [NL. (cf. It. beccabunga, G. bachbunge), fr. G. bach brook + bunge, OHG. bungo, bulb. See Beck a brook.] See Brooklime.

beccafico.c: Beccafico ‖Bec`ca*fi"co (?), n.; pl. Beccaficos (?). [It., fr. beccare to peck + fico fig.] (Zool.) A small bird. (Silvia hortensis), which is highly prized by the Italians for the delicacy of its flesh in the autumn, when it has fed on figs, grapes, etc.

becchis.c: Becchi's test Bec"chi's test (?). [After E. Becchi, Italian chemist.] (Chem.) A qualitative test for cottonseed oil, based on the fact this oil imparts a maroon color to an alcoholic solution of silver nitrate.

bechamel.c: Bechamel ‖Bech"a*mel (?), n. [F. béchamel, named from its inventor, Louis de Béchamel.] (Cookery) A rich, white sauce, prepared with butter and cream.

bechance.c: Bechance Be*chance" (?), adv. [Pref. be- for by + chance.] By chance; by accident. [Obs.] Grafton.
Bechance Be*chance", v. t. & i. To befall; to chance; to happen to.

becharm.c: Becharm Be*charm" (?), v. t. To charm; to captivate.

beche.c: Beche de mer ‖Bêche` de mer" (?). [F., lit., a sea spade.] (Zool.) The trepang.

bechic.c: Bechic Be"chic (?), a. [L. bechicus, adj., for a cough, Gr.?, fr.? cough: cf. F. béchique.] (Med.) Pertaining to, or relieving, a cough. Thomas. -- n. A medicine for relieving coughs. Quincy.

bechuanas.c: Bechuanas Bech`u*a"nas (?), n. pl. A division of the Bantus, dwelling between the Orange and Zambezi rivers, supposed to be the most ancient Bantu population of South Africa. They are divided into totemic clans; they are intelligent and progressive.

beck.c: Beck Beck, n. [OE. bek, AS. becc; akin to Icel. bekkr brook, OHG. pah, G. bach.] A small brook.
Beck Beck, n. A vat. See Back.
Beck Beck, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Becked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Becking.] [Contr. of beckon.] To nod, or make a sign with the head or hand. [Archaic] Drayton.
Beck Beck, v. t. To notify or call by a nod, or a motion of the head or hand; to intimate a command to. [Archaic]
Beck Beck, n. A significant nod, or motion of the head or hand, esp. as a call or command.

becker.c: Becker Beck"er (?), n. (Zool.) A European fish (Pagellus centrodontus); the sea bream or braise.

becket.c: Becket Beck"et (?), n. [Cf. D. bek beak, and E. beak.]

beckon.c: Beckon Beck"on, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beckoned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beckoning.] To make a significant sign to; hence, to summon, as by a motion of the hand.
Beckon Beck"on, n. A sign made without words; a beck. “At the first beckon.” Bolingbroke.

becks.c: Beck's scale Beck's scale (?). A hydrometer scale on which the zero point corresponds to sp. gr. 1.00, and the 30°-point to sp. gr. 0.85. From these points the scale is extended both ways, all the degrees being of equal length.

beclap.c: Beclap Be*clap (?), v. t. [OE. biclappen.] To catch; to grasp; to insnare. [Obs.] Chaucer.

beclip.c: Beclip Be*clip" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beclipped (?).] [AS. beclyppan; pref. be + clyppan to embrace.] To embrace; to surround. [Obs.] Wyclif.

becloud.c: Becloud Be*cloud" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beclouded; p. pr. & vb. n. Beclouding.] To cause obscurity or dimness to; to dim; to cloud.

become.c: Become Be*come" (?), v. i. [imp. Became (?); p. p. Become; p. pr. & vb. n. Becoming.] [OE. bicumen, becumen, AS. becuman to come to, to happen; akin to D. bekomen, OHG.a piquëman, Goth. biquiman to come upon, G. bekommen to get, suit. See Be-, and Come.] 1. To pass from one state to another; to enter into some state or condition, by a change from another state, or by assuming or receiving new properties or qualities, additional matter, or a new character.

Become Be*come", v. t. To suit or be suitable to; to be congruous with; to befit; to accord with, in character or circumstances; to be worthy of, or proper for; to cause to appear well; -- said of persons and things.

becoming.c: Becoming Be*com"ing, a. Appropriate or fit; congruous; suitable; graceful; befitting.
Becoming Be*com"ing, n. That which is becoming or appropriate. [Obs.]

becomingly.c: Becomingly Be*com"ing*ly, adv. In a becoming manner.

becomingness.c: Becomingness Be*com"ing*ness, n. The quality of being becoming, appropriate, or fit; congruity; fitness.

becquerel.c: Becquerel rays Becque`rel" rays" (?). (Physics) Radiations first observed by the French physicist Henri Becquerel, in working with uranium and its compounds. They consist of a mixture of alpha, beta, and gamma rays.

becripple.c: Becripple Be*crip"ple (?), v. t. To make a cripple of; to cripple; to lame. [R.] Dr. H. More.

becuiba.c: Becuiba nut Becuiba { Be*cui"ba (?), n., Be*cui"ba nut` (?) }. [Native name.] (Bot.) The nut of the Brazilian tree Myristica Bicuhyba, which yields a medicinal balsam used for rheumatism.

becuna.c: Becuna ‖Be*cu"na (?), n. [Sp.] (Zool.) A fish of the Mediterranean (Sphyræna spet). See Barracuda.

becurl.c: Becurl Be*curl" (?), v. t. To curl; to adorn with curls.

bed.c: Bed Bed (?), n. [AS. bed, bedd; akin to OS. bed, D. bed, bedde, Icel. be?r, Dan. bed, Sw. bädd, Goth. badi, OHG. betti, G. bett, bette, bed, beet a plat of ground; all of uncertain origin.] 1. An article of furniture to sleep or take rest in or on; a couch. Specifically: A sack or mattress, filled with some soft material, in distinction from the bedstead on which it is placed (as, a feather bed), or this with the bedclothes added. In a general sense, any thing or place used for sleeping or reclining on or in, as a quantity of hay, straw, leaves, or twigs.
Bed Bed, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bedding.] 1. To place in a bed. [Obs.] Bacon.
Bed Bed (?), v. i. To go to bed; to cohabit.
Bed rock Bed" rock" (?). (Mining) The solid rock underlying superficial formations. Also Fig.
Bed screw Bed" screw` (?). 1. (Naut.) A form of jack screw for lifting large bodies, and assisting in launching.
Bed steps Bed" steps` (?). Steps for mounting a bed of unusual height.

bedabble.c: Bedabble Be*dab*ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedabbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedabbling (?).] To dabble; to sprinkle or wet. Shak.

bedaff.c: Bedaff Be*daff" (?), v. t. To make a daff or fool of. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bedagat.c: Bedagat ‖Bed"a*gat (?), n. The sacred books of the Buddhists in Burmah. Malcom.

bedash.c: Bedash Be*dash" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedashed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedashing.] To wet by dashing or throwing water or other liquid upon; to bespatter. “Trees bedashed with rain.” Shak.

bedaub.c: Bedaub Be*daub" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedaubed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedaubing.] To daub over; to besmear or soil with anything thick and dirty.

bedazzle.c: Bedazzle Be*daz"zle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedazzled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedazzling (?).] To dazzle or make dim by a strong light. “Bedazzled with the sun.” Shak.

bedbug.c: Bedbug Bed"bug` (?), n. (Zool.) A wingless, bloodsucking, hemipterous insect (Cimex Lectularius), sometimes infesting houses and especially beds. See Illustration in Appendix.

bedchair.c: Bedchair Bed"chair` (?), n. A chair with adjustable back, for the sick, to support them while sitting up in bed.

bedchamber.c: Bedchamber Bed"cham`ber (?), n. A chamber for a bed; an apartment form sleeping in. Shak.

bedclothes.c: Bedclothes Bed"clothes` (?), n. pl. Blankets, sheets, coverlets, etc., for a bed. Shak.

bedcord.c: Bedcord Bed"cord` (?), n. A cord or rope interwoven in a bedstead so as to support the bed.

bedded.c: Bedded Bed"ded (?), a. Provided with a bed; as, double-bedded room; placed or arranged in a bed or beds.

bedding.c: Bedding Bed"ding (?), n. [AS. bedding, beding. See Bed.] 1. A bed and its furniture; the materials of a bed, whether for man or beast; bedclothes; litter.

bede.c: Bede Bede (?), v. t. [See Bid, v. t.] To pray; also, to offer; to proffer. [Obs.] R. of Gloucester. Chaucer.
Bede Bede, n. (Mining) A kind of pickax.

bedeck.c: Bedeck Be*deck" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedecked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedecking.] To deck, ornament, or adorn; to grace.

bedegar.c: Bedegar Bedeguar { ‖Bed"e*guar, Bed"e*gar } (?), n. [F., fr. Per. bād-āward, or bād-āwardag, prop., a kind of white thorn or thistle.] A gall produced on rosebushes, esp. on the sweetbrier or eglantine, by a puncture from the ovipositor of a gallfly (Rhodites rosæ). It was once supposed to have medicinal properties.

bedell.c: Bedell Bedel { Be"del, Be"dell } (?), n. Same as Beadle.

beden.c: Beden ‖Bed"en (?), n. (Zool.) The Abyssinian or Arabian ibex (Capra Nubiana). It is probably the wild goat of the Bible.

bedevil.c: Bedevil Be*dev"il (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedevilled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedeviling or Bedevilling.] 1. To throw into utter disorder and confusion, as if by the agency of evil spirits; to bring under diabolical influence; to torment.

bedevilment.c: Bedevilment Be*dev"il*ment (?), n. The state of being bedeviled; bewildering confusion; vexatious trouble. [Colloq.]

bedew.c: Bedew Be*dew" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedewed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedewing.] To moisten with dew, or as with dew. “Falling tears his face bedew.” Dryden.

bedewer.c: Bedewer Be*dew"er (?), n. One who, or that which, bedews.

bedewy.c: Bedewy Be*dew"y (?), a. Moist with dew; dewy. [Obs.]

bedfellow.c: Bedfellow Bed"fel`low (?), n. One who lies with another in the same bed; a person who shares one's couch.

bedphere.c: Bedphere Bedfere { Bed"fere` Bed"phere` } (?), n. [Bed + AS. fera a companion.] A bedfellow. [Obs.] Chapman.
Bedphere Bed"phere` (?), n. See Bedfere. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

bedight.c: Bedight Be*dight" (?), v. t. [p. p. Bedight, Bedighted.] To bedeck; to array or equip; to adorn. [Archaic] Milton.

bedim.c: Bedim Be*dim" (be*dĭm"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedimmed (be*dĭmd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedimming.] To make dim; to obscure or darken. Shak.

bedizen.c: Bedizen Be*diz"en (?), v. t. To dress or adorn tawdrily or with false taste.

bedizenment.c: Bedizenment Be*diz"en*ment (?), n. That which bedizens; the act of dressing, or the state of being dressed, tawdrily.

bedkey.c: Bedkey Bed"key` (?), n. An instrument for tightening the parts of a bedstead.

bedlam.c: Bedlam Bed"lam (?), n. [See Bethlehem.] 1. A place appropriated to the confinement and care of the insane; a madhouse. Abp. Tillotson.
Bedlam Bed"lam, a. Belonging to, or fit for, a madhouse. “The bedlam, brainsick duchess.” Shak.

bedlamite.c: Bedlamite Bed"lam*ite (?), n. An inhabitant of a madhouse; a madman. “Raving bedlamites.” Beattie.

bedmaker.c: Bedmaker Bed"mak`er (?), n. One who makes beds.

bedmoulding.c: Bed-moulding Bed-molding { Bed"-mold`ing Bed"-mould`ing} (bĕd"mōld`ĭng), n. (Arch.) The molding of a cornice immediately below the corona. Oxf. Gloss.

bedote.c: Bedote Be*dote" (be*dōt"), v. t. To cause to dote; to deceive. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bedouin.c: Bedouin Bed"ou*in (?), n. [F. bédouin, OF. béduin, fr. Ar. bedawī rural, living in the desert, fr. badw desert, fr. badā to live in the desert, to lead a nomadic life.] One of the nomadic Arabs who live in tents, and are scattered over Arabia, Syria, and northern Africa, esp. in the deserts. -- Bed"ou*in*ism (?), n.
Bedouin Bed"ou*in, a. Pertaining to the Bedouins; nomad.

bedpan.c: Bedpan Bed"pan` (?), n. 1. A pan for warming beds. Nares.

bedplate.c: Bedplate Bedpiece { Bed"piece` (?), Bed"plate` (?), } n. (Mach.) The foundation framing or piece, by which the other parts are supported and held in place; the bed; -- called also baseplate and soleplate.

bedpost.c: Bedpost Bed"post` (?), n. 1. One of the four standards that support a bedstead or the canopy over a bedstead.

bedquilt.c: Bedquilt Bed"quilt` (?), n. A quilt for a bed; a coverlet.

bedrabble.c: Bedrabble Be*drab"ble (?), v. t. To befoul with rain and mud; to drabble.

bedraggle.c: Bedraggle Be*drag"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedraggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedraggling (?).] To draggle; to soil, as garments which, in walking, are suffered to drag in dust, mud, etc. Swift.

bedrench.c: Bedrench Be*drench" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedrenched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedrenching.] To drench; to saturate with moisture; to soak. Shak.

bedribble.c: Bedribble Be*drib"ble (?), v. t. To dribble upon.

bedridden.c: Bedridden Bedrid { Bed"rid` (?), Bed"rid`den (?), } a. [OE. bedrede, AS. bedreda, bedrida; from bed, bedd, a bed or couch + ridda a rider; cf. OHG. pettiriso, G. bettrise. See Bed, n., and Ride, v. i. ] Confined to the bed by sickness or infirmity. “Her decrepit, sick, and bedrid father.” Shak. “The estate of a bedridden old gentleman.” Macaulay.

bedrite.c: Bedrite Bedright { Bed"right` Bed"rite` } (?), n. [Bed + right, rite.] The duty or privilege of the marriage bed. Shak.

bedrizzle.c: Bedrizzle Be*driz"zle (?), v. t. To drizzle upon.

bedroom.c: Bedroom Bed"room (?), n. 1. A room or apartment intended or used for a bed; a lodging room.

bedrop.c: Bedrop Be*drop" (?), v. t. To sprinkle, as with drops.

bedrug.c: Bedrug Be*drug" (?), v. t. To drug abundantly or excessively.

bedside.c: Bedside Bed"side` (?), n. The side of a bed.

bedsite.c: Bedsite Bed"site` (?), n. A recess in a room for a bed.

bedsore.c: Bedsore Bed"sore` (?), n. (Med.) A sore on the back or hips caused by lying for a long time in bed.

bedspread.c: Bedspread Bed"spread` (?), n. A bedquilt; a counterpane; a coverlet. [U. S.]

bedstaff.c: Bedstaff Bed"staff` (?), n.; pl. Bedstaves (?). “A wooden pin stuck anciently on the sides of the bedstead, to hold the clothes from slipping on either side.” Johnson.

bedstead.c: Bedstead Bed"stead (?), n. [Bed + stead a frame.] A framework for supporting a bed.

bedstock.c: Bedstock Bed"stock (?), n. The front or the back part of the frame of a bedstead. [Obs. or Dial. Eng.]

bedstraw.c: Bedstraw Bed"straw` (?), n. 1. Straw put into a bed. Bacon.

bedswerver.c: Bedswerver Bed"swerv`er (?), n. One who swerves from and is unfaithful to the marriage vow. [Poetic] Shak.

bedtick.c: Bedtick Bed"tick` (?), n. A tick or bag made of cloth, used for inclosing the materials of a bed.

bedtime.c: Bedtime Bed"time` (?), n. The time to go to bed. Shak.

beduck.c: Beduck Be*duck" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beducked (?).] To duck; to put the head under water; to immerse. “Deep himself beducked.” Spenser.

bedung.c: Bedung Be*dung" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedunged (?).] To cover with dung, as for manuring; to bedaub or defile, literally or figuratively. Bp. Hall.

bedust.c: Bedust Be*dust" (?), v. t. To sprinkle, soil, or cover with dust. Sherwood.

bedwarf.c: Bedwarf Be*dwarf" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedwarfed (?).] To make a dwarf of; to stunt or hinder the growth of; to dwarf. Donne.

bedye.c: Bedye Be*dye" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bedyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bedyeing.] To dye or stain.

bee.c: Bee Bee (?), p. p. of Be; -- used for been. [Obs.] Spenser.

Bee Bee (bē), n. [AS. beó; akin to D. bij and bije, Icel. bȳ, Sw. & Dan. bi, OHG. pini, G. biene, and perh. Ir. beach, Lith. bitis, Skr. bha. √97.] 1. (Zool.) An insect of the order Hymenoptera, and family Apidæ (the honeybees), or family Andrenidæ (the solitary bees.) See Honeybee.
Bee line Bee" line` (?). The shortest line from one place to another, like that of a bee to its hive when loaded with honey; an air line. “A bee line for the brig.” Kane.

beebread.c: Beebread Bee"bread` (?), n. A brown, bitter substance found in some of the cells of honeycomb. It is made chiefly from the pollen of flowers, which is collected by bees as food for their young.

beech.c: Beech Beech (?), n.; pl. Beeches (?). [OE. beche, AS. b?ce; akin to D. beuk, OHG. buocha, G. buche, Icel. beyki, Dan. bög, Sw. bok, Russ. buk, L. fagus, Gr.? oak,? to eat, Skr. bhaksh; the tree being named originally from the esculent fruit. See Book, and cf. 7th Buck, Buckwheat.] (Bot.) A tree of the genus Fagus.

beechen.c: Beechen Beech"en (?), a. [AS. b?cen.] Consisting, or made, of the wood or bark of the beech; belonging to the beech. “Plain beechen vessels.” Dryden.

beechnut.c: Beechnut Beech"nut` (?), n. The nut of the beech tree.

beechy.c: Beechy Beech"y (?), a. Of or relating to beeches.

beeeater.c: Bee-eater Bee"-eat`er (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A bird of the genus Merops, that feeds especially on bees. The European species (Merops apiaster) is remarkable for its brilliant colors. (b) An African bird of the genus Rhinopomastes.

beef.c: Beef Beef (bēf), n. [OE. boef, befe, beef, OF. boef, buef, F. bœef, fr. L. bos, bovis, ox; akin to Gr. boy^s, Skr. gō cow, and E. cow. See 2d Cow.] 1. An animal of the genus Bos, especially the common species, Bos taurus, including the bull, cow, and ox, in their full grown state; esp., an ox or cow fattened for food.
Beef Beef (bēf), a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, beef.

beefeater.c: Beefeater Beef"eat`er (bēf"ēt`ẽr), n. [Beef + eater; prob. one who eats another's beef, as his servant. Cf. AS. hlāfǣta servant, properly a loaf eater.] 1. One who eats beef; hence, a large, fleshy person.

beefsteak.c: Beefsteak Beef"steak` (bēf"stāk), n. A steak of beef; a slice of beef broiled or suitable for broiling.

beefwood.c: Beefwood Beef"wood` (?), n. An Australian tree (Casuarina), and its red wood, used for cabinetwork; also, the trees Stenocarpus salignus of New South Wales, and Banksia compar of Queensland.

beefy.c: Beefy Beef"y, a. Having much beef; of the nature of beef; resembling beef; fleshy.

beehive.c: Beehive Bee"hive` (?), n. A hive for a swarm of bees. Also used figuratively.

beehouse.c: Beehouse Bee"house` (?), n. A house for bees; an apiary.

beeld.c: Beeld Beeld (?), n. Same as Beild. Fairfax.

beelzebub.c: Beelzebub Be*el"ze*bub (?), n. The title of a heathen deity to whom the Jews ascribed the sovereignty of the evil spirits; hence, the Devil or a devil. See Baal.

beem.c: Beem Beem (bēm), n. [AS. bēme, bȳme.] A trumpet. [Obs.]

beemaster.c: Beemaster Bee"mas`ter (?), n. One who keeps bees.

been.c: Been Been (?). [OE. beon, ben, bin, p. p. of been, beon, to be. See Be.] The past participle of Be. In old authors it is also the pr. tense plural of Be. See 1st Bee.

beer.c: Beer Beer (?), n. [OE. beor, ber, AS. beór; akin to Fries. biar, Icel. bj?rr, OHG. bior, D. & G. bier, and possibly E. brew. √93, See Brew.] 1. A fermented liquor made from any malted grain, but commonly from barley malt, with hops or some other substance to impart a bitter flavor.

beerhouse.c: Beerhouse Beer"house` (?), n. A house where malt liquors are sold; an alehouse.

beery.c: Beery Beer"y (?), a. Of or resembling beer; affected by beer; maudlin.

beestings.c: Beestings Biestings { Biest"ings, Beest"ings } (?), n. pl. [OE. bestynge, AS. bȳsting, fr. bȳst, beost; akin to D. biest, OHG. biost, G. biest; of unknown origin.] The first milk given by a cow after calving. B. Jonson.

beeswax.c: Beeswax Bees"wax` (?), n. The wax secreted by bees, and of which their cells are constructed.

beeswing.c: Beeswing Bees"wing` (?), n. The second crust formed in port and some other wines after long keeping. It consists of pure, shining scales of tartar, supposed to resemble the wing of a bee.

beet.c: Beet Beet (bēt), n. [AS. bete, from L. beta.] 1. (Bot.) A biennial plant of the genus Beta, which produces an edible root the first year and seed the second year.
Beet radish Beet" rad`ish (?). Same as Beetrave.

bete.c: Bete Beete { Beete, Bete } (bēt), v. t. [AS. bētan to mend. See Better.] 1. To mend; to repair. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Bete Bete (bēt), v. t. To better; to mend. See Beete. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Bete noire ‖Bête" noire" (?). [Fr., lit. black beast.] Something especially hated or dreaded; a bugbear.

beetle.c: Beetle Bee"tle (bē"t'l), n. [OE. betel, AS. bītl, b?tl, mallet, hammer, fr. beátan to beat. See Beat, v. t.] 1. A heavy mallet, used to drive wedges, beat pavements, etc.
Beetle Bee"tle (bē"t'l), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beetled (-t'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Beetling.] 1. To beat with a heavy mallet.

Beetle Bee"tle, n. [OE. bityl, bittle, AS. bītel, fr. bītan to bite. See Bite, v. t.] Any insect of the order Coleoptera, having four wings, the outer pair being stiff cases for covering the others when they are folded up. See Coleoptera.
Beetle Bee"tle, v. i. [See Beetlebrowed.] To extend over and beyond the base or support; to overhang; to jut.
Beetle brow Bee"tle brow` (?). An overhanging brow.

beetlebrowed.c: Beetle-browed Bee"tle-browed` (?), a. [OE. bitelbrowed; cf. OE. bitel, adj., sharp, projecting, n., a beetle. See Beetle an insect.] Having prominent, overhanging brows; hence, lowering or sullen.

beetlestock.c: Beetlestock Bee"tle*stock` (?), n. The handle of a beetle.

beetrave.c: Beetrave Beet"rave` (?), n. [F. betterave; bette beet + rave radish.] The common beet (Beta vulgaris).

beeve.c: Beeve Beeve (?), n. [Formed from beeves, pl. of beef.] A beef; a beef creature.

beeves.c: Beeves Beeves (bēvz), n. plural of Beef, the animal.

befall.c: Befall Be*fall" (?), v. t. [imp. Befell (?); p. p. Befallen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Befalling.] [AS. befeallan; pref. be- + feallan to fall.] To happen to.
Befall Be*fall", v. i. To come to pass; to happen.

befit.c: Befit Be*fit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Befitting.] To be suitable to; to suit; to become.

befitting.c: Befitting Be*fit"ting, a. Suitable; proper; becoming; fitting.

befittingly.c: Befittingly Be*fit"ting*ly, adv. In a befitting manner; suitably.

beflatter.c: Beflatter Be*flat"ter (?), v. t. To flatter excessively.

beflower.c: Beflower Be*flow"er (?), v. t. To besprinkle or scatter over with, or as with, flowers. Hobbes.

befog.c: Befog Be*fog" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befogged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Befogging (?).] 1. To involve in a fog; -- mostly as a participle or part. adj.

befool.c: Befool Be*fool" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befooled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Befooling.] [OE. befolen; pref. be- + fol fool.] 1. To fool; to delude or lead into error; to infatuate; to deceive.

before.c: Before Be*fore" (?), prep. [OE. beforen, biforen, before, AS. beforan; pref. be- + foran, fore, before. See Be-, and Fore.] 1. In front of; preceding in space; ahead of; as, to stand before the fire; before the house.
Before Be*fore", adv. 1. On the fore part; in front, or in the direction of the front; -- opposed to in the rear.

beforehand.c: Beforehand Be*fore"hand`, a. In comfortable circumstances as regards property; forehanded.

befoul.c: Befoul Be*foul" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befouled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Befouling.] [Cf. AS. bef?lan; pref. be- + f?lan to foul. See Foul, a.] 1. To make foul; to soil.

befriend.c: Befriend Be*friend" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befriended; p. pr. & vb. n. Befriending.] To act as a friend to; to favor; to aid, benefit, or countenance.

befrill.c: Befrill Be*frill" (?), v. t. To furnish or deck with a frill.

befringe.c: Befringe Be*fringe" (?), v. t. To furnish with a fringe; to form a fringe upon; to adorn as with fringe. Fuller.

befuddle.c: Befuddle Be*fud"dle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Befuddled (?)] To becloud and confuse, as with liquor.

beg.c: Beg Beg (?), n. [Turk. beg, pronounced bay. Cf. Bey, Begum.] A title of honor in Turkey and in some other parts of the East; a bey.

Beg Beg (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Begging.] [OE. beggen, perh. fr. AS. bedecian (akin to Goth. bedagwa beggar), biddan to ask. (Cf. Bid, v. t.); or cf. beghard, beguin.] 1. To ask earnestly for; to entreat or supplicate for; to beseech.
Beg Beg, v. i. To ask alms or charity, especially to ask habitually by the wayside or from house to house; to live by asking alms.

begem.c: Begem Be*gem" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begemmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Begemming.] To adorn with gems, or as with gems.

beget.c: Beget Be*get" (?), v. t. [imp. Begot (?), (Archaic) Begat (?); p. p. Begot, Begotten (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Begetting.] [OE. bigiten, bigeten, to get, beget, AS. begitan to get; pref. be- + gitan. See Get, v. t. ] 1. To procreate, as a father or sire; to generate; -- commonly said of the father.

begetter.c: Begetter Be*get"ter (?), n. One who begets; a father.

beggable.c: Beggable Beg"ga*ble (?), a. Capable of being begged.

beggar.c: Beggar Beg"gar (?), n. [OE. beggere, fr. beg.] 1. One who begs; one who asks or entreats earnestly, or with humility; a petitioner.
Beggar Beg"gar, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beggared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beggaring.] 1. To reduce to beggary; to impoverish; as, he had beggared himself. Milton.

beggarhood.c: Beggarhood Beg"gar*hood (?), n. The condition of being a beggar; also, the class of beggars.

beggarliness.c: Beggarliness Beg"gar*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being beggarly; meanness.

beggarly.c: Beggarly Beg"gar*ly (?), a. 1. In the condition of, or like, a beggar; suitable for a beggar; extremely indigent; poverty-stricken; mean; poor; contemptible. “A bankrupt, beggarly fellow.” South. “A beggarly fellowship.” Swift. “Beggarly elements.” Gal. iv. 9.
Beggarly Beg"gar*ly, adv. In an indigent, mean, or despicable manner; in the manner of a beggar.

beggars.c: Beggar's lice Beg"gar's lice` (?). (Bot.) The prickly fruit or seed of certain plants (as some species of Echinospermum and Cynoglossum) which cling to the clothing of those who brush by them.

Beggar's ticks Beg"gar's ticks` (?). The bur marigold (Bidens) and its achenes, which are armed with barbed awns, and adhere to clothing and fleeces with unpleasant tenacity; -- also called beggar-ticks.

beggary.c: Beggary Beg"gar*y (?), n. [OE. beggerie. See Beggar, n.] 1. The act of begging; the state of being a beggar; mendicancy; extreme poverty.

beguard.c: Beguard Beghard { Be*ghard" Be*guard" } (?), n. [F. bégard, béguard; cf. G. beghard, LL. Beghardus, Begihardus, Begardus. Prob. from the root of beguine + -ard or -hard. See Beguine.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of an association of religious laymen living in imitation of the Beguines. They arose in the thirteenth century, were afterward subjected to much persecution, and were suppressed by Innocent X. in 1650. Called also Beguins.

begild.c: Begild Be*gild" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begilded or Begilt (?).] To gild. B. Jonson.

begin.c: Begin Be*gin" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Began (?), Begun (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beginning (?).] [AS. beginnan (akin to OS. biginnan, D. & G. beginnen, OHG. biginnan, Goth., du-ginnan, Sw. begynna, Dan. begynde); pref. be- + an assumed ginnan. √31. See Gin to begin.] 1. To have or commence an independent or first existence; to take rise; to commence.
Begin Be*gin", v. t. 1. To enter on; to commence.

beginner.c: Beginner Be*gin"ner (?), n. One who begins or originates anything. Specifically: A young or inexperienced practitioner or student; a tyro.

beginning.c: Beginning Be*gin"ning (?), n. 1. The act of doing that which begins anything; commencement of an action, state, or space of time; entrance into being or upon a course; the first act, effort, or state of a succession of acts or states.

begird.c: Begird Be*gird" (?), v. t. [imp. Begirt (?), Begirded; p. p. Begirt; p. pr. & vb. n. Begirding.] [AS. begyrdan (akin to Goth. bigairdan); pref. be- + gyrdan to gird.] 1. To bind with a band or girdle; to gird.

begirdle.c: Begirdle Be*gir"dle (?), v. t. To surround as with a girdle.

begirt.c: Begirt Be*girt" (?), v. t. To encompass; to begird. Milton.

beglerbeg.c: Beglerbeg ‖Beg"ler*beg` (?), n. [Turk. beglerbeg, fr. beg, pl. begler. See Beg, n.] The governor of a province of the Ottoman empire, next in dignity to the grand vizier.

begnaw.c: Begnaw Be*gnaw" (?), v. t. [p. p. Begnawed (?), (R.) Begnawn (?).] [AS. begnagan; pref. be- + gnagan to gnaw.] To gnaw; to eat away; to corrode.

begod.c: Begod Be*god" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begodded.] To exalt to the dignity of a god; to deify. [Obs.] “Begodded saints.” South.

begohm.c: Begohm Beg"ohm` (?), n. (Elec.) A unit of resistance equal to one billion ohms, or one thousand megohms.

begone.c: Begone Be*gone" (?), interj. [Be, v. i. + gone, p. p.] Go away; depart; get you gone.
Begone Be*gone", p. p. [OE. begon, AS. bigān; pref. be- + gān to go.] Surrounded; furnished; beset; environed (as in woe-begone). [Obs.] Gower. Chaucer.

begonia.c: Begonia Be*go"ni*a (be*gō"nĭ*ȧ), n. [From Michel Begon, a promoter of botany.] (Bot.) A genus of plants, mostly of tropical America, many species of which are grown as ornamental plants. The leaves are curiously one-sided, and often exhibit brilliant colors.

begore.c: Begore Be*gore" (be*gōr"), v. t. To besmear with gore.

begot.c: Begot Be*got" (be*gŏt"), imp. & p. p. of Beget.

begrave.c: Begrave Be*grave" (?), v. t. [Pref. be- + grave; akin to G. begraben, Goth. bigraban to dig a ditch around.] To bury; also, to engrave. [Obs.] Gower.

begrease.c: Begrease Be*grease" (?), v. t. To soil or daub with grease or other oily matter.

begrime.c: Begrime Be*grime" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begrimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Begriming.] To soil with grime or dirt deeply impressed or rubbed in.

begrimer.c: Begrimer Be*grim"er (?), n. One who, or that which, begrimes.

begrudge.c: Begrudge Be*grudge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Begrudged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Begrudging.] To grudge; to envy the possession of.

beguile.c: Beguile Be*guile" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beguiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beguiling.] 1. To delude by guile, artifice, or craft; to deceive or impose on, as by a false statement; to lure.

beguilement.c: Beguilement Be*guile"ment (?), n. The act of beguiling, or the state of being beguiled.

beguiler.c: Beguiler Be*guil"er (?), n. One who, or that which, beguiles.

beguiling.c: Beguiling Be*guil"ing, a. Alluring by guile; deluding; misleading; diverting. -- Be*guil"ing*ly, adv.

beguinage.c: Beguinage ‖Be`gui`nage" (?), n. [F.] A collection of small houses surrounded by a wall and occupied by a community of Beguines.

beguine.c: Beguine ‖Be`guine" (?), n. [F. béguine; LL. beguina, beghina; fr. Lambert le Bègue (the Stammerer) the founder of the order. (Du Cange.)] A woman belonging to one of the religious and charitable associations or communities in the Netherlands, and elsewhere, whose members live in beguinages and are not bound by perpetual vows.

begum.c: Begum ‖Be"gum (?), n. [Per., fr. Turk., perh. properly queen mother, fr. Turk. beg (see Beg, n.) + Ar. umm mother.] In the East Indies, a princess or lady of high rank. Malcom.

behalf.c: Behalf Be*half" (?), n. [OE. on-behalve in the name of, bihalven by the side of, fr. AS. healf half, also side, part: akin to G. halb half, halber on account of. See Be-, and Half, n.] Advantage; favor; stead; benefit; interest; profit; support; defense; vindication.

behappen.c: Behappen Be*hap"pen (?), v. t. To happen to. [Obs.]

behave.c: Behave Be*have" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Behaved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Behaving.] [AS. behabban to surround, restrain, detain (akin to G. gehaben (obs.) to have, sich gehaben to behave or carry one's self); pref. be- + habban to have. See Have, v. t. ] 1. To manage or govern in point of behavior; to discipline; to handle; to restrain. [Obs.]
Behave Be*have", v. i. To act; to conduct; to bear or carry one's self; as, to behave well or ill.

behavior.c: Behavior Be*hav"ior (?), n. Manner of behaving, whether good or bad; mode of conducting one's self; conduct; deportment; carriage; -- used also of inanimate objects; as, the behavior of a ship in a storm; the behavior of the magnetic needle.

behead.c: Behead Be*head" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beheaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Beheading.] [OE. bihefden, AS. beheáfdian; pref. be- + heáfod head. See Head.] To sever the head from; to take off the head of.

beheld.c: Beheld Be*held" (?), imp. & p. p. of Behold.

behemoth.c: Behemoth Be"he*moth (?), n. [Heb. behemōth, fr. Egyptian P-ehe-maut hippopotamus.] 1. An animal, probably the hippopotamus, described in Job xl. 15-24.

behn.c: Behn Behen { Be"hen (?), Behn } (?), n. [Per. & Ar. bahman, behmen, an herb, whose leaves resemble ears of corn, saffron.] (Bot.) (a) The Centaurea behen, or saw-leaved centaury. (b) The Cucubalus behen, or bladder campion, now called Silene inflata. (c) The Statice limonium, or sea lavender.

behest.c: Behest Be*hest" (?), n. [OE. biheste promise, command, AS. behǣs promise; pref. be- + hǣs command. See Hest, Hight.] 1. That which is willed or ordered; a command; a mandate; an injunction.
Behest Be*hest", v. t. To vow. [Obs.] Paston.

behete.c: Behete Be*hete" (?), v. t. See Behight. [Obs.] Chaucer.

behight.c: Behight Be*hight" (?), v. t. [imp. Behight; p. p. Behight, Behoten.] [OE. bihaten, AS. behātan to vow, promise; pref. be- + hātan to call, command. See Hight, v.] [Obs. in all its senses.] 1. To promise; to vow.
Behight Be*hight", n. A vow; a promise. [Obs.] Surrey.

behind.c: Behind Be*hind" (?), prep. [AS. behindan; pref. be- + hindan. See Hind, a.] 1. On the side opposite the front or nearest part; on the back side of; at the back of; on the other side of; as, behind a door; behind a hill.
Behind Be*hind", adv. 1. At the back part; in the rear. “I shall not lag behind.” Milton.
Behind Be*hind", n. The backside; the rump. [Low]

behither.c: Behither Be*hith"er (?), prep. On this side of. [Obs.]

behold.c: Behold Be*hold" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beheld (?) (p. p. formerly Beholden (?), now used only as a p. a.); p. pr. & vb. n. Beholding.] [OE. bihalden, biholden, AS. behealdan to hold, have in sight; pref. be- + healdan to hold, keep; akin to G. behalten to hold, keep. See Hold.] To have in sight; to see clearly; to look at; to regard with the eyes.
Behold Be*hold", v. i. To direct the eyes to, or fix them upon, an object; to look; to see.

beholden.c: Beholden Be*hold"en (?), p. a. [Old p. p. of behold, used in the primitive sense of the simple verb hold.] Obliged; bound in gratitude; indebted.

beholder.c: Beholder Be*hold"er (?), n. One who beholds; a spectator.

beholding.c: Beholding Be*hold"ing, n. The act of seeing; sight; also, that which is beheld. Shak.

beholdingness.c: Beholdingness Be*hold"ing*ness, n., The state of being obliged or beholden. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

behoof.c: Behoof Be*hoof" (?), n. [OE. to bihove for the use of, AS. beh?f advantage, a word implied in beh?flīc necessary; akin to Sw. behof, Dan. behov, G. behuf, and E. heave, the root meaning to seize, hence the meanings “to hold, make use of.” See Heave, v. t.] Advantage; profit; benefit; interest; use.

behoovable.c: Behoovable Be*hoov"a*ble (?), a. Supplying need; profitable; advantageous. [Obs.] Udall.

behoove.c: Behoove Be*hoove" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Behooved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Behooving.] [OE. bihoven, behoven, AS. beh?fian to have need of, fr. beh?f. See Behoof.] To be necessary for; to be fit for; to be meet for, with respect to necessity, duty, or convenience; -- mostly used impersonally.
Behoove Be*hoove" (?), v. i. To be necessary, fit, or suitable; to befit; to belong as due. Chaucer.

behooveful.c: Behooveful Be*hoove"ful (?), a. Advantageous; useful; profitable. [Archaic] -- Be*hoove"ful*ly, adv. -- Be*hoove"ful*ness, n. [Archaic]

behove.c: Behove Be*hove" (?), v., and derivatives. See Behoove, &c.

behovely.c: Behovely Be*hove"ly, a. & adv. Useful, or usefully. [Obs.]

behowl.c: Behowl Be*howl" (?), v. t. To howl at. [Obs.]

beild.c: Beild Beild (?), n. [Prob. from the same root as build, v. t.] A place of shelter; protection; refuge. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] [Also written bield and beeld.]

being.c: Being Be"ing (?), p. pr. from Be. Existing.
Being Be"ing, n. 1. Existence, as opposed to nonexistence; state or sphere of existence.
Being Be"ing, adv. Since; inasmuch as. [Obs. or Colloq.]

bejade.c: Bejade Be*jade" (?), v. t. To jade or tire. [Obs.] Milton.

bejape.c: Bejape Be*jape" (?), v. t. To jape; to laugh at; to deceive. [Obs.] Chaucer.
