bejaundice.c: Bejaundice Be*jaun"dice (?), v. t. To infect with jaundice.

bejewel.c: Bejewel Be*jew"el (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bejeweled or Bejewelled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bejeweling or Bejewelling.] To ornament with a jewel or with jewels; to spangle. “Bejeweled hands.” Thackeray.

bejuco.c: Bejuco ‖Be*ju"co (?), n. [Sp., a reed or woody vine.] Any climbing woody vine of the tropics with the habit of a liane; in the Philippines, esp. any of various species of Calamus, the cane or rattan palm.

bejumble.c: Bejumble Be*jum"ble (?), v. t. To jumble together.

beknave.c: Beknave Be*knave" (?), v. t. To call knave. [Obs.] Pope.

beknow.c: Beknow Be*know" (?), v. t. To confess; to acknowledge. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bel.c: Bel Bel (?), n. The Babylonian name of the god known among the Hebrews as Baal. See Baal. Baruch vi. 41.

Bel Bel (bĕl), n. [Hind., fr. Skr. bilva.] A thorny rutaceous tree (Ægle marmelos) of India, and its aromatic, orange-like fruit; -- called also Bengal quince, golden apple, wood apple. The fruit is used medicinally, and the rind yields a perfume and a yellow dye.

belabor.c: Belabor Be*la"bor (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belabored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belaboring.] 1. To ply diligently; to work carefully upon. “If the earth is belabored with culture, it yieldeth corn.” Barrow.

belaccoyle.c: Bel-accoyle Bel`-ac*coyle" (?), n. [F. bel beautiful + accueil reception.] A kind or favorable reception or salutation. [Obs.]

belace.c: Belace Be*lace" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belaced (?).]

belam.c: Belam Be*lam" (?), v. t. [See Lam.] To beat or bang. [Prov. & Low, Eng.] Todd.

belamour.c: Belamour Bel"a*mour (?), n. [F. bel amour fair love.] 1. A lover. [Obs.] Spenser.

belamy.c: Belamy Bel"a*my (?), n. [F. bel ami fair friend.] Good friend; dear friend. [Obs.] Chaucer.

belate.c: Belate Be*late" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belated; p. pr. & vb. n. Belating.] To retard or make too late. Davenant.

belated.c: Belated Be*lat"ed, a. Delayed beyond the usual time; too late; overtaken by night; benighted. “Some belated peasant.” Milton. -- Be*lat"ed*ness, n. Milton.

belaud.c: Belaud Be*laud" (?), v. t. To laud or praise greatly.

belay.c: Belay Be*lay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belaid, Belayed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belaying.] [For senses 1 & 2, D. beleggen to cover, belay; akin to E. pref. be-, and lay to place: for sense 3, OE. beleggen, AS. belecgan. See pref. Be-, and Lay to place.] 1. To lay on or cover; to adorn. [Obs.]

belaying.c: Belaying pin Be*lay"ing pin` (be*lā"ĭng pĭn`). (Naut.) A strong pin in the side of a vessel, or by the mast, round which ropes are wound when they are fastened or belayed.

belch.c: Belch Belch (bĕlch; 224), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belched (bĕlch); p. pr. & vb. n. Belching.] [OE. belken, AS. bealcan, akin to E. bellow. See Bellow, v. i.] 1. To eject or throw up from the stomach with violence; to eruct.
Belch Belch, v. i. 1. To eject wind from the stomach through the mouth; to eructate.
Belch Belch, n. 1. The act of belching; also, that which is belched; an eructation.

belcher.c: Belcher Belch"er (?), n. One who, or that which, belches.

beldame.c: Beldame Beldam { Bel"dam Bel"dame } (?), n. [Pref. bel-, denoting relationship + dame mother: cf. F. belledame fair lady, It. belladonna. See Belle, and Dame.]

beleaguer.c: Beleaguer Be*lea"guer (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beleaguered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beleaguering.] [D. belegeren (akin to G. belagern, Sw. belägra, Dan. beleire); pref. be- = E. be- + leger bed, camp, army, akin to E. lair. See Lair.] To surround with an army so as to preclude escape; to besiege; to blockade.

beleave.c: Beleave Be*leave" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Beleft (?).] To leave or to be left. [Obs.] May.

belecture.c: Belecture Be*lec"ture (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belectured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belecturing.] To vex with lectures; to lecture frequently.

belee.c: Belee Be*lee" (?), v. t. To place under the lee, or unfavorably to the wind. Shak.

belemnite.c: Belemnite Be*lem"nite (?), n. [Gr.? dart, fr.? dart, fr.? to throw: cf. F. bélemnite.] (Paleon.) A conical calcareous fossil, tapering to a point at the lower extremity, with a conical cavity at the other end, where it is ordinarily broken; but when perfect it contains a small chambered cone, called the phragmocone, prolonged, on one side, into a delicate concave blade; the thunderstone. It is the internal shell of a cephalopod related to the sepia, and belonging to an extinct family. The belemnites are found in rocks of the Jurassic and Cretaceous ages. -- Bel*em*nit"ic, a.

beleper.c: Beleper Be*lep"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belepered (?).] To infect with leprosy. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

belesprit.c: Bel-esprit ‖Bel"-es*prit" (?), n.; pl. Beaux-esprits (?). [F., fine wit.] A fine genius, or man of wit. “A man of letters and a bel esprit.” W. Irving.

belfry.c: Belfry Bel"fry (?), n. [OE. berfray movable tower used in sieges, OF. berfreit, berfroit, F. beffroi, fr. MHG. bervrit, bercvrit, G. bergfriede, fr. MHG. bergen to protect (G. bergen to conceal) + vride peace, protection, G. friede peace; in compounds often taken in the sense of security, or place of security; orig. therefore a place affording security. G. friede is akin to E. free. See Burg, and Free.] 1. (Mil. Antiq.) A movable tower erected by besiegers for purposes of attack and defense.

belgard.c: Belgard Bel*gard" (?), n. [It. bel guardo.] A sweet or loving look. [Obs.] Spenser.

belgian.c: Belgian Bel"gi*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Belgium. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Belgium.
Belgian block Belgian block. An oblong, often nearly cubical, block of some tough stone, esp. granite, used as a material for street pavements. Its usual diameter is 5 to 7 inches.

belgic.c: Belgic Bel"gic (?), a. [L. Belgicus, fr. Belgae the Belgians.] 1. Of or pertaining to the Belgæ, a German tribe who anciently possessed the country between the Rhine, the Seine, and the ocean.

belgravian.c: Belgravian Bel*gra"vi*an (?), a. Belonging to Belgravia (a fashionable quarter of London, around Pimlico), or to fashionable life; aristocratic.

belial.c: Belial Be"li*al (?), n. [Heb. beli ya'al; beli without + ya'al profit.] An evil spirit; a wicked and unprincipled person; the personification of evil.

belibel.c: Belibel Be*li"bel (?), v. t. [See Libel, v. t. ] To libel or traduce; to calumniate. Fuller.

belie.c: Belie Be*lie" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belying (?).] [OE. bilien, bili?en, AS. beleógan; pref. be- + leógan to lie. See Lie, n.] 1. To show to be false; to convict of, or charge with, falsehood.

belief.c: Belief Be*lief" (?), n. [OE. bileafe, bileve; cf. AS. geleáfa. See Believe.] 1. Assent to a proposition or affirmation, or the acceptance of a fact, opinion, or assertion as real or true, without immediate personal knowledge; reliance upon word or testimony; partial or full assurance without positive knowledge or absolute certainty; persuasion; conviction; confidence; as, belief of a witness; the belief of our senses.

beliefful.c: Beliefful Be*lief"ful (?), a. Having belief or faith.

believable.c: Believable Be*liev"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being believed; credible. -- Be*liev"a*ble*ness, n. -- Be*liev`a*bil"i*ty (?), n.

believe.c: Believe Be*lieve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Believed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Believing.] [OE. bileven (with pref. be- for AS. ge-), fr. AS. gel?fan, gel?fan; akin to D. gelooven, OHG. gilouban, G. glauben, OS. gil?bian, Goth. galaubjan, and Goth. liubs dear. See Lief, a., Leave, n.] To exercise belief in; to credit upon the authority or testimony of another; to be persuaded of the truth of, upon evidence furnished by reasons, arguments, and deductions of the mind, or by circumstances other than personal knowledge; to regard or accept as true; to place confidence in; to think; to consider; as, to believe a person, a statement, or a doctrine.
Believe Be*lieve", v. i. 1. To have a firm persuasion, esp. of the truths of religion; to have a persuasion approaching to certainty; to exercise belief or faith.

believer.c: Believer Be*liev"er (?), n. 1. One who believes; one who is persuaded of the truth or reality of some doctrine, person, or thing.

believing.c: Believing Be*liev"ing, a. That believes; having belief. -- Be*liev"ing*ly, adv.

belight.c: Belight Be*light" (?), v. t. To illuminate. [Obs.] Cowley.

belike.c: Belike Be*like" (?), adv. [Pref. be- (for by) + like.] It is likely or probably; perhaps. [Obs. or Archaic] -- Be*like"ly, adv.

belime.c: Belime Be*lime" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belimed (?).] To besmear or insnare with birdlime.

belittle.c: Belittle Be*lit"tle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belittled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belittling.] To make little or less in a moral sense; to speak of in a depreciatory or contemptuous way. T. Jefferson.

belive.c: Belive Be*live" (?), adv. [Cf. Live, a.] Forthwith; speedily; quickly. [Obs.] Chaucer.

belk.c: Belk Belk (?), v. t. [See Belch.] To vomit. [Obs.]

bell.c: Bell Bell (?), n. [AS. belle, fr. bellan to bellow. See Bellow.] 1. A hollow metallic vessel, usually shaped somewhat like a cup with a flaring mouth, containing a clapper or tongue, and giving forth a ringing sound on being struck.
Bell Bell (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belling.] To put a bell upon; as, to bell the cat.
Bell Bell, v. i. To develop bells or corollas; to take the form of a bell; to blossom; as, hops bell.
Bell Bell, v. t. [AS. bellan. See Bellow.] To utter by bellowing. [Obs.]
Bell Bell, v. i. To call or bellow, as the deer in rutting time; to make a bellowing sound; to roar.
Bell animalcule Bell" an`i*mal"cule (?). (Zool.) An infusorian of the family Vorticellidæ, common in fresh-water ponds.
Bell bearer Bell" bear`er (?). (Zool.) A Brazilian leaf hopper (Bocydium tintinnabuliferum), remarkable for the four bell-shaped appendages of its thorax.

Bell crank Bell" crank` (?). A lever whose two arms form a right angle, or nearly a right angle, having its fulcrum at the apex of the angle. It is used in bell pulls and in changing the direction of bell wires at angles of rooms, etc., and also in machinery.

Bell jar Bell" jar` (?). (Phys.) A glass vessel, varying in size, open at the bottom and closed at the top like a bell, and having a knob or handle at the top for lifting it. It is used for a great variety of purposes; as, with the air pump, and for holding gases, also for keeping the dust from articles exposed to view.
Bell metal Bell" met`al (?). A hard alloy or bronze, consisting usually of about three parts of copper to one of tin; -- used for making bells.
Bell pepper Bell" pep`per (?). (Bot.) A species of Capsicum, or Guinea pepper (Capsicum annuum). It is the red pepper of the gardens.
Bell process Bell process. (Iron Metal.) The process of washing molten pig iron by adding iron oxide, proposed by I. Lowthian Bell of England about 1875.
Bell system of control Bell system of control. (Aëronautics) See Cloche.

belladonna.c: Belladonna Bel`la*don"na (?), n. [It., literally fine lady; bella beautiful + donna lady.] (Bot.) (a) An herbaceous European plant (Atropa belladonna) with reddish bell-shaped flowers and shining black berries. The whole plant and its fruit are very poisonous, and the root and leaves are used as powerful medicinal agents. Its properties are largely due to the alkaloid atropine which it contains. Called also deadly nightshade. (b) A species of Amaryllis (Amaryllis belladonna); the belladonna lily.

bellarmine.c: Bellarmine Bel"lar*mine (?), n. A stoneware jug of a pattern originated in the neighborhood of Cologne, Germany, in the 16th century. It has a bearded face or mask supposed to represent Cardinal Bellarmine, a leader in the Roman Catholic Counter Reformation, following the Reformation; -- called also graybeard, longbeard.

bellbird.c: Bellbird Bell"bird` (?), n. [So called from their notes.] (Zool.) (a) A South and Central American bird of the genus Casmarhincos, and family Cotingidæ, of several species; the campanero. (b) The Myzantha melanophrys of Australia.

belle.c: Belle Belle (bĕl), n. [F. belle, fem. of bel, beau, beautiful, fine. See Beau.] A young lady of superior beauty and attractions; a handsome lady, or one who attracts notice in society; a fair lady.

belled.c: Belled Belled (bĕld), a. Hung with a bell or bells.

belleek.c: Belleek ware Bel*leek" ware (?). A porcelainlike kind of decorative pottery with a high gloss, which is sometimes iridescent. A very fine kind is made at Belleek in Ireland.

bellelettrist.c: Belle-lettrist Belle-let"trist (?), n. One versed in belles-lettres.

bellerophon.c: Bellerophon ‖Bel*ler"o*phon (?), n. (Paleon.) A genus of fossil univalve shells, believed to belong to the Heteropoda, peculiar to the Paleozoic age.

belleslettres.c: Belles-lettres ‖Belles-let"tres (?), n. pl. [F.] Polite or elegant literature; the humanities; -- used somewhat vaguely for literary works in which imagination and taste are predominant.

belletristical.c: Belletristical Belletristic { Bel`le*tris"tic (?), Bel`le*tris"tic*al (?), } a. Occupied with, or pertaining to, belles-lettres. “An unlearned, belletristic trifler.” M. Arnold.

bellfaced.c: Bell-faced Bell"-faced` (?), a. Having the striking surface convex; -- said of hammers.

bellflower.c: Bellflower Bell"flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) A plant of the genus Campanula; -- so named from its bell-shaped flowers.
Bellflower Bell"flow`er, n. [F. bellefleur, lit., beautiful flower.] A kind of apple. The yellow bellflower is a large, yellow winter apple. [Written also bellefleur.]

bellibone.c: Bellibone Bel"li*bone (?), n. [F. belle et bonne, beautiful and good.] A woman excelling both in beauty and goodness; a fair maid. [Obs.] Spenser.

bellical.c: Bellical Bellic { Bel"lic (?), Bel"li*cal (?), } a. [L. bellicus. See Bellicose.] Of or pertaining to war; warlike; martial. [Obs.] “Bellic Cæsar.” Feltham.

bellicose.c: Bellicose Bel"li*cose` (?), a. [L. bellicosus, fr. bellicus of war, fr. bellum war. See Duel.] Inclined to war or contention; warlike; pugnacious.

bellicosely.c: Bellicosely Bel"li*cose`ly, adv. In a bellicose manner.

bellied.c: Bellied Bel"lied (?), a. Having (such) a belly; puffed out; -- used in composition; as, pot-bellied; shad-bellied.

belligerency.c: Belligerency Belligerence { Bel*lig"er*ence (?), Bel*lig"er*en*cy (?), } n. The quality of being belligerent.

belligerent.c: Belligerent Bel*lig"er*ent (?), a. [L. bellum war + gerens, -entis, waging, p. pr. of gerere to wage: cf. F. belligérant. See Bellicose, Jest.] 1. Waging war; carrying on war. “Belligerent powers.” E. Everett.
Belligerent Bel*lig"er*ent, n. A nation or state recognized as carrying on war; a person engaged in warfare.

belligerently.c: Belligerently Bel*lig"er*ent*ly, adv. In a belligerent manner; hostilely.

belling.c: Belling Bell"ing (?), n. [From Bell to bellow.] A bellowing, as of a deer in rutting time. Johnson.

bellipotent.c: Bellipotent Bel*lip"o*tent (?), a. [L. bellipotens; bellum war + potens powerful, p. pr. of posse to be able.] Mighty in war; armipotent. [R.] Blount.

bellman.c: Bellman Bell"man (?), n. A man who rings a bell, especially to give notice of anything in the streets. Formerly, also, a night watchman who called the hours. Milton.

bellmouthed.c: Bell-mouthed Bell"-mouthed` (?), a. Expanding at the mouth; as, a bell-mouthed gun. Byron.

bellona.c: Bellona ‖Bel*lo"na (?), n. [L., from bellum war.] (Rom. Myth.) The goddess of war.

bellow.c: Bellow Bel"low (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bellowed; p. pr. & vb. n. Bellowing.] [OE. belwen, belowen, AS. bylgean, fr. bellan; akin to G. bellen, and perh. to L. flere to weep, OSlav. bleja to bleat, Lith. balsas voice. Cf. Bell, n. & v., Bawl, Bull.] 1. To make a hollow, loud noise, as an enraged bull.
Bellow Bel"low, v. t. To emit with a loud voice; to shout; -- used with out. “Would bellow out a laugh.” Dryden.
Bellow Bel"low, n. A loud resounding outcry or noise, as of an enraged bull; a roar.

bellower.c: Bellower Bel"low*er (?), n. One who, or that which, bellows.

bellows.c: Bellows Bel"lows (?), n. sing. & pl. [OE. bely, below, belly, bellows, AS. bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly. Bellows is prop. a pl. and the orig. sense is bag. See Belly.] An instrument, utensil, or machine, which, by alternate expansion and contraction, or by rise and fall of the top, draws in air through a valve and expels it through a tube for various purposes, as blowing fires, ventilating mines, or filling the pipes of an organ with wind.
Bellows fish Bel"lows fish` (?). (Zool.) A European fish (Centriscus scolopax), distinguished by a long tubular snout, like the pipe of a bellows; -- called also trumpet fish, and snipe fish.

bellshaped.c: Bell-shaped Bell"-shaped` (-shāpt`), a. Having the shape of a wide-mouthed bell; campanulate.

bells.c: Bell's palsy Bell's palsy. Paralysis of the facial nerve, producing distortion of one side of the face.

belluine.c: Belluine Bel"lu*ine (?), a. [L. belluinus, fr. bellua beast.] Pertaining to, or like, a beast; brutal. [R.]

bellwether.c: Bellwether Bell"weth`er (?), n. 1. A wether, or sheep, which leads the flock, with a bell on his neck.

bellwort.c: Bellwort Bell"wort" (?), n. (Bot.) A genus of plants (Uvularia) with yellowish bell-shaped flowers.

belly.c: Belly Bel"ly (bĕl"ly̆), n.; pl. Bellies (-lĭz). [OE. bali, bely, AS. belg, bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly; akin to Icel. belgr bag, bellows, Sw. bälg, Dan. bælg, D. & G. balg, cf. W. bol the paunch or belly, dim. boly, Ir. bolg. Cf. Bellows, Follicle, Fool, Bilge.] 1. That part of the human body which extends downward from the breast to the thighs, and contains the bowels, or intestines; the abdomen.
Belly Bel"ly, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bellied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bellying.] To cause to swell out; to fill. [R.]
Belly Bel"ly, v. i. To swell and become protuberant, like the belly; to bulge.

bellyache.c: Bellyache Bel"ly*ache` (?), n. Pain in the bowels; colic.

bellyband.c: Bellyband Bel"ly*band` (?), n. 1. A band that passes under the belly of a horse and holds the saddle or harness in place; a girth.

bellycheat.c: Bellycheat Bel"ly*cheat` (?), n. An apron or covering for the front of the person. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

bellycheer.c: Bellycheer Bel"ly*cheer` (?), n. [Perh. from F. belle chère.] Good cheer; viands. [Obs.] “Bellycheer and banquets.” Rowlands. “Loaves and bellycheer.” Milton.
Bellycheer Bel"ly*cheer`, v. i. To revel; to feast. [Obs.]

bellyful.c: Bellyful Bel"ly*ful (?), n. As much as satisfies the appetite. Hence: A great abundance; more than enough. Lloyd.

bellygod.c: Belly-god Bel"ly-god` (?), n. One whose great pleasure it is to gratify his appetite; a glutton; an epicure.

bellypinched.c: Belly-pinched Bel"ly-pinched` (?), a. Pinched with hunger; starved. “The belly-pinched wolf.” Shak.

belock.c: Belock Be*lock" (be*lŏk"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belocked (be*lŏkt").] [Pref. be- + lock: cf. AS. belūcan.] To lock, or fasten as with a lock. [Obs.] Shak.

belomancy.c: Belomancy Bel"o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr.?;? arrow +? a diviner: cf. F. bélomancie.] A kind of divination anciently practiced by means of marked arrows drawn at random from a bag or quiver, the marks on the arrows drawn being supposed to foreshow the future. Encyc. Brit.

belong.c: Belong Be*long" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Belonged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Belonging.] [OE. belongen (akin to D. belangen to concern, G. belangen to attain to, to concern); pref. be- + longen to desire. See Long, v. i.] 1. To be the property of; as, Jamaica belongs to Great Britain.
Belong Be*long" (?), v. t. To be deserved by. [Obs.]

belonging.c: Belonging Be*long"ing, n. [Commonly in the pl.] 1. That which belongs to one; that which pertains to one; hence, goods or effects. “Thyself and thy belongings.” Shak.

belonite.c: Belonite Bel"o*nite (?), n. [Gr.? a needle.] (Min.) Minute acicular or dendritic crystalline forms sometimes observed in glassy volcanic rocks.

belooche.c: Belooche Beloochee { Bel*oo"che Bel*oo"chee } (?), a. Of or pertaining to Beloochistan, or to its inhabitants. -- n. A native or an inhabitant of Beloochistan.

belord.c: Belord Be*lord" (?), v. t. 1. To act the lord over.

belove.c: Belove Be*love" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beloved (?).] [OE. bilufien. See pref. Be-, and Love, v. t.] To love. [Obs.] Wodroephe.

beloved.c: Beloved Be*loved" (?), p. p. & a. Greatly loved; dear to the heart.

below.c: Below Be*low" (?), prep. [Pref. be- by + low.] 1. Under, or lower in place; beneath not so high; as, below the moon; below the knee. Shak.
Below Be*low", adv. 1. In a lower place, with respect to any object; in a lower room; beneath.

belowt.c: Belowt Be*lowt" (?), v. t. To treat as a lout; to talk abusively to. [Obs.] Camden.

belsire.c: Belsire Bel"sire` (?), n. [Pref. bel- + sire. Cf. Beldam.] A grandfather, or ancestor. “His great belsire Brute.” [Obs.] Drayton.

belswagger.c: Belswagger Bel"swag`ger (?), n. [Contr. from bellyswagger.] A lewd man; also, a bully. [Obs.] Dryden.

belt.c: Belt Belt (bĕlt), n. [AS. belt; akin to Icel. belti, Sw. bälte, Dan. bælte, OHG. balz, L. balteus, Ir. & Gael. balt border, belt.] 1. That which engirdles a person or thing; a band or girdle; as, a lady's belt; a sword belt.
Belt Belt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Belted; p. pr. & vb. n. Belting.] To encircle with, or as with, a belt; to encompass; to surround.

belted.c: Belted Belt"ed (?), a. 1. Encircled by, or secured with, a belt; as, a belted plaid; girt with a belt, as an honorary distinction; as, a belted knight; a belted earl.

beltin.c: Beltin Beltein { Bel"tein (?), Bel"tin } (?), n. See Beltane.

belting.c: Belting Belt"ing (?), n. The material of which belts for machinery are made; also, belts, taken collectively.

beluga.c: Beluga Be*lu"ga (be*lū"gȧ), n. [Russ. bieluga a sort of large sturgeon, prop. white fish, fr. bieluii white. The whale is now commonly called bieluka in Russian.] 1. (Zool.) A cetacean allied to the dolphins.

belute.c: Belute Be*lute" (be*lūt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beluted; p. pr. & vb. n. Beluting.] [Pref. be- + L. lutum mud.] To bespatter, as with mud. [R.] Sterne.

belvedere.c: Belvedere Bel`ve*dere" (?), n. [It., fr. bello, bel, beautiful + vedere to see.] (Arch.) A small building, or a part of a building, more or less open, constructed in a place commanding a fine prospect.

belzebuth.c: Belzebuth ‖Bel"ze*buth (?), n. [From Beelzebub.] (Zool.) A spider monkey (Ateles belzebuth) of Brazil.

bemad.c: Bemad Be*mad" (?), v. t. To make mad. [Obs.] Fuller.

bemangle.c: Bemangle Be*man"gle (?), v. t. To mangle; to tear asunder. [R.] Beaumont.

bemask.c: Bemask Be*mask" (?), v. t. To mask; to conceal.

bemaster.c: Bemaster Be*mas"ter (?), v. t. To master thoroughly.

bemaul.c: Bemaul Be*maul" (?), v. t. To maul or beat severely; to bruise. “In order to bemaul Yorick.” Sterne.

bemaze.c: Bemaze Be*maze (?), v. t. [OE. bimasen; pref. be- + masen to maze.] To bewilder.

bemean.c: Bemean Be*mean" (?), v. t. To make mean; to lower. C. Reade.

bemeet.c: Bemeet Be*meet" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bemet (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bemeeting.] To meet. [Obs.]

bemete.c: Bemete Be*mete" (?), v. t. To mete. [Obs.] Shak.

bemingle.c: Bemingle Be*min"gle (?), v. t. To mingle; to mix.

bemire.c: Bemire Be*mire" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bemired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bemiring.] To drag through, encumber with, or fix in, the mire; to soil by passing through mud or dirt.

bemist.c: Bemist Be*mist" (?), v. t. To envelop in mist. [Obs.]

bemoan.c: Bemoan Be*moan" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bemoaned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bemoaning.] [OE. bimenen, AS. bem?nan; pref. be- + m?nan to moan. See Moan.] To express deep grief for by moaning; to express sorrow for; to lament; to bewail; to pity or sympathize with.

bemock.c: Bemock Be*mock" (?), v. t. To mock; to ridicule.

bemoil.c: Bemoil Be*moil" (?), v. t. [Pref. be- + moil, fr. F. mouiller to wet; but cf. also OE. bimolen to soil, fr. AS. māl spot: cf. E. mole.] To soil or encumber with mire and dirt. [Obs.] Shak.

bemol.c: Bemol Be"mol (bē"mŏl), n. [F. bémol, fr. bé ♭ + mol soft.] (Mus.) The sign ♭; the same as B flat. [Obs.]

bemonster.c: Bemonster Be*mon"ster (?), v. t. To make monstrous or like a monster. [Obs.] Shak.

bemourn.c: Bemourn Be*mourn" (?), v. t. To mourn over. Wyclif.

bemuddle.c: Bemuddle Be*mud"dle (?), v. t. To muddle; to stupefy or bewilder; to confuse.

bemuffle.c: Bemuffle Be*muf"fle (?), v. t. To cover as with a muffler; to wrap up.

bemuse.c: Bemuse Be*muse" (?), v. t. To muddle, daze, or partially stupefy, as with liquor.

ben.c: Ben nut Ben { Ben (?), Ben" nut` } (?). [Ar. bān, name of the tree.] (Bot.) The seed of one or more species of moringa; as, oil of ben. See Moringa.
Ben Ben, adv. & prep. [AS. binnan; pref. be- by + innan within, in in.] Within; in; in or into the interior; toward the inner apartment. [Scot.]
Ben Ben, n. [See Ben, adv.] The inner or principal room in a hut or house of two rooms; -- opposed to but, the outer apartment. [Scot.]
Ben Ben. An old form of the pl. indic. pr. of Be. [Obs.]
Ben Bene { ‖Bene, Ben } (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A hoglike mammal of New Guinea (Porcula papuensis).

bename.c: Bename Be*name" (?), v. t. [p. p. Benamed, Benempt.] To promise; to name. [Obs.]

bench.c: Bench Bench (?), n.; pl. Benches (?). [OE. bench, benk, AS. benc; akin to Sw. bänk, Dan bænk, Icel. bekkr, OS., D., & G. bank. Cf. Bank, Beach.] 1. A long seat, differing from a stool in its greater length.
Bench Bench (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Benched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Benching.] 1. To furnish with benches.
Bench Bench, v. i. To sit on a seat of justice. [R.] Shak.

bench mark benchmark benchmark, bench mark. (Surveying) 1. Any permanent mark to which other levels may be referred. such as: (a) A horizontal mark at the water's edge with reference to which the height of tides and floods may be measured. (b) a surveyer's mark on a permanent object of predetermined position and elevation used as a reference point.

Bench warrant Bench" war`rant (?). (Law) A process issued by a presiding judge or by a court against a person guilty of some contempt, or indicted for some crime; -- so called in distinction from a justice's warrant.

bencher.c: Bencher Bench"er (?), n. 1. (Eng. Law) One of the senior and governing members of an Inn of Court.

bend.c: Bend Bend (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bended or Bent (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bending.] [AS. bendan to bend, fr. bend a band, bond, fr. bindan to bind. See Bind, v. t., and cf. 3d & 4th Bend.] 1. To strain or move out of a straight line; to crook by straining; to make crooked; to curve; to make ready for use by drawing into a curve; as, to bend a bow; to bend the knee.
Bend Bend, v. i. 1. To be moved or strained out of a straight line; to crook or be curving; to bow.

Bend Bend, n. [See Bend, v. t., and cf. Bent, n.] 1. A turn or deflection from a straight line or from the proper direction or normal position; a curve; a crook; as, a slight bend of the body; a bend in a road.
Bend Bend, n. [AS. bend. See Band, and cf. the preceding noun.] 1. A band. [Obs.] Spenser.

bendable.c: Bendable Bend"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being bent.

bender.c: Bender Bend"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, bends.

bending.c: Bending Bend"ing, n. The marking of the clothes with stripes or horizontal bands. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bendlet.c: Bendlet Bend"let (?), n. [Bend + -let: cf. E. bandlet.] (Her.) A narrow bend, esp. one half the width of the bend.

bendy.c: Bendy Ben"dy (?), a. [From Bend a band.] (Her.) Divided into an even number of bends; -- said of a shield or its charge. Cussans.

bene.c: Bene Be"ne (?), n. [AS. bēn.] A prayer; boon. [Archaic]
Bene placito ‖Be`ne plac"i*to (bē`ne plăs"ĭ*to; It. bā`na plä"che*to). [It. beneplacito pleasure, fr. L. bene well + placitus pleasing.] 1. At or during pleasure.

beneath.c: Beneath Be*neath" (?), prep. [OE. benethe, bineoðen, AS. beneoðan, benyðan; pref. be- + neoðan, nyðan, downward, beneath, akin to E. nether. See Nether.] 1. Lower in place, with something directly over or on; under; underneath; hence, at the foot of. “Beneath the mount.” Ex. xxxii. 19.
Beneath Be*neath" (?), adv. 1. In a lower place; underneath.

benedicite.c: Benedicite ‖Ben`e*dic"i*te (?), n. [L., (imperative pl.,) bless ye, praise ye.] A canticle (the Latin version of which begins with this word) which may be used in the order for morning prayer in the Church of England. It is taken from an apocryphal addition to the third chapter of Daniel.
Benedicite ‖Ben`e*dic"i*te, interj. [See Benedicite, n.] An exclamation corresponding to Bless you!.

benedick.c: Benedick Benedict { Ben"e*dict (?), Ben"e*dick (?), } n. [From Benedick, one of the characters in Shakespeare's play of “Much Ado about Nothing.”] A married man, or a man newly married.

benedict.c: Benedict Ben"e*dict, a. [L. benedictus, p. p. of benedicere to bless. See Benison, and cf. Bennet.] Having mild and salubrious qualities. [Obs.] Bacon.

benedictine.c: Benedictine Ben`e*dic"tine (?), a. Pertaining to the monks of St. Benedict, or St. Benet.
Benedictine Ben`e*dic"tine, n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a famous order of monks, established by St. Benedict of Nursia in the sixth century. This order was introduced into the United States in 1846.

benediction.c: Benediction Ben`e*dic"tion (?), n. [L. benedictio: cf. F. bénédiction. See Benison.] 1. The act of blessing.

benedictional.c: Benedictional Ben`e*dic"tion*al (?), n. A book of benedictions.

benedictionary.c: Benedictionary Ben`e*dic"tion*a*ry (?), n. A collected series of benedictions.

benedictive.c: Benedictive Ben`e*dic"tive (?), a. Tending to bless. Gauden.

benedictory.c: Benedictory Ben`e*dic"to*ry (?), a. Expressing wishes for good; as, a benedictory prayer. Thackeray.

benedictus.c: Benedictus ‖Ben`e*dic"tus (?), n. [L., blessed. See Benedict, a.] The song of Zacharias at the birth of John the Baptist (Luke i. 68); -- so named from the first word of the Latin version.

benefaction.c: Benefaction Ben`e*fac"tion (?), n. [L. benefactio, fr. benefacere to do good to one; bene well + facere to do. See Benefit.] 1. The act of conferring a benefit. Johnson.

benefactor.c: Benefactor Ben`e*fac"tor (?),n. [L.] One who confers a benefit or benefits. Bacon.

benefactress.c: Benefactress Ben`e*fac"tress, n. A woman who confers a benefit.

benefic.c: Benefic Be*nef"ic (?), a. [L. beneficus. See Benefice.] Favorable; beneficent. Milton.

benefice.c: Benefice Ben"e*fice (?), n. [F. bénéfice, L. beneficium, a kindness, in LL. a grant of an estate, fr. L. beneficus beneficent; bene well + facere to do. See Benefit.]
Benefice Ben"e*fice, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beneficed.] To endow with a benefice.

beneficed.c: Beneficed Ben"e*ficed (?), a. Possessed of a benefice or church preferment. “Beneficed clergymen.” Burke.

beneficeless.c: Beneficeless Ben"e*fice*less (?), a. Having no benefice. “Beneficeless precisians.” Sheldon.

beneficence.c: Beneficence Be*nef"i*cence (?), n. [L. beneficentia, fr. beneficus: cf. F. bénéficence. See Benefice.] The practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity; bounty springing from purity and goodness.

beneficent.c: Beneficent Be*nef`i*cent (?), a. Doing or producing good; performing acts of kindness and charity; characterized by beneficence.

beneficently.c: Beneficently Be*nef"i*cent*ly (be*nĕf"ĭ*seint*ly̆), adv. In a beneficent manner; with beneficence.

beneficial.c: Beneficial Ben`e*fi"cial (?), a. [Cf. F. bénéficial, LL. beneficialis.] 1. Conferring benefits; useful; profitable; helpful; advantageous; serviceable; contributing to a valuable end; -- followed by to.

beneficially.c: Beneficially Ben`e*fi"cial*ly, adv. In a beneficial or advantageous manner; profitably; helpfully.

beneficialness.c: Beneficialness Ben`e*fi"cial*ness, n. The quality of being beneficial; profitableness.

beneficiary.c: Beneficiary Ben`e*fi"ci*a*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. bénéficiaire, LL. beneficiarius.] 1. Holding some office or valuable possession, in subordination to another; holding under a feudal or other superior; having a dependent and secondary possession.
Beneficiary Ben`e*fi"ci*a*ry, n.; pl. Beneficiaries (?). 1. A feudatory or vassal; hence, one who holds a benefice and uses its proceeds. Ayliffe.

beneficiate.c: Beneficiate Ben`e*fi"ci*ate (?), v. t. [Sp. beneficiar to benefit, to work mines.] (Mining) To reduce (ores). -- Ben`e*fi`ci*a"tion (?), n.

benefit.c: Benefit Ben"e*fit (?), n. [OE. benefet, benfeet, bienfet, F. bienfait, fr. L. benefactum; bene well (adv. of bonus good) + factum, p. p. of facere to do. See Bounty, and Fact.] 1. An act of kindness; a favor conferred.
Benefit Ben"e*fit, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Benefited; p. pr. & vb. n. Benefitting.] To be beneficial to; to do good to; to advantage; to advance in health or prosperity; to be useful to; to profit.
Benefit Ben"e*fit, v. i. To gain advantage; to make improvement; to profit; as, he will benefit by the change.

Benefit society Benefit society. A society or association formed for mutual insurance, as among tradesmen or in labor unions, to provide for relief in sickness, old age, and for the expenses of burial. Usually called friendly society in Great Britain.

benefiter.c: Benefiter Ben"e*fit`er (?), n. One who confers a benefit; -- also, one who receives a benefit.

beneme.c: Beneme Be*neme" (?), v. t. [AS. ben?man. Cf. Benim.] To deprive (of), or take away (from). [Obs.]

benempt.c: Benempt Be*nempt" (?), p. p. of Bename. 1. Promised; vowed. [Obs.] Spenser.

benet.c: Benet Be*net" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Benetted.] To catch in a net; to insnare. Shak.

benevolence.c: Benevolence Be*nev"o*lence (?), n. [OF. benevolence, L. benevolentia. See Benevolent.] 1. The disposition to do good; good will; charitableness; love of mankind, accompanied with a desire to promote their happiness.

benevolent.c: Benevolent Be*nev"o*lent (?), a. [L. benevolens, -entis; bene well (adv. of bonus good) + volens, p. pr. of volo I will, I wish. See Bounty, and Voluntary.] Having a disposition to do good; possessing or manifesting love to mankind, and a desire to promote their prosperity and happiness; disposed to give to good objects; kind; charitable. -- Be*nev"o*lent*ly, adv.

benevolous.c: benevolous be*nev"o*lous (?), a. [L. benevolus.] Kind; benevolent. [Obs.] T. Puller.

bengal.c: Bengal Ben*gal" (?), prop. n. 1. A province in India, giving its name to various stuffs, animals, etc.

bengali.c: Bengali Bengalee { Ben*gal"ee, Ben*gal"i } (?), prop. n. The language spoken in Bengal.

bengalese.c: Bengalese Ben`gal*ese" (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to Bengal. -- n. sing. & pl. A native or natives of Bengal.

benight.c: benight be*night" (be*nīt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Benighted; p. pr. & vb. n. Benighting.] 1. To involve in darkness; to shroud with the shades of night; to obscure. [Archaic]

benightment.c: Benightment Be*night"ment (?), n. The condition of being benighted.

benign.c: Benign Be*nign" (?), a. [OE. benigne, bening, OF. benigne, F. bénin, fem. bénigne, fr. L. benignus, contr. from benigenus; bonus good + root of genus kind. See Bounty, and Genus.] 1. Of a kind or gentle disposition; gracious; generous; favorable; benignant.

benignant.c: Benignant Be*nig"nant (?), a. [LL. benignans, p. pr. of benignare, from L. benignus. See Benign.] Kind; gracious; favorable. -- Be*nig"nant*ly, adv.

benignity.c: Benignity Be*nig"ni*ty (?), n. [OE. benignite, F. bénignité, OF. bénigneté, fr. L. benignitas. See Benign.] 1. The quality of being benign; goodness; kindness; graciousness. “Benignity of aspect.” Sir W. Scott.

benignly.c: Benignly Be*nign"ly (?), adv. In a benign manner.

benim.c: Benim Be*nim" (?), v. t. [AS. beniman. See Benumb, and cf. Nim.] To take away. [Obs.]

benison.c: Benison Ben"i*son (?), n. [OE. beneysun, benesoun, OF. beneï?un, beneïson, fr. L. benedictio, fr. benedicere to bless; bene (adv. of bonus good) + dicere to say. See Bounty, and Diction, and cf. Benediction.] Blessing; beatitude; benediction. Shak.

benitier.c: Benitier ‖Bé*ni"tier` (?), n. [F., fr. bénir to bless.] (R. C. Ch.) A holy-water stoup. Shipley.

benjamin.c: Benjamin Ben"ja*min (?), n. [Corrupted from benzoin.] See Benzoin.
Benjamin Ben"ja*min, n. A kind of upper coat for men. [Colloq. Eng.]

benjamite.c: Benjamite Ben"ja*mite (?), n. A descendant of Benjamin; one of the tribe of Benjamin. Judg. iii. 15.

benne.c: Benne Ben"ne (?), n. [Malay bijen.] (Bot.) The name of two plants (Sesamum orientale and Sesamum indicum), originally Asiatic; -- also called oil plant. From their seeds an oil is expressed, called benne oil or sesame oil, used mostly for making soap. In the southern United States the seeds are used in candy. [Also spelled benni.]

bennet.c: Bennet Ben"net (?), n. [F. benoîte, fr. L. benedicta, fem. of benedictus, p. p., blessed. See Benedict, a.] (Bot.) The common yellow-flowered avens of Europe (Geum urbanum); herb bennet. The name is sometimes given to other plants, as the hemlock, valerian, etc.

bent.c: Bent Bent (bĕnt), imp. & p. p. of Bend.
Bent Bent, a. & p. p. 1. Changed by pressure so as to be no longer straight; crooked; as, a bent pin; a bent lever.
Bent Bent, n. [See Bend, n. & v.] 1. The state of being curved, crooked, or inclined from a straight line; flexure; curvity; as, the bent of a bow. [Obs.] Wilkins.
Bent Bent (?), n. [AS. beonet; akin to OHG. pinuz, G. binse, rush, bent grass; of unknown origin.] 1. A reedlike grass; a stalk of stiff, coarse grass.
Bent grass Bent" grass` (?). (Bot.) Same as Bent, a kind of grass.

benthal.c: Benthal Ben"thal (?), a. [Gr.? the depth of the sea.] Relating to the deepest zone or region of the ocean.

benthamic.c: Benthamic Ben*tham"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to Bentham or Benthamism.

benthamism.c: Benthamism Ben"tham*ism (?), n. That phase of the doctrine of utilitarianism taught by Jeremy Bentham; the doctrine that the morality of actions is estimated and determined by their utility; also, the theory that the sensibility to pleasure and the recoil from pain are the only motives which influence human desires and actions, and that these are the sufficient explanation of ethical and jural conceptions.

benthamite.c: Benthamite Ben"tham*ite (?), n. One who believes in Benthamism.

benthos.c: Benthos ‖Ben"thos (bĕn"thŏs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. be`nqos depth of the sea.] The bottom of the sea, esp. of the deep oceans; hence (Bot. & Zool.), the fauna and flora of the sea bottom; -- opposed to plankton.

benting.c: Benting time Bent"ing time" (?). The season when pigeons are said to feed on bents, before peas are ripe.

benty.c: Benty Bent"y (bĕnt"y̆), a. 1. Abounding in bents, or the stalks of coarse, stiff, withered grass; as, benty fields.

benumb.c: Benumb Be*numb" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Benumbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Benumbing.] [OE. binomen, p. p. of binimen to take away, AS. beniman; pref. be + niman to take. See Numb, a., and cf. Benim.] To make torpid; to deprive of sensation or sensibility; to stupefy; as, a hand or foot benumbed by cold.

benumbed.c: Benumbed Be*numbed" (?), a. Made torpid; numbed; stupefied; deadened; as, a benumbed body and mind. -- Be*numbed"ness, n.

benumbment.c: Benumbment Be*numb"ment (?), n. Act of benumbing, or state of being benumbed; torpor. Kirby.

benzal.c: Benzal Ben"zal (?), n. [Benzoic + aldehyde.] (Chem.) A compound radical, C6H5.CH=, of the aromatic series, related to benzyl and benzoyl; -- used adjectively or in combination.

benzamide.c: Benzamide Ben*zam"ide (?), n. [Benzoin + amide.] (Chem.) A transparent crystalline substance, C6H5.CO.NH2, obtained by the action of ammonia upon chloride of benzoyl, as also by several other reactions with benzoyl compounds.

benzene.c: Benzene Ben"zene (?), n. [From Benzoin.] (Chem.) A volatile, very inflammable liquid, C6H6, contained in the naphtha produced by the destructive distillation of coal, from which it is separated by fractional distillation. The name is sometimes applied also to the impure commercial product or benzole, and also, but rarely, to a similar mixed product of petroleum.

benzile.c: Benzile Ben"zile (?), n. [From Benzoin.] (Chem.) A yellowish crystalline substance, C6H5.CO.CO.C6H5, formed from benzoin by the action of oxidizing agents, and consisting of a doubled benzoyl radical.

benzine.c: Benzine Ben"zine (?), n. [From Benzoin.] (Chem.) 1. A liquid consisting mainly of the lighter and more volatile hydrocarbons of petroleum or kerosene oil, used as a solvent and for cleansing soiled fabrics; -- called also petroleum spirit, petroleum benzine. Varieties or similar products are gasoline, naphtha, rhigolene, ligroin, etc.

benzoate.c: Benzoate Ben"zo*ate (?), n. [Cf. F. benzoate.] (Chem.) A salt formed by the union of benzoic acid with any salifiable base.

benzoic.c: Benzoic Ben*zo"ic (bĕn*zō"ĭk), a. [Cf. F. benzoïque.] Pertaining to, or obtained from, benzoin.

benzoin.c: Benzoin Ben*zoin" (bĕn*zoin"), n. [Cf. F. benjoin, Sp. benjui, Pg. beijoin; all fr. Ar. lubān-jāwī incense form Sumatra (named Java in Arabic), the first syllable being lost. Cf. Benjamin.] 1. A resinous substance, dry and brittle, obtained from the Styrax benzoin, a tree of Sumatra, Java, etc., having a fragrant odor, and slightly aromatic taste. It is used in the preparation of benzoic acid, in medicine, and as a perfume.

benzoinated.c: Benzoinated Ben*zoin"a*ted (?), a. (Med.) Containing or impregnated with benzoin; as, benzoinated lard.

benzol.c: Benzol Benzole { Ben"zole Ben"zol } (?), n. [Benzoin + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) An impure benzene, used in the arts as a solvent, and for various other purposes. See Benzene.

benzoline.c: Benzoline Ben"zo*line (?), n. (Chem.) (a) Same as Benzole. (b) Same as Amarine. [R.] Watts.

benzonaphtol.c: Benzonaphtol Benzonaphthol { Ben`zo*naph"thol (?), n. Also Ben`zo*naph"tol }. [Benzoin + naphthol.] (Chem.) A white crystalline powder used as an intestinal antiseptic; beta-naphthol benzoate.

benzosol.c: Benzosol Ben"zo*sol (?), n. (Pharm.) Guaiacol benzoate, used as an intestinal antiseptic and as a substitute for creosote in phthisis. It is a colorless crystalline pewder.

benzoyl.c: Benzoyl Ben"zoyl (?), n. [Benzoic + Gr.? wood. See -yl.] (Chem.) A compound radical, C6H5.CO-; the base of benzoic acid, of the oil of bitter almonds, and of an extensive series of compounds. [Formerly written also benzule.]

benzyl.c: Benzyl Ben"zyl (?), n. [Benzoic + -yl.] (Chem.) A compound radical, C6H5.CH2, related to toluene and benzoic acid; -- commonly used adjectively.

bepaint.c: Bepaint Be*paint" (?), v. t. To paint; to cover or color with, or as with, paint.

bepelt.c: Bepelt Be*pelt" (?), v. t. To pelt roundly.

bepinch.c: Bepinch Be*pinch" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bepinched (?).] To pinch, or mark with pinches. Chapman.

beplaster.c: Beplaster Be*plas"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beplastered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beplastering.] To plaster over; to cover or smear thickly; to bedaub.

bepommel.c: Bepommel Be*pom"mel (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bepommeled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bepommeling.] To pommel; to beat, as with a stick; figuratively, to assail or criticise in conversation, or in writing. Thackeray.

bepowder.c: Bepowder Be*pow"der (?), v. t. To sprinkle or cover with powder; to powder.

bepraise.c: Bepraise Be*praise" (?), v. t. To praise greatly or extravagantly. Goldsmith.

beprose.c: Beprose Be*prose" (?), v. t. To reduce to prose. [R.] “To beprose all rhyme.” Mallet.

bepurple.c: Bepurple Be*pur"ple (?), v. t. To tinge or dye with a purple color.

bequeath.c: Bequeath Be*queath" (be*kwēth"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bequeathed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bequeathing.] [OE. biquethen, AS. becweðan to say, affirm, bequeath; pref. be- + cweðan to say, speak. See Quoth.] 1. To give or leave by will; to give by testament; -- said especially of personal property.

bequeathable.c: Bequeathable Be*queath"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being bequeathed.

bequeathal.c: Bequeathal Be*queath"al (?), n. The act of bequeathing; bequeathment; bequest. Fuller.

bequeathment.c: Bequeathment Be*queath"ment (?), n. The act of bequeathing, or the state of being bequeathed; a bequest.

bequest.c: Bequest Be*quest" (?), n. [OE. biquest, corrupted fr. bequide; pref. be- + AS. cwide a saying, becweðan to bequeath. The ending -est is probably due to confusion with quest. See Bequeath, Quest.] 1. The act of bequeathing or leaving by will; as, a bequest of property by A. to B.
Bequest Be*quest", v. t. To bequeath, or leave as a legacy. [Obs.] “All I have to bequest.” Gascoigne.

bequethen.c: Bequethen Be*queth"en (?), old p. p. of Bequeath. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bequote.c: Bequote Be*quote" (?), v. t. To quote constantly or with great frequency.

berain.c: Berain Be*rain (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Berained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beraining.] To rain upon; to wet with rain. [Obs.] Chaucer.

berate.c: Berate Be*rate" (be*rāt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Berated; p. pr. & vb. n. Berating.] [See 2nd rate, v. t..] To rate or chide vehemently; to scold. Holland. Motley.

berattle.c: Berattle Be*rat"tle (be*răt"t'l), v. t. To make rattle; to scold vociferously; to cry down. [Obs.] Shak.

beray.c: Beray Be*ray" (be*rā"), v. t. [Pref. be + ray to defile.] To make foul; to soil; to defile. [Obs.] Milton.

berbe.c: Berbe ‖Berbe (bẽrb), n. [Cf. Berber, Barb a Barbary horse.] (Zool.) An African genet (Genetta pardina). See Genet.

berber.c: Berber Ber"ber (bẽr"bẽr), n. [See Barbary.] A member of a race somewhat resembling the Arabs, but often classed as Hamitic, who were formerly the inhabitants of the whole of North Africa from the Mediterranean southward into the Sahara, and who still occupy a large part of that region; -- called also Kabyles. Also, the language spoken by this people.

berberine.c: Berberine Ber"ber*ine (?), n. (Chem.) An alkaloid obtained, as a bitter, yellow substance, from the root of the barberry, gold thread, and other plants.

berceuse.c: Berceuse ‖Ber`ceuse" (?), n. [F.] (Mus.) A vocal or instrumental composition of a soft tranquil character, having a lulling effect; a cradle song.

berdash.c: Berdash Ber"dash (?), n. A kind of neckcloth. [Obs.]

bereave.c: Bereave Be*reave" (be*rēv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bereaved (be*rēvd"), Bereft (be*rĕft"); p. pr. & vb. n. Bereaving.] [OE. bireven, AS. bereáfian. See Be-, and Reave.]

bereavement.c: Bereavement Be*reave"ment (be*rēv"meint), n. The state of being bereaved; deprivation; esp., the loss of a relative by death.

bereft.c: Bereft Be*reft" (be*rĕft"), imp. & p. p. of Bereave.

berenices.c: Berenice's Hair Ber`e*ni"ce's Hair` (?). [See Berenice's Locks, in Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.] (Astron.) See Coma Berenices, under Coma.

berg.c: Berg Berg (?), n. [√95. See Barrow hill, and cf. Iceberg.] A large mass or hill, as of ice.

bergamot.c: Bergamot Ber"ga*mot (bẽr"gȧ*mŏt), n. [F. bergamote, fr. It. bergamotta; prob. a corruption of Turk. beg armūdi a lord's pear.] 1. (Bot.) (a) A tree of the Orange family (Citrus bergamia), having a roundish or pear-shaped fruit, from the rind of which an essential oil of delicious odor is extracted, much prized as a perfume. Also, the fruit. (b) A variety of mint (Mentha aquatica, var. glabrata).

bergander.c: Bergander Ber"gan*der (?), n. [Berg, for burrow + gander a male goose? Cf. G. bergente, Dan. gravgaas.] (Zool.) A European duck (Anas tadorna). See Sheldrake.

bergeret.c: Bergeret Ber"ger*et (?), n. [OF. bergerete, F. berger a shepherd.] A pastoral song. [Obs.]

bergmeal.c: Bergmeal Berg"meal (?), n. [G. berg mountain + mehl meal.] (Min.) An earthy substance, resembling fine flour. It is composed of the shells of infusoria, and in Lapland and Sweden is sometimes eaten, mixed with flour or ground birch bark, in times of scarcity. This name is also given to a white powdery variety of calcite.

bergomask.c: Bergomask Ber"go*mask (?), n. A rustic dance, so called in ridicule of the people of Bergamo, in Italy, once noted for their clownishness.

bergschrund.c: Bergschrund ‖Berg"schrund` (?), n. [G., lit., mountain gap.] (Phys. Geog.) The crevasse or series of crevasses, usually deep and often broad, frequently occurring near the head of a mountain glacier, about where the névé field joins the valley portion of the glacier.

bergstock.c: Bergstock ‖Berg"stock` (?), n. [G., lit., mountain stick.] A long pole with a spike at the end, used in climbing mountains; an alpenstock.

bergylt.c: Bergylt Ber"gylt (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) The Norway haddock. See Rosefish.

berhyme.c: Berhyme Be*rhyme" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Berhymed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Berhyming.] To mention in rhyme or verse; to rhyme about. Shak.

beriberi.c: Beriberi ‖Be`ri*be"ri (?), n. [Singhalese beri weakness.] An acute disease occurring in India, characterized by multiple inflammatory changes in the nerves, producing great muscular debility, a painful rigidity of the limbs, and cachexy.

bering.c: Bering Sea Controversy Be"ring Sea Controversy (?). A controversy (1886 -- 93) between Great Britain and the United States as to the right of Canadians not licensed by the United States to carry on seal fishing in the Bering Sea, over which the United States claimed jurisdiction as a mare clausum. A court of arbitration, meeting in Paris in 1893, decided against the claim of the United States, but established regulations for the preservation of the fur seal.

berkeleian.c: Berkeleian Berke*le"ian (bẽrk*lē"ain), a. Of or relating to Bishop Berkeley or his system of idealism; as, Berkeleian philosophy. -- Berke"ley*ism, n.

berlin.c: Berlin Ber"lin (?), n. [The capital of Germany] 1. A four-wheeled carriage, having a sheltered seat behind the body and separate from it, invented in the 17th century, at Berlin.

berme.c: Berme Berm { Berm Berme } (?), n. [F. berme, of German origin; cf. G. brame, bräme, border, akin to E. brim.] 1. (Fort.) A narrow shelf or path between the bottom of a parapet and the ditch.

bermuda.c: Bermuda grass Ber*mu"da grass` (?). (Bot.) A kind of grass (Cynodon Dactylon) esteemed for pasture in the Southern United States. It is a native of Southern Europe, but is now wide-spread in warm countries; -- called also scutch grass, and in Bermuda, devil grass.
Bermuda lily Ber*mu"da lil"y. (Bot.) The large white lily (Lilium longiflorum eximium, syn. Lilium Harrisii) which is extensively cultivated in Bermuda.

berna.c: Berna fly Ber"na fly` (?). (Zool.) A Brazilian dipterous insect of the genus Trypeta, which lays its eggs in the nostrils or in wounds of man and beast, where the larvæ do great injury.

bernardine.c: Bernardine Ber"nar*dine (?), a. Of or pertaining to St. Bernard of Clairvaux, or to the Cistercian monks. -- n. A Cistercian monk.

bernese.c: Bernese Ber*nese" (?), a. Pertaining to the city or canton of Bern, in Switzerland, or to its inhabitants. -- n. sing. & pl. A native or natives of Bern.

bernicle.c: Bernicle Ber"ni*cle (?), n. [OE. bernak, bernacle; cf. OF. bernac; prob. fr. LL. bernacula for hibernicula, bernicula, fr. Hibernia; the birds coming from Hibernia or Ireland. Cf. 1st Barnacle.] A bernicle goose. [Written also barnacle.]

berob.c: Berob Be*rob" (?), v. t. To rob; to plunder. [Obs.]

beroe.c: Beroe ‖Ber"o*e (?), n. [L. Beroe, one of the Oceanidæ Gr.?: cf. F. beroé.] (Zool.) A small, oval, transparent jellyfish, belonging to the Ctenophora.

berretta.c: Berretta Ber*ret"ta (?), n. [It., fr. LL. birrettum, berretum, a cap, dim. of L. birrus, birrum, a cloak to keep off rain, cf. Gr.? tawny, red: cf. Sp. birreta, Pg. barrete, and E. Barret.] A square cap worn by ecclesiastics of the Roman Catholic Church. A cardinal's berretta is scarlet; that worn by other clerics is black, except that a bishop's is lined with green. [Also spelt beretta, biretta, etc.]

berried.c: Berried Ber"ried (?), a. Furnished with berries; consisting of a berry; baccate; as, a berried shrub.

berry.c: Berry Ber"ry (?), n.; pl. Berries. [OE. berie, AS. berie, berige; akin to D. bes, G. beere, OS. and OHG. beri, Icel. ber, Sw. bär, Goth. basi, and perh. Skr. bhas to eat.] 1. Any small fleshy fruit, as the strawberry, mulberry, huckleberry, etc.
Berry Ber"ry, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Berried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Berrying.] To bear or produce berries.
Berry Ber"ry, n. [AS. beorh. See Barrow a hill.] A mound; a hillock. W. Browne.

berrying.c: Berrying Ber"ry*ing, n. A seeking for or gathering of berries, esp. of such as grow wild.

berseem.c: Berseem Ber*seem" (?), n. [Ar. bershīm clover.] An Egyptian clover (Trifolium alexandrinum) extensively cultivated as a forage plant and soil-renewing crop in the alkaline soils of the Nile valley, and now introduced into the southwestern United States. It is more succulent than other clovers or than alfalfa. Called also Egyptian clover.

berserker.c: Berserker Berserk { Ber"serk (?), Ber"serk*er (?), } n. [Icel. berserkr.] 1. (Scand. Myth.) One of a class of legendary heroes, who fought frenzied by intoxicating liquors, and naked, regardless of wounds. Longfellow.

berth.c: Berth Berth (bẽrth), n. [From the root of bear to produce, like birth nativity. See Birth.] [Also written birth.]
Berth Berth, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Berthed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Berthing.] 1. To give an anchorage to, or a place to lie at; to place in a berth; as, she was berthed stem to stern with the Adelaide.

bertha.c: Bertha Ber"tha (?), n. [F. berthe, fr. Berthe, a woman's name.] A kind of collar or cape worn by ladies.

berthage.c: Berthage Berth"age (?), n. A place for mooring vessels in a dock or harbor.

berthierite.c: Berthierite Ber"thi*er*ite (?), n. [From Berthier, a French naturalist.] (Min.) A double sulphide of antimony and iron, of a dark steel-gray color.

berthing.c: Berthing Berth"ing (?), n. (Naut.) The planking outside of a vessel, above the sheer strake. Smyth.

bertillon.c: Bertillon system Ber`til`lon" sys"tem (?). [After Alphonse Bertillon, French anthropologist.] A system for the identification of persons by a physical description based upon anthropometric measurements, notes of markings, deformities, color, impression of thumb lines, etc.

bertram.c: Bertram Ber"tram (?), n. [Corrupted fr. L. pyrethrum, Gr.? a hot spicy plant, fr.? fire.] (Bot.) Pellitory of Spain (Anacyclus pyrethrum).

berycoid.c: Berycoid Ber"y*coid (bĕr"ĭ*koid), a. [NL. beryx, the name of the typical genus + -oid.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Berycidæ, a family of marine fishes.

beryl.c: Beryl Ber"yl (bĕr"ĭl), n. [F. béryl, OF. beril, L. beryllus, Gr. bh`ryllos, prob. fr. Skr. vaiḍūrya. Cf. Brilliant.] (Min.) A mineral of great hardness, and, when transparent, of much beauty. It occurs in hexagonal prisms, commonly of a green or bluish green color, but also yellow, pink, and white. It is a silicate of aluminum and beryllium. The aquamarine is a transparent, sea-green variety used as a gem. The emerald is another variety highly prized in jewelry, and distinguished by its deep color, which is probably due to the presence of a little oxide of chromium.

berylline.c: Berylline Ber"yl*line (?), a. Like a beryl; of a light or bluish green color.

beryllium.c: Beryllium Be*ryl"li*um (?), n. [NL.] (Chem.) A metallic element found in the beryl. See Glucinum.

berylloid.c: Berylloid Ber"yl*loid (?), n. [Beryl + -oid.] (Crystallog.) A solid consisting of a double twelve-sided pyramid; -- so called because the planes of this form occur on crystals of beryl.

besayle.c: Besayle Besaile Besaiel { Be*saiel", Be*saile", Be*sayle" (?) }, n. [OF. beseel, F. bisaïeul, fr. L. bis twice + LL. avolus, dim. of L. avus grandfather.] 1. A great-grandfather. [Obs.]

besaint.c: Besaint Be*saint" (?), v. t. To make a saint of.

bescatter.c: Bescatter Be*scat"ter (?), v. t. 1. To scatter over.

bescorn.c: Bescorn Be*scorn" (?), v. t. To treat with scorn. “Then was he bescorned.” Chaucer.

bescratch.c: Bescratch Be*scratch" (?), v. t. To tear with the nails; to cover with scratches.

bescrawl.c: Bescrawl Be*scrawl" (?), v. t. To cover with scrawls; to scribble over. Milton.

bescreen.c: Bescreen Be*screen" (?), v. t. To cover with a screen, or as with a screen; to shelter; to conceal. Shak.

bescribble.c: Bescribble Be*scrib"ble (?), v. t. To scribble over. “Bescribbled with impertinences.” Milton.

bescummer.c: Bescummer Bescumber { Be*scum"ber (?), Be*scum"mer (?), } v. t. [Pref. be- + scumber, scummer.] To discharge ordure or dung upon. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

besee.c: Besee Be*see" (?), v. t. & i. [AS. beseón; pref. be- +?eón to see.] To see; to look; to mind. [Obs.] Wyclif.

beseech.c: Beseech Be*seech" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besought (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beseeching.] [OE. bisechen, biseken (akin to G. besuchen to visit); pref. be- + sechen, seken, to seek. See Seek.] 1. To ask or entreat with urgency; to supplicate; to implore.
Beseech Be*seech", n. Solicitation; supplication. [Obs. or Poetic] Shak.

beseeching.c: Beseeching Be*seech"ing, a. Entreating urgently; imploring; as, a beseeching look. -- Be*seech"ing*ly, adv. -- Be*seech"ing*ness, n.

beseechment.c: Beseechment Be*seech"ment (?), n. The act of beseeching or entreating earnestly. [R.] Goodwin.

beseek.c: Beseek Be*seek" (?), v. t. To beseech. [Obs.] Chaucer.

beseem.c: Beseem Be*seem" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beseemed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beseeming.] [Pref. be- + seem.] Literally: To appear or seem (well, ill, best, etc.) for (one) to do or to have. Hence: To be fit, suitable, or proper for, or worthy of; to become; to befit.
Beseem Be*seem", v. i. To seem; to appear; to be fitting. [Obs.] “As beseemed best.” Spenser.

beseeming.c: Beseeming Be*seem"ing, a. Becoming; suitable. [Archaic] -- Be*seem"ing*ly, adv. -- Be*seem"ing*ness, n.

beseen.c: Beseen Be*seen" (?), a. [Properly the p. p. of besee.]

beset.c: Beset Be*set" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beset; p. pr. & vb. n. Besetting.] [AS. besettan (akin to OHG. bisazjan, G. besetzen, D. bezetten); pref. be- + settan to set. See Set.] 1. To set or stud (anything) with ornaments or prominent objects.

besetment.c: Besetment Be*set"ment (?), n. The act of besetting, or the state of being beset; also, that which besets one, as a sin. “Fearing a besetment.” Kane.

besetter.c: Besetter Be*set"ter (?), n. One who, or that which, besets.

besetting.c: Besetting Be*set"ting, a. Habitually attacking, harassing, or pressing upon or about; as, a besetting sin.

beshine.c: Beshine Be*shine" (be*shīn"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beshone; p. pr. & vb. n. Beshining.] To shine upon; to illumine.

beshow.c: Beshow ‖Be*show" (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A large food fish (Anoplopoma fimbria) of the north Pacific coast; -- called also candlefish.

beshrew.c: Beshrew Be*shrew" (?), v. t. To curse; to execrate.

beshroud.c: Beshroud Be*shroud" (?), v. t. To cover with, or as with, a shroud; to screen.

beshut.c: Beshut Be*shut" (?), v. t. To shut up or out. [Obs.]

beside.c: Beside Be*side" (?), prep. [OE. biside, bisiden, bisides, prep. and adv., beside, besides; pref. be- by + side. Cf. Besides, and see Side, n.] 1. At the side of; on one side of. “Beside him hung his bow.” Milton.
Beside Besides { Be*sides" (?), Be*side" (?), } adv. [OE. Same as beside, prep.; the ending -s is an adverbial one, prop. a genitive sign.] 1. On one side. [Obs.] Chaucer. Shak.

besides.c: Besides Be*sides (?), prep. Over and above; separate or distinct from; in addition to; other than; else than. See Beside, prep., 3, and Syn. under Beside.

besiege.c: Besiege Be*siege" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besieged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besieging.] [OE. bisegen; pref. be- + segen to siege. See Siege.] To beset or surround with armed forces, for the purpose of compelling to surrender; to lay siege to; to beleaguer; to beset.

besiegement.c: Besiegement Be*siege"ment (?), n. The act of besieging, or the state of being besieged. Golding.

besieger.c: Besieger Be*sie"ger (?), n. One who besieges; -- opposed to the besieged.

besieging.c: Besieging Be*sie"ging (?), a. That besieges; laying siege to. -- Be*sie"ging*ly, adv.

besit.c: Besit Be*sit" (?), v. t. [Pref. be- + sit.] To suit; to fit; to become. [Obs.]

beslave.c: Beslave Be*slave" (?), v. t. To enslave. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

beslaver.c: Beslaver Be*slav"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beslavered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beslavering.] To defile with slaver; to beslobber.

beslime.c: Beslime Be*slime" (?), v. t. To daub with slime; to soil. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

beslobber.c: Beslobber Be*slob"ber (?), v. t. To slobber on; to smear with spittle running from the mouth. Also Fig.: as, to beslobber with praise.

besmear.c: Besmear Be*smear" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besmeared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besmearing.] To smear with any viscous, glutinous matter; to bedaub; to soil.

besmirch.c: Besmirch Be*smirch" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besmirched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besmirching.] To smirch or soil; to discolor; to obscure. Hence: To dishonor; to sully. Shak.

besmoke.c: Besmoke Be*smoke" (?), v. t. 1. To foul with smoke.

besmut.c: Besmut Be*smut" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besmutted; p. pr. & vb. n. Besmutting.] [Pref. be- + smut: cf. AS. besmītan, and also OE. besmotren.] To blacken with smut; to foul with soot.

besnow.c: Besnow Be*snow" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besnowed (?).] [OE. bisnewen, AS. besnīwan; pref. be- + snīwan to snow.] 1. To scatter like snow; to cover thick, as with snow flakes. [R.] Gower.

besnuff.c: Besnuff Be*snuff" (?), v. t. To befoul with snuff. Young.

besogne.c: Besogne Be*sogne" (?), n. [F. bisogne.] A worthless fellow; a bezonian. [Obs.]

besom.c: Besom Be"som (?), n. [OE. besme, besum, AS. besma; akin to D. bezem, OHG pesamo, G. besen; of uncertain origin.] A brush of twigs for sweeping; a broom; anything which sweeps away or destroys. [Archaic or Fig.]
Besom Be"som, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besomed (?).] To sweep, as with a besom. [Archaic or Poetic] Cowper.

besomer.c: Besomer Be"som*er (?), n. One who uses a besom. [Archaic]

besort.c: Besort Be*sort" (?), v. t. To assort or be congruous with; to fit, or become. [Obs.]
Besort Be*sort", n. Befitting associates or attendants. [Obs.]

besot.c: Besot Be*sot" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besotted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besotting.] To make sottish; to make dull or stupid; to stupefy; to infatuate.

besotted.c: Besotted Be*sot"ted, a. Made sottish, senseless, or infatuated; characterized by drunken stupidity, or by infatuation; stupefied. “Besotted devotion.” Sir W. Scott. -- Be*sot"ted*ly, adv. -- Be*sot"ted*ness, n. Milton.

besottingly.c: Besottingly Be*sot"ting*ly, adv. In a besotting manner.

bespangle.c: Bespangle Be*span"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bespangled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespangling (?).] To adorn with spangles; to dot or sprinkle with something brilliant or glittering.

bespatter.c: Bespatter Be*spat"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bespattered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespattering.] 1. To soil by spattering; to sprinkle, esp. with dirty water, mud, or anything which will leave foul spots or stains.

bespawl.c: Bespawl Be*spawl" (?), v. t. To daub, soil, or make foul with spawl or spittle. [Obs.] Milton.

bespeak.c: Bespeak Be*speak" (?), v. t. [imp. Bespoke (?), Bespake (Archaic); p. p. Bespoke, Bespoken (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespeaking.] [OE. bispeken, AS. besprecan, to speak to, accuse; pref. be- + sprecan to speak. See Speak.] 1. To speak or arrange for beforehand; to order or engage against a future time; as, to bespeak goods, a right, or a favor.
Bespeak Be*speak", v. i. To speak. [Obs.] Milton.
Bespeak Be*speak", n. A bespeaking. Among actors, a benefit (when a particular play is bespoken.) “The night of her bespeak.” Dickens.

bespeckle.c: Bespeckle Be*spec"kle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bespeckled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespeckling.] To mark with speckles or spots. Milton.

bespew.c: Bespew Be*spew" (?), v. t. To soil or daub with spew; to vomit on.

bespice.c: Bespice Be*spice" (?), v. t. To season with spice, or with some spicy drug. Shak.

bespirt.c: Bespirt Be*spirt" (?), v. t. Same as Bespurt.

bespit.c: Bespit Be*spit (be*spĭt"), v. t. [imp. Bespit; p. p. Bespit, Bespitten (-t'n); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespitting.] To daub or soil with spittle. Johnson.

bespoke.c: Bespoke Be*spoke" (be*spōk"), imp. & p. p. of Bespeak.

bespot.c: Bespot Be*spot" (be*spŏt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bespotted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bespotting.] To mark with spots, or as with spots.

bespread.c: Bespread Be*spread" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bespread; p. pr. & vb. n. Bespreading.] To spread or cover over.

besprent.c: Besprent Be*sprent" (?), p. p. [OE. bespreynt, p. p. of besprengen, bisprengen, to besprinkle, AS. besprengan, akin to D. & G. besprengen; pref. be- + sprengan to sprinkle. See Sprinkle.] Sprinkled over; strewed.

besprinkle.c: Besprinkle Be*sprin"kle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Besprinkled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besprinkling (?).] To sprinkle over; to scatter over.

besprinkler.c: Besprinkler Be*sprin"kler (?), n. One who, or that which, besprinkles.

besprinkling.c: Besprinkling Be*sprin"kling (?), n. The act of sprinkling anything; a sprinkling over.

bespurt.c: Bespurt Be*spurt" (?), v. t. To spurt on or over; to asperse. [Obs.] Milton.

bessemer.c: Bessemer steel Bes"se*mer steel` (?). Steel made directly from cast iron, by burning out a portion of the carbon and other impurities that the latter contains, through the agency of a blast of air which is forced through the molten metal; -- so called from Sir Henry Bessemer, an English engineer, the inventor of the process.

best.c: Best Best (bĕst), a.; superl. of Good. [AS. besta, best, contr. from betest, betst, betsta; akin to Goth. batists, OHG. pezzisto, G. best, beste, D. best, Icel. beztr, Dan. best, Sw. bäst. This word has no connection in origin with good. See Better.] 1. Having good qualities in the highest degree; most good, kind, desirable, suitable, etc.; most excellent; as, the best man; the best road; the best cloth; the best abilities.
Best Best, n. Utmost; highest endeavor or state; most nearly perfect thing, or being, or action; as, to do one's best; to the best of our ability.
Best Best, adv.; superl. of Well. 1. In the highest degree; beyond all others. “Thou serpent! That name best befits thee.” Milton.
Best Best, v. t. To get the better of. [Colloq.]

bestad.c: Bestad Be*stad" (?), imp. & p. p. of Bestead. Beset; put in peril. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bestar.c: Bestar Be*star" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestarred (?).] To sprinkle with, or as with, stars; to decorate with, or as with, stars; to bestud. “Bestarred with anemones.” W. Black.

bestead.c: Bestead Be*stead" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestead or Bested, also (Obs.) Bestad. In sense 3 imp. also Besteaded.] [Pref. be- + stead a place.] 1. To put in a certain situation or condition; to circumstance; to place. [Only in p. p.]

bestial.c: Bestial Bes"tial (?), a. [F. bestial, L. bestialis, fr. bestia beast. See Beast.] 1. Belonging to a beast, or to the class of beasts.
Bestial Bes"tial, n. A domestic animal; also collectively, cattle; as, other kinds of bestial. [Scot.]

bestiality.c: Bestiality Bes*tial"i*ty (?), n. [F. bestialité.] 1. The state or quality of being bestial.

bestialize.c: Bestialize Bes"tial*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestialized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bestializing.] To make bestial, or like a beast; to degrade; to brutalize.

bestially.c: Bestially Bes"tial*ly, adv. In a bestial manner.

bestiary.c: Bestiary Bes"ti*a*ry (?), n. [LL. bestiarium, fr. L. bestiarius pert. to beasts, fr. bestia beast: cf. F. bestiaire.] A treatise on beasts; esp., one of the moralizing or allegorical beast tales written in the Middle Ages.

bestick.c: Bestick Be*stick" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestuck (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Besticking.] To stick over, as with sharp points pressed in; to mark by infixing points or spots here and there; to pierce.

bestill.c: Bestill Be*still" (?), v. t. To make still.

bestir.c: Bestir Be*stir" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestirred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bestirring.] To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor; -- usually with the reciprocal pronoun.

bestorm.c: Bestorm Be*storm" (?), v. i. & t. To storm. Young.

bestow.c: Bestow Be*stow" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bestowing.] [OE. bestowen; pref. be- + stow a place. See Stow.] 1. To lay up in store; to deposit for safe keeping; to stow; to place; to put. “He bestowed it in a pouch.” Sir W. Scott.

bestowal.c: Bestowal Be*stow"al (?), n. The act of bestowing; disposal.

bestowment.c: Bestowment Be*stow"ment (?), n. 1. The act of giving or bestowing; a conferring or bestowal.

bestraught.c: Bestraught Be*straught" (?), a. [Pref. be- + straught; prob. here used for distraught.] Out of one's senses; distracted; mad. [Obs.] Shak.

bestrew.c: Bestrew Be*strew" (?), v. t. [imp. Bestrewed (?); p. p. Bestrewed, Bestrown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bestrewing.] To strew or scatter over; to besprinkle. [Spelt also bestrow.] Milton.

bestride.c: Bestride Be*stride" (?), v. t. [imp. Bestrode (?), (Obs. or R.) Bestrid (?); p. p. Bestridden (?), Bestrid, Bestrode; p. pr. & vb. n. Bestriding.] [AS. bestrīdan; pref. be- + strīdan to stride.] 1. To stand or sit with anything between the legs, or with the legs astride; to stand over

bestrode.c: Bestrode Be*strode" (?), imp. & p. p. of Bestride.

bestud.c: Bestud Be*stud" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bestudded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bestudding.] To set or adorn, as with studs or bosses; to set thickly; to stud; as, to bestud with stars. Milton.

beswike.c: Beswike Be*swike", v. t. [AS. beswīcan; be- + swīcan to deceive, entice; akin to OS. swīkan, OHG. swīhhan, Icel. svīkja.] To lure; to cheat. [Obs.] Gower.

bet.c: Bet Bet (?), n. [Prob. from OE. abet abetting, OF. abet, fr. abeter to excite, incite. See Abet.] That which is laid, staked, or pledged, as between two parties, upon the event of a contest or any contingent issue; the act of giving such a pledge; a wager. “Having made his bets.” Goldsmith.
Bet Bet, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bet, Betted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betting.] To stake or pledge upon the event of a contingent issue; to wager.
Bet Bet, imp. & p. p. of Beat. [Obs.]
Bet Bet, a. & adv. An early form of Better. [Obs.]

beta.c: Beta Be"ta (?), n. [Gr. bh^ta.] The second letter of the Greek alphabet, B, β. See B, and cf. etymology of Alphabet.

Beta rays Be"ta rays (?). (Physics) a form of ionizing radiation emitted by radioactive substances (such as radium), more penetrating than alpha rays, and consisting of negatively charged electrons. The electrons are the same kind of particle as those of cathode rays, but have much higher velocities (about 35,000 to 180,000 miles per second). They are readily deflected by a magnetic or electric field.

betacismus.c: Betacismus Betacism { Be"ta*cism (?), ‖Be`ta*cis"mus (?) }, n. Excessive or extended use of the b sound in speech, due to conversion of other sounds into it, as through inability to distinguish them from b, or because of difficulty in pronouncing them.

betaine.c: Betaine Be"ta*ine (?), n. [From beta, generic name of the beet.] (Chem.) A nitrogenous base, C5H11NO2, produced artificially, and also occurring naturally in beet-root molasses and its residues, from which it is extracted as a white crystalline substance; -- called also lycine and oxyneurine. It has a sweetish taste.

betake.c: Betake Be*take" (?), v. t. [imp. Betook (?); p. p. Betaken (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betaking.] [Pref. be- + take.] 1. To take or seize. [Obs.] Spenser.

betaught.c: Betaught Be*taught" (be*tät"),a. [p. p. of OE. bitechen, AS. betǣcan, to assign, deliver. See Teach.] Delivered; committed in trust. [Obs.]

beteela.c: Beteela Be*tee"la (?), n. [Pg. beatilha.] An East India muslin, formerly used for cravats, veils, etc. [Obs.]

beteem.c: Beteem Be*teem" (?), v. t. [Pref. be- + an old verb teem to be fitting; cf. D. betamen to beseem, G. ziemen, Goth. gatiman, and E. tame. See Tame, a.] 1. To give; to bestow; to grant; to accord; to consent. [Obs.] Spenser. Milton.

betel.c: Betel Be"tel (bē"t'l), n. [Pg., fr. Tamil veṭṭilei, prop. meaning, a mere leaf.] (Bot.) A species of pepper (Piper betle), the leaves of which are chewed, with the areca or betel nut and a little shell lime, by the inhabitants of the East Indies. It is a woody climber with ovate many-nerved leaves.
Betel nut Be"tel nut` (?). The nutlike seed of the areca palm, chewed in the East with betel leaves (whence its name) and shell lime.

betelguese.c: Betelguese Bet"el*guese (bĕt"ĕl*jēz), n. [F. Bételgeuse, of Arabic origin.] (Astron.) A bright star of the first magnitude, near one shoulder of Orion. [Written also Betelgeux and Betelgeuse.]

bethabara.c: Bethabara wood Beth*ab"a*ra wood` (?). (Bot.) A highly elastic wood, used for fishing rods, etc. The tree is unknown, but it is thought to be East Indian.

bethel.c: Bethel Beth"el (bĕth"ĕl), n. [Heb. bēth-el house of God.]

bethink.c: Bethink Be*think" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bethought (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bethinking.] [AS. beþencan; pref. be- + þencan to think. See Think.] To call to mind; to recall or bring to recollection, reflection, or consideration; to think; to consider; -- generally followed by a reflexive pronoun, often with of or that before the subject of thought.
Bethink Be*think", v. i. To think; to recollect; to consider. “Bethink ere thou dismiss us.” Byron.

bethlehem.c: Bethlehem Beth"le*hem (?), n. [Heb. bēth-lekhem house of food; bēth house + lekhem food, lākham to eat. Formerly the name of a hospital for the insane, in London, which had been the priory of St. Mary of Bethlehem. Cf. Bedlam.] 1. A hospital for lunatics; -- corrupted into bedlam.

bethlemite.c: Bethlemite Bethlehemite { Beth"le*hem*ite (?), Beth"lem*ite (?), } n. 1. An inhabitant of Bethlehem in Judea.

bethought.c: Bethought Be*thought" (?), imp. & p. p. of Bethink.

bethrall.c: Bethrall Be*thrall" (?), v. t. To reduce to thralldom; to inthrall. [Obs.] Spenser.

bethumb.c: Bethumb Be*thumb" (?), v. t. To handle; to wear or soil by handling; as books. Poe.

bethump.c: Bethump Be*thump" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bethumped (?), or Bethumpt; p. pr. & vb. n. Bethumping.] To beat or thump soundly. Shak.

betide.c: Betide Be*tide" (be*tīd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betided (?), Obs. Betid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betiding.] [OE. bitiden; pref. bi-, be- + tiden, fr. AS. tīdan, to happen, fr. tīd time. See Tide.] To happen to; to befall; to come to; as, woe betide the wanderer.
Betide Be*tide", v. i. To come to pass; to happen; to occur.

betimes.c: Betimes Betime { Be*time" (?), Be*times" (?), } adv. [Pref. be- (for by) + time; that is, by the proper time. The -s is an adverbial ending.] 1. In good season or time; before it is late; seasonably; early.

betitle.c: Betitle Be*ti"tle (?), v. t. To furnish with a title or titles; to entitle. [Obs.] Carlyle.

betoken.c: Betoken Be*to"ken (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betokened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betokening.] 1. To signify by some visible object; to show by signs or tokens.

beton.c: Beton ‖Bé`ton" (?), n. [F. béton, fr. L. bitumen bitumen.] (Masonry) The French name for concrete; hence, concrete made after the French fashion.

betongue.c: Betongue Be*tongue" (?), v. t. To attack with the tongue; to abuse; to insult.

betony.c: Betony Bet"o*ny (?), n.; pl. Betonies (?). [OE. betony, betany, F. betoine, fr. L. betonica, vettonica.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Betonica (Linn.).

betorn.c: Betorn Be*torn" (?), a. Torn in pieces; tattered.

betoss.c: Betoss Be*toss (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betossed (?).] To put in violent motion; to agitate; to disturb; to toss. “My betossed soul.” Shak.

betrap.c: Betrap Be*trap" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betrapped (?).] 1. To draw into, or catch in, a trap; to insnare; to circumvent. Gower.

betray.c: Betray Be*tray" (be*trā"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betrayed (-trād"); p. pr. & vb. n. Betraying.] [OE. betraien, bitraien; pref. be- + OF. traïr to betray, F. trahir, fr. L. tradere. See Traitor.] 1. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; to give up treacherously or faithlessly; as, an officer betrayed the city.

betrayal.c: Betrayal Be*tray"al (?) n. The act or the result of betraying.

betrayer.c: Betrayer Be*tray"er (?), n. One who, or that which, betrays.

betrim.c: Betrim Be*trim" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betrimmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betrimming.] To set in order; to adorn; to deck, to embellish; to trim. Shak.

betroth.c: Betroth Be*troth" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betrothed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Betrothing.] [Pref. be- + troth, i. e., truth. See Truth.] 1. To contract to any one for a marriage; to engage or promise in order to marriage; to affiance; -- used esp. of a woman.

betrothal.c: Betrothal Be*troth"al (?), n. The act of betrothing, or the fact of being betrothed; a mutual promise, engagement, or contract for a future marriage between the persons betrothed; betrothment; affiance. “The feast of betrothal.” Longfellow.

betrothment.c: Betrothment Be*troth"ment (?), n. The act of betrothing, or the state of being betrothed; betrothal.

betrust.c: Betrust Be*trust" (?), v. t. To trust or intrust. [Obs.]

betrustment.c: Betrustment Be*trust"ment (?), n. The act of intrusting, or the thing intrusted. [Obs.] Chipman.

betso.c: Betso ‖Bet"so (?), n. [It. bezzo.] A small brass Venetian coin. [Obs.]

better.c: Better Bet"ter (?), a.; compar. of Good. [OE. betere, bettre, and as adv. bet, AS. betera, adj., and bet, adv.; akin to Icel. betri, adj., betr, adv., Goth. batiza, adj., OHG. bezziro, adj., baz, adv., G. besser, adj. and adv., bass, adv., E. boot, and prob. to Skr. bhadra excellent. See Boot advantage, and cf. Best, Batful.] 1. Having good qualities in a greater degree than another; as, a better man; a better physician; a better house; a better air.
Better Bet"ter, n. 1. Advantage, superiority, or victory; -- usually with of; as, to get the better of an enemy.

Better Bet"ter, adv.; compar. of Well. 1. In a superior or more excellent manner; with more skill and wisdom, courage, virtue, advantage, or success; as, Henry writes better than John; veterans fight better than recruits.

Better Bet"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bettered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bettering.] [AS. beterian, betrian, fr. betera better. See Better, a.] 1. To improve or ameliorate; to increase the good qualities of.
Better Bet"ter, v. i. To become better; to improve. Carlyle.
Better Bet"ter, n. One who bets or lays a wager.

betterment.c: Betterment Bet"ter*ment (?), n. 1. A making better; amendment; improvement. W. Montagu.

bettermost.c: Bettermost Bet"ter*most` (?), a. Best. [R.] “The bettermost classes.” Brougham.

betterness.c: Betterness Bet"ter*ness, n. 1. The quality of being better or superior; superiority. [R.] Sir P. Sidney.

bettong.c: Bettong ‖Bet"tong (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A small, leaping Australian marsupial of the genus Bettongia; the jerboa kangaroo.

bettor.c: Bettor Bet"tor (?), n. One who bets; a better. Addison.

betty.c: Betty Bet"ty (?), n. 1. [Supposed to be a cant word, from Betty, for Elizabeth, as such an instrument is also called Bess (i. e., Elizabeth) in the Canting Dictionary of 1725, and Jenny (i. e., Jane).] A short bar used by thieves to wrench doors open. [Written also bettee.]

betulin.c: Betulin Bet"u*lin (?), n. [L. betula birch tree.] (Chem.) a term originally applied to a substance obtained as a resin or tar by extraction from the outer bark of the common European white birch (Betula alba); now referring to the chemical compound (C30H50O2) having a cyclopentanophenanthrene ring system, which is the main constituent of that extract, and which may be obtained crystalline; -- called also birch camphor. Watts.

betumble.c: Betumble Be*tum"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betumbled (?).] To throw into disorder; to tumble. [R.]

betutor.c: Betutor Be*tu"tor (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Betutored (?).] To tutor; to instruct. Coleridge.
