between.c: Between Be*tween" (?), prep. [OE. bytwene, bitweonen, AS. betweónan, betweónum; prefix be- by + a form fr. AS. twā two, akin to Goth. tweihnai two apiece. See Twain, and cf. Atween, Betwixt.] 1. In the space which separates; betwixt; as, New York is between Boston and Philadelphia.
Between Be*tween", n. Intermediate time or space; interval. [Poetic & R.] Shak.

betwixt.c: Betwixt Be*twixt" (?), prep. [OE. betwix, bitwix, rarely bitwixt, AS. betweox, betweohs, betweoh, betwīh; pref. be- by + a form fr. AS. twā two. See Between.]

beurre.c: Beurre ‖Beur*ré" (?), n. [F., fr. beurre butter.] (Bot.) A beurré (or buttery) pear, one with the meat soft and melting; -- used with a distinguishing word; as, Beurré d'Anjou; Beurré Clairgeau.

bevel.c: Bevel Bev"el (?), n. [C. F. biveau, earlier buveau, Sp. baivel; of unknown origin. Cf. Bevile.] 1. Any angle other than a right angle; the angle which one surface makes with another when they are not at right angles; the slant or inclination of such surface; as, to give a bevel to the edge of a table or a stone slab; the bevel of a piece of timber.
Bevel Bev"el, a. 1. Having the slant of a bevel; slanting.
Bevel Bev"el, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Beveled (?) or Bevelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Beveling or Bevelling.] To cut to a bevel angle; to slope the edge or surface of.
Bevel Bev"el, v. i. To deviate or incline from an angle of 90°, as a surface; to slant.

Bevel gear Bev"el gear` (?). (Mech.) A kind of gear in which the two wheels working together lie in different planes, and have their teeth cut at right angles to the surfaces of two cones whose apices coincide with the point where the axes of the wheels would meet.

bevelled.c: Bevelled Beveled { Bev"eled, Bev"elled } (?), a. 1. Formed to a bevel angle; sloping; as, the beveled edge of a table.

bevelment.c: Bevelment Bev"el*ment (?), n. (Min.) The replacement of an edge by two similar planes, equally inclined to the including faces or adjacent planes.

bever.c: Bever Be"ver (?), n. [OE. bever a drink, drinking time, OF. beivre, boivre, to drink, fr. L. bibere.] A light repast between meals; a lunch. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
Bever Be"ver, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bevered (?).] To take a light repast between meals. [Obs.]

beverage.c: Beverage Bev"er*age (?), n. [OF. bevrage, F. breuvage, fr. beivre to drink, fr. L. bibere. Cf. Bib, v. t., Poison, Potable.] 1. Liquid for drinking; drink; -- usually applied to drink artificially prepared and of an agreeable flavor; as, an intoxicating beverage.

bevile.c: Bevile Bev"ile (?), n. [See Bevel.] (Her.) A chief broken or opening like a carpenter's bevel. Encyc. Brit.

bevilled.c: Bevilled Beviled { Bev"iled, Bev"illed } (?), a. (Her.) Notched with an angle like that inclosed by a carpenter's bevel; -- said of a partition line of a shield.

bevy.c: Bevy Bev"y (?), n.; pl. Bevies (?). [Perhaps orig. a drinking company, fr. OF. bevée (cf. It. beva) a drink, beverage; then, perh., a company in general, esp. of ladies; and last applied by sportsmen to larks, quails, etc. See Beverage.] 1. A company; an assembly or collection of persons, especially of ladies.

bewail.c: Bewail Be*wail" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bewailing.] To express deep sorrow for, as by wailing; to lament; to wail over.
Bewail Be*wail", v. i. To express grief; to lament. Shak.

bewailable.c: Bewailable Be*wail"a*ble (?), a. Such as may, or ought to, be bewailed; lamentable.

bewailer.c: Bewailer Be*wail"er (?), n. One who bewails or laments.

bewailing.c: Bewailing Be*wail"ing, a. Wailing over; lamenting. -- Be*wail"ing*ly, adv.

bewailment.c: Bewailment Be*wail"ment (?), n. The act of bewailing.

bewake.c: Bewake Be*wake" (?), v. t. & i. To keep watch over; to keep awake. [Obs.] Gower.

beware.c: Beware Be*ware" (?), v. i. [Be, imperative of verb to be + ware. See Ware, Wary.] 1. To be on one's guard; to be cautious; to take care; -- commonly followed by of or lest before the thing that is to be avoided.
Beware Be*ware" (be*wâr"), v. t. To avoid; to take care of; to have a care for. [Obs.] “Priest, beware your beard.” Shak.

bewash.c: Bewash Be*wash" (?), v. t. To drench or souse with water. “Let the maids bewash the men.” Herrick.

beweep.c: Beweep Be*weep" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewept (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Beweeping.] [AS. bew?pan; pref. be- + weep.] To weep over; to deplore; to bedew with tears. “His timeless death beweeping.” Drayton.
Beweep Be*weep", v. i. To weep. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bewet.c: Bewet Be*wet" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewet, Bewetted.] To wet or moisten. Gay.

bewhore.c: Bewhore Be*whore" (?), v. t. 1. To corrupt with regard to chastity; to make a whore of. J. Fletcher.

bewig.c: Bewig Be*wig" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewigged (?).] To cover (the head) with a wig. Hawthorne.

bewilder.c: Bewilder Be*wil"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewildered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bewildering.] [Pref. be- + wilder.] To lead into perplexity or confusion, as for lack of a plain path; to perplex with mazes; or in general, to perplex or confuse greatly.

bewildered.c: Bewildered Be*wil"dered (?), a. Greatly perplexed; as, a bewildered mind.

bewilderedness.c: Bewilderedness Be*wil"dered*ness (?), n. The state of being bewildered; bewilderment. [R.]

bewildering.c: Bewildering Be*wil"der*ing (?), a. Causing bewilderment or great perplexity; as, bewildering difficulties. -- Be*wil"der*ing*ly, adv.

bewilderment.c: Bewilderment Be*wil"der*ment (?), n. 1. The state of being bewildered.

bewinter.c: Bewinter Be*win"ter (?), v. t. To make wintry. [Obs.]

bewit.c: Bewit Bew"it (?), n. [Cf. OF. buie bond, chain, fr. L. boja neck collar, fetter. Cf. Buoy.] A double slip of leather by which bells are fastened to a hawk's legs.

bewitch.c: Bewitch Be*witch" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewitched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bewitching.] 1. To gain an ascendency over by charms or incantations; to affect (esp. to injure) by witchcraft or sorcery.

bewitchedness.c: Bewitchedness Be*witch"ed*ness (?), n. The state of being bewitched. Gauden.

bewitchery.c: Bewitchery Be*witch"er*y (?), n. The power of bewitching or fascinating; bewitchment; charm; fascination.

bewitching.c: Bewitching Be*witch"ing, a. Having power to bewitch or fascinate; enchanting; captivating; charming. -- Be*witch"ing*ly, adv. -- Be*witch"ing*ness, n.

bewitchment.c: Bewitchment Be*witch"ment (?), n. 1. The act of bewitching, or the state of being bewitched. Tylor.

bewonder.c: Bewonder Be*won"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewondered (?).] 1. To fill with wonder. [Obs.]

bewrap.c: Bewrap Be*wrap" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewrapped (?).] To wrap up; to cover. Fairfax.

bewray.c: Bewray Be*wray" (be*rā"), v. t. To soil. See Beray.

Bewray Be*wray", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bewrayed (-rād"); p. pr. & vb. n. Bewraying.] [OE. bewraien, biwreyen; pref. be- + AS. wrēgan to accuse, betray; akin to OS. wrōgian, OHG. ruogēn, G. rügen, Icel. rægja, Goth. wrōhjan to accuse.] To expose; to reveal; to disclose; to betray. [Obs. or Archaic]

bewrayer.c: Bewrayer Be*wray"er (-ẽr), n. One who, or that which, bewrays; a revealer. [Obs. or Archaic] Addison.

bewreke.c: Bewreke Be*wreke" (?), v. t. [Pref. be- + wreak.] To wreak; to avenge. [Obs.] Ld. Berners.

bewrought.c: Bewrought Be*wrought" (?), a. [Pref. be- + wrought, p. p. of work, v. t. ] Embroidered. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

bey.c: Bey Bey (bā), n. [See Beg a bey.] A governor of a province or district in the Turkish dominions; also, in some places, a prince or nobleman; a beg; as, the bey of Tunis.

beylic.c: Beylic Bey"lic (?), n. [Turk.] The territory ruled by a bey.

beyond.c: Beyond Be*yond" (?), prep. [OE. biyonde, biȝeonde, AS. begeondan, prep. and adv.; pref. be- + geond yond, yonder. See Yon, Yonder.] 1. On the further side of; in the same direction as, and further on or away than.
Beyond Be*yond" (?), adv. Further away; at a distance; yonder.

bezant.c: Bezant Be*zant" (?), n. [See Byzant.] 1. A gold coin of Byzantium or Constantinople, varying in weight and value, usually (those current in England) between a sovereign and a half sovereign. There were also white or silver bezants. [Written also besant, byzant, etc.]

bezantler.c: Bez-antler Bez`-ant"ler (?), n. [L. bis twice (OF. bes) + E. antler.] The second branch of a stag's horn.

bezel.c: Bezel Bez"el (bĕz"ĕl), n. [From an old form of F. biseau sloping edge, prob. fr. L. bis double. See Bi-.] The rim which encompasses and fastens a jewel or other object, as the crystal of a watch, in the cavity in which it is set.

bezique.c: Bezique Bé*zique" (ba*zēk"), n. [F. bésigue.] A game at cards in which various combinations of cards in the hand, when declared, score points.

bezoar.c: Bezoar Be"zoar (?), n. [F. bézoard, fr. Ar. bāzahr, bādizahr, fr. Per. pād-zahr bezoar; pād protecting + zahr poison; cf. Pg. & Sp. bezoar.] A calculous concretion found in the intestines of certain ruminant animals (as the wild goat, the gazelle, and the Peruvian llama) formerly regarded as an unfailing antidote for poison, and a certain remedy for eruptive, pestilential, or putrid diseases. Hence: Any antidote or panacea.

bezoardic.c: Bezoardic Bez`o*ar"dic (?), a. [Cf. F. bézoardique, bézoartique.] Pertaining to, or compounded with, bezoar. -- n. A medicine containing bezoar.

bezoartical.c: Bezoartical Bezoartic { Bez`o*ar"tic (?), Bez`o*ar"tic*al (?), } a. [See Bezoardic.] Having the qualities of an antidote, or of bezoar; healing. [Obs.]

bezonian.c: Bezonian Be*zo"ni*an (?), n. [Cf. F. besoin need, want, It bisogno.] A low fellow or scoundrel; a beggar.

bezpopovtsy.c: Bezpopovtsy ‖Bez`po*pov"tsy (?), n. [Russ.; bez without + popovtsy, a derivative of pop priest.] A Russian sect. See Raskolnik.

bezzle.c: Bezzle Bez"zle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bezzled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bezzling (?).] [OF. besillier, besiler, to maltreat, pillage; or shortened fr. embezzle. Cf. Embezzle.] To plunder; to waste in riot. [Obs.]
Bezzle Bez"zle, v. i. To drink to excess; to revel. [Obs.]

bhang.c: Bhang Bhang (?), n. [Per. bang; cf. Skr. bhangā hemp.] An astringent and narcotic drug made from the dried leaves and seed capsules of wild hemp (Cannabis Indica), and chewed or smoked in the East as a means of intoxication. See Hasheesh.

bheestie.c: Bheestie Bheesty { Bhees"ty, Bhees"tie (?) }, n. [Written also bhistee, bhisti, etc.] [Per. bihishtī lit., heavenly.] A water carrier, as to a household or a regiment. [India]

bhisti.c: Bhisti Bhistee { Bhis"tee (?), Bhis"ti (?) }, n. Same as Bheesty. [India]

bhunder.c: Bhunder ‖Bhun"der (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) An Indian monkey (Macacus Rhesus), protected by the Hindus as sacred. See Rhesus.

bi.c: Bi- Bi- (?). [L. bis twice, which in composition drops the -s, akin to E. two. See Bis-, Two, and cf. Di-, Dis-.]

biacid.c: Biacid Bi*ac"id (?), a. [Pref. bi- + acid.] (Chem.) Having two hydrogen atoms which can be replaced by negative atoms or radicals to form salts; -- said of bases. See Diacid.

biacuminate.c: Biacuminate Bi`a*cu"mi*nate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + acuminate.] (Bot.) Having points in two directions.

biangular.c: Biangular Bi*an"gu*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + angular.] Having two angles or corners.

biangulated.c: Biangulated Biangulate { Bi*an"gu*late (?), Bi*an"gu*la`ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + angulate, angulated.] Biangular.

biannual.c: Biannual Bi*an"nu*al (?), a. [Pref. bi- + annual.] Occurring twice a year; half-yearly; semiannual.

biantheriferous.c: Biantheriferous Bi*an`ther*if"er*ous (?), a. [Pref. bi- + antherigerous.] (Bot.) Having two anthers.

biarticulate.c: Biarticulate Bi`ar*tic"u*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + articulate.] (Zool.) Having, or consisting of, tow joints.

bias.c: Bias Bi"as (bī"ais), n.; pl. Biases (-ĕz). [F. biasis, perh. fr. LL. bifax two-faced; L. bis + facies face. See Bi-, and cf. Face.] 1. A weight on the side of the ball used in the game of bowls, or a tendency imparted to the ball, which turns it from a straight line.
Bias Bi"as, a. 1. Inclined to one side; swelled on one side. [Obs.] Shak.
Bias Bi"as, adv. In a slanting manner; crosswise; obliquely; diagonally; as, to cut cloth bias.
Bias Bi"as, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Biased (bī"aist); p. pr. & vb. n. Biasing.] To incline to one side; to give a particular direction to; to influence; to prejudice; to prepossess.

biauriculate.c: Biauriculate Bi`au*ric"u*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + auriculate.] 1. (Anat.) Having two auricles, as the heart of mammals, birds, and reptiles.

biaxial.c: Biaxial Biaxal { Bi*ax"al (?), Bi*ax"i*al (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + axal, axial.] (Opt.) Having two axes; as, biaxial polarization; biaxial crystals. Brewster. -- Bi*ax"i*al*ly, adv.

bib.c: Bib Bib (?), n. [From Bib, v., because the bib receives the drink that the child slavers from the mouth.] 1. A small piece of cloth worn by children over the breast, to protect the clothes.
Bib Bib, v. i. To drink; to sip; to tipple.

bibbe.c: Bibbe Bib { Bib, Bibbe } (?), v. t. [L. bibere. See Beverage, and cf. Imbibe.] To drink; to tipple. [Obs.]

bibacious.c: Bibacious Bi*ba"cious (?), a. [L. bibax, bibacis, fr. bibere. See Bib.] Addicted to drinking.

bibacity.c: Bibacity Bi*bac"i*ty (?), n. The practice or habit of drinking too much; tippling. Blount.

bibasic.c: Bibasic Bi*ba"sic (?), a. [Pref. bi- + basic.] (Chem.) Having to hydrogen atoms which can be replaced by positive or basic atoms or radicals to form salts; -- said of acids. See Dibasic.

bibb.c: Bibb Bibb (bĭb), n. A bibcock. See Bib, n., 3.

bibber.c: Bibber Bib"ber (?), n. One given to drinking alcoholic beverages too freely; a tippler; -- chiefly used in composition; as, winebibber.

bibblebabble.c: Bibble-babble Bib"ble-bab"ble (?), n. [A reduplication of babble.] Idle talk; babble. Shak.

bibbs.c: Bibbs Bibbs (bĭbz), n. pl. (Naut.) Pieces of timber bolted to certain parts of a mast to support the trestletrees.

bibcock.c: Bibcock Bib"cock` (bĭb"kŏk), n. A cock or faucet having a bent down nozzle. Knight.

bibelot.c: Bibelot ‖Bi`be*lot" (?), n. [F.] A small decorative object without practical utility.

bibitory.c: Bibitory Bib"i*to*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to drinking or tippling.

bible.c: Bible Bi"ble (bī"b'l), n. [F. bible, L. biblia, pl., fr. Gr. bibli`a, pl. of bibli`on, dim. of bi`blos, by`blos, book, prop. Egyptian papyrus.] 1. A book. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bibler.c: Bibler Bib"ler (bĭb"lẽr), n. [See Bib, v. t.] A great drinker; a tippler. [Written also bibbler and bibbeler.]

biblical.c: Biblical Bib"li*cal (bĭb"lĭ*kail), a. Pertaining to, or derived from, the Bible; as, biblical learning; biblical authority.

biblicality.c: Biblicality Bib`li*cal"i*ty (-kăl"ĭ*ty̆), n. The quality of being biblical; a biblical subject. [R.]

biblically.c: Biblically Bib"li*cal*ly (?), adv. According to the Bible.

biblicism.c: Biblicism Bib"li*cism (?), n. [Cf. F. biblicisme.] Learning or literature relating to the Bible. [R.]

biblicist.c: Biblicist Bib"li*cist (?), n. One skilled in the knowledge of the Bible; a demonstrator of religious truth by the Scriptures.

bibliographer.c: Bibliographer Bib`li*og"ra*pher (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? book +? to write: cf. F. bibliographe.] One who writes, or is versed in, bibliography.

bibliographical.c: Bibliographical Bibliographic { Bib`li*o*graph"ic (?), Bib`li*o*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. bibliographique.] Pertaining to bibliography, or the history of books. -- Bib`li*o*graph"ic*al*ly, adv.

bibliography.c: Bibliography Bib`li*og"ra*phy (bĭb`lĭ*ŏg"rȧ*fy̆) n.; pl. Bibliographies (?). [Gr. bibliografi`a: cf. F. bibliographie.] 1. a history or description of books and manuscripts, with notices of the different editions, the times when they were printed, etc.

bibliolatrist.c: Bibliolatrist Bibliolater { Bib`li*ol"a*ter (bĭb`lĭ*ŏl"ȧ*tẽr), Bib`li*ol"a*trist (bĭb`lĭ*ŏl"ȧ*trĭst), } n. [See. Bibliolatry.] A worshiper of books; especially, a worshiper of the Bible; a believer in its verbal inspiration. De Quincey.

bibliolatry.c: Bibliolatry Bib`li*ol"a*try (bĭb`lĭ*ŏl"ȧ*try̆), n. [Gr. bibli`on book + latrei`a service, worship, latrey`ein to serve.] Book worship, esp. of the Bible; -- applied by Roman Catholic divines to the exaltation of the authority of the Bible over that of the pope or the church, and by Protestants to an excessive regard to the letter of the Scriptures. Coleridge. F. W. Newman.

bibliomancy.c: Bibliomancy Bib"li*o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr.? book + -mancy: cf. F. bibliomancie.] A kind of divination, performed by selecting passages of Scripture at hazard, and drawing from them indications concerning future events.

bibliomania.c: Bibliomania Bib`li*o*ma"ni*a (?), n. [Gr.? book +? madness: cf. F. bibliomanie.] A mania for acquiring books.

bibliomaniac.c: Bibliomaniac Bib`li*o*ma"ni*ac (?), n. One who has a mania for books. -- a. Relating to a bibliomaniac.

bibliomaniacal.c: Bibliomaniacal Bib`li*o*ma*ni"ac*al (?), a. Pertaining to a passion for books; relating to a bibliomaniac.

bibliopegic.c: Bibliopegic Bib`li*o*peg"ic (-pĕj"ĭk), a. [Gr. bibli`on book + phgny`naito make fast.] Relating to the binding of books. [R.]

bibliopegistic.c: Bibliopegistic Bib`li*op`e*gis"tic (bĭb`lĭ*ŏp`e*jĭs"tĭk), a. Pertaining to the art of binding books. [R.] Dibdin.

bibliopegy.c: Bibliopegy Bib`li*op"e*gy (?), n. [See Bibliopegic.] The art of binding books. [R.]

bibliophile.c: Bibliophile Bib"li*o*phile (?), n. [Gr.? book +? to love: cf. F. bibliophile.] A lover of books.

bibliophilist.c: Bibliophilist Bib`li*oph"i*list (?), n. A lover of books.

bibliophobia.c: Bibliophobia Bib`li*o*pho"bi*a (?), n. [Gr.? book +? to fear.] A dread of books. [R.]

bibliopole.c: Bibliopole Bib"li*o*pole (?), n. [L. bibliopola, Gr.?;? book +? to sell: cf. F. bibliopole.] One who sells books.

bibliopolar.c: Bibliopolar Bibliopolic { Bib`li*o*pol"ic (?), Bib`li*op"o*lar } (?), a. [See Bibliopole.] Of or pertaining to the sale of books. “Bibliopolic difficulties.” Carlyle.

bibliopolism.c: Bibliopolism Bib`li*op"o*lism (?), n. The trade or business of selling books.

bibliopolistic.c: Bibliopolistic Bib`li*op`o*lis"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to bibliopolism. Dibdin.

bibliotaphist.c: Bibliotaphist Bibliotaph { Bib"li*o*taph (?), Bib`li*ot"a*phist (?), } n. [Gr.? book +? a burial.] One who hides away books, as in a tomb. [R.] Crabb.

bibliothecal.c: Bibliothecal Bib`li*o*the"cal (?), a. [L. bibliothecalis. See Bibliotheke.] Belonging to a library. Byrom.

bibliothecary.c: Bibliothecary Bib`li*oth"e*ca*ry (?), n. [L. bibliothecarius: cf. F. bibliothécaire.] A librarian. [Obs.] Evelin.

bibliotheke.c: Bibliotheke Bib"li*o*theke (?), n. [L. bibliotheca, Gr.?;? book +? a case, box, fr.? to place: cf. F. bibliothèque.] A library. [Obs.] Bale.

biblist.c: Biblist Bib"list (?), n. [Cf. F. bibliste. See Bible.]

bibracteate.c: Bibracteate Bi*brac"te*ate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + bracteate.] (Bot.) Furnished with, or having, two bracts.

bibulous.c: Bibulous Bib"u*lous (?), a. [L. bibulus, fr. bibere to drink. See Bib, v. t. ] 1. Readily imbibing fluids or moisture; spongy; as, bibulous blotting paper.

bibulously.c: Bibulously Bib"u*lous*ly, adv. In a bibulous manner; with profuse imbibition or absorption. De Quincey.

bicalcarate.c: Bicalcarate Bi*cal"ca*rate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + calcarate.] Having two spurs, as the wing or leg of a bird.

bicallous.c: Bicallous Bicallose { Bi*cal"lose (?), Bi*cal"lous (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + callose, callous.] (Bot.) Having two callosities or hard spots. Gray.

bicameral.c: Bicameral Bi*cam"er*al (?), a. [Pref. bi- + camera.] Consisting of, or including, two chambers, or legislative branches. Bentham.

bicapsular.c: Bicapsular Bi*cap"su*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + capsular: cf. F. bicapsulaire.] (Bot.) Having two capsules; as, a bicapsular pericarp.

bicarbonate.c: Bicarbonate Bi*car"bon*ate (?), n. [Pref. bi- + carbonate.] (Chem.) A carbonate in which but half the hydrogen of the acid is replaced by a positive element or radical, thus making the proportion of the acid to the positive or basic portion twice what it is in the normal carbonates; an acid carbonate; -- sometimes called supercarbonate.

bicarinate.c: Bicarinate Bi*car"i*nate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + carinate.] (Biol.) Having two keel-like projections, as the upper palea of grasses.

bicaudal.c: Bicaudal Bi*cau"dal (?), a. [Pref. bi- + caudal.] Having, or terminating in, two tails.

bicaudate.c: Bicaudate Bi*cau"date (?), a. [Pref. bi- + caudate.] Two-tailed; bicaudal.

bicched.c: Bicched Bic"ched (?), a. [Of unknown origin.] Pecked; pitted; notched. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bise.c: Bise Bice { Bice, Bise } (?), n. [F. bis, akin to It. bigio light gray, tawny.] (Paint.) A pale blue pigment, prepared from the native blue carbonate of copper, or from smalt; -- called also blue bice.
Bise ‖Bise (?), n. [F.] A cold north wind which prevails on the northern coasts of the Mediterranean and in Switzerland, etc.; -- nearly the same as the mistral.

bicentenary.c: Bicentenary Bi*cen"te*na*ry (?), a. [Pref. bi- + centenary.] Of or pertaining to two hundred, esp. to two hundred years; as, a bicentenary celebration. -- n. The two hundredth anniversary, or its celebration.

bicentennial.c: Bicentennial Bi`cen*ten"ni*al, a. [Pref. bi- + centennial.] 1. Consisting of two hundred years.
Bicentennial Bi`cen*ten"ni*al, n. The two hundredth year or anniversary, or its celebration.

bicephalous.c: Bicephalous Bi*ceph"a*lous (?), a. [Pref. bi- + cephalous: cf. F. bicéphale.] Having two heads.

biceps.c: Biceps ‖Bi"ceps (?), n. [L., two-headed; bis twice + caput head. See Capital.] (Anat.) A muscle having two heads or origins; -- applied particularly to a flexor in the arm, and to another in the thigh.

bichir.c: Bichir ‖Bi*chir" (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A remarkable ganoid fish (Polypterus bichir) found in the Nile and other African rivers. See Brachioganoidei.

bichloride.c: Bichloride Bi*chlo"ride (?), n. [Pref. bi- + chloride.] (Chem.) A compound consisting of two atoms of chlorine with one or more atoms of another element; -- called also dichloride.

bichromate.c: Bichromate Bi*chro"mate (?), n. [Pref. bi- + chromate.] (Chem.) A salt containing two parts of chromic acid to one of the other ingredients; as, potassium bichromate; -- called also dichromate.

bichromatize.c: Bichromatize Bi*chro"ma*tize (?), v. t. To combine or treat with a bichromate, esp. with bichromate of potassium; as, bichromatized gelatine.

bicipital.c: Bicipital Bi*cip"i*tal (?), a. [L. biceps, bicipitis: cf. F. bicipital. See Biceps.] 1. (Anat.) (a) Having two heads or origins, as a muscle. (b) Pertaining to a biceps muscle; as, bicipital furrows, the depressions on either side of the biceps of the arm.

bicipitous.c: Bicipitous Bi*cip"i*tous (?), a. Having two heads; bicipital. “Bicipitous serpents.” Sir T. Browne.

bicker.c: Bicker Bick"er, n. [See Beaker.] A small wooden vessel made of staves and hoops, like a tub. [Prov. Eng.]

Bicker Bick"er (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bickered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bickering.] [OE. bikeren, perh. fr. Celtic; cf. W. bicra to fight, bicker, bicre conflict, skirmish; perh. akin to E. beak.] 1. To skirmish; to exchange blows; to fight. [Obs.]
Bicker Bick"er, n. 1. A skirmish; an encounter. [Obs.]

bickering.c: Bickering Bick"er*ing, n. 1. A skirmishing. “Frays and bickerings.” Milton.

bickern.c: Bickern Bick"ern (?), n. [F. bigorne. See Bicorn.] An anvil ending in a beak or point (orig. in two beaks); also, the beak or horn itself.

bickford.c: Bickford match Bickford fuze Bickford fuse { Bick"ford fuse or Bick"ford fuze, or Bickford match (?) }. A fuse used in blasting, consisting of a long cylinder of explosive material inclosed in a varnished wrapping of rope or hose. It burns from 2 to 4 feet a minute.

bicolligate.c: Bicolligate Bi*col"li*gate (?), a. [L. bis twice + colligatus, p. p. See Colligate, v. t. ] (Zool.) Having the anterior toes connected by a basal web.

bicolored.c: Bicolored Bicolor { Bi"col`or (?), Bi"col`ored (?), } a. [L. bicolor; bis twice + color color.] Of two colors.

biconcave.c: Biconcave Bi*con"cave (?), a. [Pref. bi- + concave.] Concave on both sides; as, biconcave vertebræ.

biconjugate.c: Biconjugate Bi*con"ju*gate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + conjugate, a.] (Bot.) Twice paired, as when a petiole forks twice. Gray.

biconvex.c: Biconvex Bi*con"vex (?), a. [Pref. bi- + convex.] Convex on both sides; as, a biconvex lens.

bicornous.c: Bicornous Bicorned Bicorn { Bi"corn (?), Bi"corned (?), Bi*cor"nous (?), } a. [L. bicornis; bis twice + cornu horn: cf. F. bicorne. Cf. Bickern.] Having two horns; two-horned; crescentlike.

bicorporal.c: Bicorporal Bi*cor"po*ral (?), a. [Pref. bi- + corporal.] Having two bodies.

bicorporate.c: Bicorporate Bi*cor"po*rate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + corporate.] (Her.) Double-bodied, as a lion having one head and two bodies.

bicostate.c: Bicostate Bi*cos"tate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + costate.] (Bot.) Having two principal ribs running longitudinally, as a leaf.

bicrenate.c: Bicrenate Bi*cre"nate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + crenate.] (Bot.) Twice crenated, as in the case of leaves whose crenatures are themselves crenate.

bicrescentic.c: Bicrescentic Bi`cres*cen"tic (?), a. [Pref. bi- + crescent.] Having the form of a double crescent.

bicrural.c: Bicrural Bi*cru"ral (?), a. [Pref. bi- + crural.] Having two legs. Hooker.

bicuspidate.c: Bicuspidate Bicuspid { Bi*cus"pid (?), Bi*cus"pid*ate (?), } a. [See pref. Bi-, and Cuspidate.] Having two points or prominences; ending in two points; -- said of teeth, leaves, fruit, etc.

bicuspid.c: Bicuspid Bi*cus"pid, n. (Anat.) One of the two double-pointed teeth which intervene between the canines (cuspids) and the molars, on each side of each jaw. See Tooth, n.

bicycle.c: Bicycle Bi"cy*cle (?), n. [Pref. bi- + cycle.] A light vehicle having two wheels one behind the other. It has a saddle seat and is propelled by the rider's feet acting on cranks or levers.

bicycler.c: Bicycler Bi"cy*cler (?), n. One who rides a bicycle.

bicycling.c: Bicycling Bi"cy*cling (?), n. The use of a bicycle; the act or practice of riding a bicycle.

bicyclism.c: Bicyclism Bi"cy*clism (?), n. The art of riding a bicycle.

bid.c: Bid Bid (bĭd), v. t. [imp. Bade (băd), Bid, (Obs.) Bad; p. p. Bidden (?), Bid; p. pr. & vb. n. Bidding.] [OE. bidden, prop to ask, beg, AS. biddan; akin to OS. biddian, Icel. biðja, OHG. bittan, G. bitten, to pray, ask, request, and E. bead, also perh. to Gr. teiqein to persuade, L. fidere to trust, E. faith, and bide. But this word was early confused with OE. beden, beoden, AS. beódan, to offer, command; akin to Icel. bjōða, Goth. biudan (in comp.), OHG. biotan to command, bid, G. bieten, D. bieden, to offer, also to Gr. pynqa`nesqai to learn by inquiry, Skr. budh to be awake, to heed, present OSlav. budēti to be awake, E. bode, v. The word now has the form of OE. bidden to ask, but the meaning of OE. beden to command, except in “to bid beads.” √30.]
Bid Bid (?), imp. & p. p. of Bid.

Bid Bid, n. An offer of a price, especially at auctions; a statement of a sum which one will give for something to be received, or will take for something to be done or furnished; that which is offered.
Bid Bid, v. i. [See Bid, v. t.] 1. To pray. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bidale.c: Bidale Bid"ale` (?), n. [Bid + ale.] An invitation of friends to drink ale at some poor man's house, and there to contribute in charity for his relief. [Prov. Eng.]

bidarka.c: Bidarka Bidarkee { Bi*dar"kee (?), Bi*dar"ka (?) }, n. [Russ. baidarka, dim. Cf. Baidar.] A portable boat made of skins stretched on a frame. [Alaska] The Century.

bidder.c: Bidder Bid"der (?), n. [AS. biddere. ] One who bids or offers a price. Burke.

biddery.c: Biddery ware Bid"der*y ware` (?). [From Beder or Bidar a town in India.] A kind of metallic ware made in India. The material is a composition of zinc, tin, and lead, in which ornaments of gold and silver are inlaid or damascened. [Spelt also bidry, bidree, bedery, beder.]

bidding.c: Bidding Bid"ding, n. 1. Command; order; a proclamation or notifying. “Do thou thy master's bidding.” Shak.
Bidding prayer Bid"ding prayer` (?). 1. (R. C. Ch.) The prayer for the souls of benefactors, said before the sermon.

biddy.c: Biddy Bid"dy (?), n. [Etymology uncertain.] A name used in calling a hen or chicken. Shak.
Biddy Bid"dy, n. [A familiar form of Bridget.] An Irish serving woman or girl. [Colloq.]

bide.c: Bide Bide (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bided; p. pr. & vb. n. Biding.] [OE. biden, AS. bīdan; akin to OHG. bītan, Goth. beidan, Icel. bī??; perh. orig., to wait with trust, and akin to bid. See Bid, v. t., and cf. Abide.] 1. To dwell; to inhabit; to abide; to stay.
Bide Bide, v. t. 1. To encounter; to remain firm under (a hardship); to endure; to suffer; to undergo.

bident.c: Bident Bi"dent (?), n. [L. bidens, -entis, having two prongs; bis twice + dens a tooth.] An instrument or weapon with two prongs.

bidental.c: Bidental Bi*den"tal (?), a. Having two teeth. Swift.

bidentate.c: Bidentate Bi*den"tate (?), a. (Bot. & Zool.) Having two teeth or two toothlike processes; two-toothed.

bidet.c: Bidet Bi*det" (?), n. [F. bidet, perh. fr. Celtic; cr. Gael. bideach very little, diminutive, bidein a diminutive animal, W. bidan a weakly or sorry wretch.]

bidigitate.c: Bidigitate Bi*dig"i*tate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + digitate.] Having two fingers or fingerlike projections.

bielas.c: Biela's comet Bie"la's com"et (?). (Astron.) A periodic coment, discovered by Biela in 1826, which revolves around the sun in 6.6 years. The November meteors (Andromedes or Bielids) move in its orbit, and may be fragments of the comet.

bield.c: Bield Bield (?), n. A shelter. Same as Beild. [Scot.]

bielid.c: Bielid Bie"lid (?), n. (Astron.) See Andromede and cf. Biela's comet.

biennial.c: Biennial Bi*en"ni*al (?), a. [L. biennalis and biennis, fr. biennium a space of two years; bis twice + annus year. Cf. Annual.] 1. Happening, or taking place, once in two years; as, a biennial election.
Biennial Bi*en"ni*al, n. 1. Something which takes place or appears once in two years; esp. a biennial examination.

biennially.c: Biennially Bi*en"ni*al*ly, adv. Once in two years.

bier.c: Bier Bier (?), n. [OE. bæe, beere, AS. b?r, b?re; akin to D. baar, OHG. bāra, G. bahre, Icel barar, D? baare, L. feretrum, Gr.?, from the same?? bear to produce. See 1st Bear, and cf. Barrow.] 1. A handbarrow or portable frame on which a corpse is placed or borne to the grave.

bierbalk.c: Bierbalk Bier"balk` (bēr"bäk`), n. [See Bier, and Balk, n.] A church road (e. g., a path across fields) for funerals. [Obs.] Homilies.

bifacial.c: Bifacial Bi*fa"cial (?), a. [Pref. bi- + facial.] Having the opposite surfaces alike.

bifarious.c: Bifarious Bi*fa"ri*ous (?), a. [L. bifarius; bis twice + fari to speak. Cf. Gr.? twofold;? twice +? to say.] 1. Twofold; arranged in two rows.

bifariously.c: Bifariously Bi*fa"ri*ous*ly, adv. In a bifarious manner.

biferous.c: Biferous Bif"er*ous (?), a. [L. bifer; bis twice + ferre to bear.] Bearing fruit twice a year.

biffin.c: Biffin Bif"fin (?), n. [Cf. Beaufin.] 1. A sort of apple peculiar to Norfolk, Eng. Wright.

bifid.c: Bifid Bi"fid (?), a. [L. bifidus; bis twice + root of findere to cleave or split: cf. F. bifide.] Cleft to the middle or slightly beyond the middle; opening with a cleft; divided by a linear sinus, with straight margins.

bifilar.c: Bifilar Bi*fi"lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + filar.] Two-threaded; involving the use of two threads; as, bifilar suspension; a bifilar balance.

biflabellate.c: Biflabellate Bi`fla*bel"late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + flabellate.] (Zool.) Flabellate on both sides.

biflagellate.c: Biflagellate Bi`fla*gel"late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + flagellate.] Having two long, narrow, whiplike appendages.

biflorous.c: Biflorous Biflorate { Bi*flo"rate (?), Bi*flo"rous (?), } a. [L. bis twice + flos, floris, flower.] (Bot.) Bearing two flowers; two-flowered.

bifocal.c: Bifocal Bi"fo`cal (?), a. [Pref. bi-+ focal.] Having two foci, as some spectacle lenses.

bifold.c: Bifold Bi"fold (?), a. [Pref. bi- + fold.] Twofold; double; of two kinds, degrees, etc. Shak.

bifoliate.c: Bifoliate Bi*fo"li*ate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + foliate.] (Bot.) Having two leaves; two-leaved.

bifoliolate.c: Bifoliolate Bi*fo"li*o*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + foliolate.] (Bot.) Having two leaflets, as some compound leaves.

biforate.c: Biforate Bif"o*rate (?), a. [L. bis twice + foratus, p. p. of forare to bore or pierce.] (Bot.) Having two perforations.

biforine.c: Biforine Bif"o*rine (?), n. [L. biforis, biforus, having two doors; bis twice + foris door.] (Bot.) An oval sac or cell, found in the leaves of certain plants of the order Araceæ. It has an opening at each end through which raphides, generated inside, are discharged.

biform.c: Biform Bi"form (?), a. [L. biformis; bis twice + forma shape: cf. F. biforme.] Having two forms, bodies, or shapes. Croxall.

biformed.c: Biformed Bi"formed (?), a. [Pref. bi- + form.] Having two forms. Johnson.

biforous.c: Biforous Bif"o*rous (?), a. [L. biforis having two doors; bis twice, two + foris door.] See Biforate.

bifronted.c: Bifronted Bi*front"ed (?), a. [Pref. bi- + front.] Having two fronts. “Bifronted Janus.” Massinger.

bifurcated.c: Bifurcated Bifurcate { Bi*fur"cate (?), Bi*fur"ca*ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + furcate.] 1. Two-pronged; forked.

bifurcate.c: Bifurcate Bi*fur"cate (?), v. i. To divide into two branches.

bifurcation.c: Bifurcation Bi`fur*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. bifurcation.] A forking, or division into two branches.

bifurcous.c: Bifurcous Bi*fur"cous (?), a. [L. bifurcus; bis twice + furca fork.] See Bifurcate, a. [R.] Coles.

big.c: Big Big (bĭg), a. [Compar. Bigger; superl. Biggest.] [Perh. from Celtic; cf. W. beichiog, beichiawg, pregnant, with child, fr. baich burden, Arm. beac'h; or cf. OE. bygly, Icel. biggiligr, (properly) habitable; (then) magnigicent, excellent, fr. OE. biggen, Icel. byggja, to dwell, build, akin to E. be.] 1. Having largeness of size; of much bulk or magnitude; of great size; large. “He's too big to go in there.” Shak.
Big Bend State Big Bend State. Tennessee; -- a nickname.

bigg.c: Bigg Big { Big, Bigg }, n. [OE. bif, bigge; akin to Icel. bygg, Dan. byg, Sw. bjugg.] (Bot.) Barley, especially the hardy four-rowed kind.

Bigg Big { Big, Bigg }, v. t. [OE. biggen, fr. Icel. byggja to inhabit, to build, b?a (neut.) to dwell (active) to make ready. See Boor, and Bound.] To build. [Scot. & North of Eng. Dial.] Sir W. Scott.
Bigg Bigg (?), n. & v. See Big, n. & v.

bigam.c: Bigam Big"am (?), n. [L. bigamus twice married: cf. F. bigame. See Bigamy.] A bigamist. [Obs.]

bigamist.c: Bigamist Big"a*mist (?), n. [Cf. Digamist.] One who is guilty of bigamy. Ayliffe.

bigamous.c: Bigamous Big"a*mous (?), a. Guilty of bigamy; involving bigamy; as, a bigamous marriage.

bigamy.c: Bigamy Big"a*my (?), n. [OE. bigamie, fr. L. bigamus twice married; bis twice + Gr.? marriage; prob. akin to Skt. jāmis related, and L. gemini twins, the root meaning to bind, join: cf. F. bigamie. Cf. Digamy.] (Law) The offense of marrying one person when already legally married to another. Wharton.

bigaroon.c: Bigaroon Bigarreau { Big`ar*reau" (?), Big`a*roon" (?), } n. [F. bigarreau, fr. bigarré variegated.] (Bot.) The large white-heart cherry.

bigbellied.c: Big-bellied Big"-bel`lied (?), a. Having a great belly; as, a big-bellied man or flagon; advanced in pregnancy.

bigeminate.c: bigeminate bi*gem"i*nate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + geminate.] (Bot.) Having a forked petiole, and a pair of leaflets at the end of each division; biconjugate; twice paired; -- said of a decompound leaf.

bigential.c: bigential bi*gen"tial (?), a. [Pref. bi- + L. gens, gentis, tribe.] (Zool.) Including two tribes or races of men.

bigeye.c: Bigeye Big"eye` (?), n. (Zool.) A fish of the genus Priacanthus, remarkable for the large size of the eye.

biggen.c: Biggen Big"gen (?), v. t. & i. To make or become big; to enlarge. [Obs. or Dial.] Steele.

biggin.c: Biggin Big"gin (?), n. [F. béguin, prob. from the cap worn by the Béguines. Cf. Beguine, Biggon.] A child's cap; a hood, or something worn on the head.
Biggin Big"gin, n. A coffeepot with a strainer or perforated metallic vessel for holding the ground coffee, through which boiling water is poured; -- so called from Mr. Biggin, the inventor.

bigging.c: Bigging Biggin { Big"gin, Big"ging, } n. [OE. bigging. See Big, Bigg, v. t.] A building. [Obs.]

biggonnet.c: Biggonnet Biggon { Big"gon (?), Big"gon*net (?), } n. [F. béguin and OF. beguinet, dim of béguin. See Biggin a cap.] A cap or hood with pieces covering the ears.

bigha.c: Bigha ‖Big"ha (?), n. A measure of land in India, varying from a third of an acre to an acre.

bighorn.c: Bighorn Big"horn` (?), n. (Zool.) The Rocky Mountain sheep (Ovis montana or Caprovis montana); called also bighorn sheep.

bight.c: Bight Bight (bīt), n. [OE. biȝt a bending; cf. Sw. & Dan. bugt bend, bay; fr. AS. byht, fr. būgan. √88. Cf. Bout, Bought a bend, and see Bow, v.] 1. A corner, bend, or angle; a hollow; as, the bight of a horse's knee; the bight of an elbow.

biglandular.c: Biglandular Bi*glan"du*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + glandular.] Having two glands, as a plant.

bigly.c: Bigly Big"ly (?), adv. [From Big, a.] In a tumid, swelling, blustering manner; haughtily; violently.

bigness.c: Bigness Big"ness, n. The state or quality of being big; largeness; size; bulk.

bignonia.c: Bignonia Big*no"ni*a (?), prop. n. [Named from the Abbé Bignon.] 1. (Bot.) A large genus of American, mostly tropical, climbing shrubs, having compound leaves and showy somewhat tubular flowers. Bignonia capreolata is the cross vine of the Southern United States. The trumpet creeper (also called the trumpet vine), with large red tubular flowers, was formerly considered to be of this genus, but is now classified as Campsis radicans.

bignoniaceous.c: Bignoniaceous Big*no`ni*a"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Of pertaining to, or resembling, the family of plants of which the trumpet flower (also called trumpet creeper and trumpet vine) is an example.

bigot.c: Bigot Big"ot (?), n. [F. bigot a bigot or hypocrite, a name once given to the Normans in France. Of unknown origin; possibly akin to Sp. bigote a whisker; hombre de bigote a man of spirit and vigor; cf. It. s-bigottire to terrify, to appall. Wedgwood and others maintain that bigot is from the same source as Beguine, Beghard.]

bigoted.c: Bigoted Big"ot*ed, a. Obstinately and blindly attached to some creed, opinion practice, or ritual; unreasonably devoted to a system or party, and illiberal toward the opinions of others. “Bigoted to strife.” Byron.

bigotedly.c: Bigotedly Big"ot*ed*ly, adv. In the manner of a bigot.

bigotry.c: Bigotry Big"ot*ry (?), n. [Cf. F. bigoterie.] 1. The state of mind of a bigot; obstinate and unreasoning attachment of one's own belief and opinions, with narrow-minded intolerance of beliefs opposed to them.

bigwig.c: Bigwig Big"wig` (?), n. [Big,a.+ wig.] A person of consequence; as, the bigwigs of society. [Jocose]

bigwigged.c: Big-wigged Big"-wigged` (?), a. characterized by pomposity of manner. [Eng.]

bihydroguret.c: Bihydroguret Bi`hy*drog"u*ret (?), n. [Pref. bi- + hydroguret.] (Chem.) A compound of two atoms of hydrogen with some other substance. [Obs.]

bijou.c: Bijou ‖Bi*jou" (?), n.; pl. Bijoux (?). [F.; of uncertain origin.] A trinket; a jewel; -- a word applied to anything small and of elegant workmanship.

bijoutry.c: Bijoutry Bi*jou"try (?), n. [F. bijouterie. See Bijou.] Small articles of virtu, as jewelry, trinkets, etc.

bijugate.c: Bijugate Bij"u*gate (?), a. [L. bis twice + jugatus, p. p. of jugare to join.] (Bot.) Having two pairs, as of leaflets.

bijugous.c: Bijugous Bij"u*gous (?), a. [L. bijugus yoked two together; bis twice + jugum yoke, pair.] (Bot.) Bijugate.

bike.c: Bike Bike (?), n. [Ethymol. unknown.] A nest of wild bees, wasps, or ants; a swarm. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

bikh.c: Bikh ‖Bikh (?), n. [Hind., fr. Skr. visha poison.] (Bot.) The East Indian name of a virulent poison extracted from Aconitum ferox or other species of aconite: also, the plant itself.

bilabiate.c: Bilabiate Bi*la"bi*ate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + labiate.] (Bot.) Having two lips, as the corols of certain flowers.

bilaciniate.c: Bilaciniate Bi`la*cin"i*ate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + laciniate.] Doubly fringed.

bilalo.c: Bilalo ‖Bi*la"lo (?), n. A two-masted passenger boat or small vessel, used in the bay of Manila.

bilamellated.c: Bilamellated Bilamellate { Bi*lam"el*late (?), Bi*lam"el*la`ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + lamellate.] (Bot.) Formed of two plates, as the stigma of the Mimulus; also, having two elevated ridges, as in the lip of certain flowers.

bilaminate.c: Bilaminate Bilaminar { Bi*lam"i*nar (?), Bi*lam"i*nate (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + laminar, laminate.] Formed of, or having, two laminæ, or thin plates.

bilander.c: Bilander Bil"an*der (?), n. [D. bijlander; bij by + land land, country.] (Naut.) A small two-masted merchant vessel, fitted only for coasting, or for use in canals, as in Holland.

bilateral.c: Bilateral Bi*lat"er*al (?), a. [Pref. bi- + lateral: cf. F. bilatéral.] 1. Having two sides; arranged upon two sides; affecting two sides or two parties.

bilaterality.c: Bilaterality Bi*lat`er*al"i*ty (?), n. State of being bilateral.

bilberry.c: Bilberry Bil"ber*ry (?), n.; pl. Bilberries (?). [Cf. Dan. böllebær bilberry, where bölle is perh. akin to E. ball.] 1. (Bot.) The European whortleberry (Vaccinium myrtillus); also, its edible bluish black fruit.

bilbo.c: Bilbo Bil"bo (?), n.; pl. Bilboes (?). 1. A rapier; a sword; so named from Bilbao, in Spain. Shak.

bilboquet.c: Bilboquet ‖Bil"bo*quet (?), n. [F.] The toy called cup and ball.

bilcock.c: Bilcock Bil"cock (?), n. (Zool.) The European water rail.

bildstein.c: Bildstein ‖Bild"stein (?), n. [G., fr. bild image, likeness + stein stone.] Same as Agalmatolite.

bile.c: Bile Bile (?), n. [L. bilis: cf. F. bile.] 1. (Physiol.) A yellow, or greenish, viscid fluid, usually alkaline in reaction, secreted by the liver. It passes into the intestines, where it aids in the digestive process. Its characteristic constituents are the bile salts, and coloring matters.
Bile Bile, n. [OE. byle, bule, bele, AS. b?le, b?l; skin to D. buil, G. beule, and Goth. ufbauljan to puff up. Cf. Boil a tumor, Bulge.] A boil. [Obs. or Archaic]

bilection.c: Bilection Bi*lec"tion (?), n. (Arch.) That portion of a group of moldings which projects beyond the general surface of a panel; a bolection.

bilestone.c: Bilestone Bile"stone` (?), n. [Bile + stone.] A gallstone, or biliary calculus. See Biliary. E. Darwin.

bilge.c: Bilge Bilge (?), n. [A different orthography of bulge, of same origin as belly. Cf. Belly, Bulge.] 1. The protuberant part of a cask, which is usually in the middle.
Bilge Bilge (bĭlj), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bilged (bĭljd); p. pr. & vb. n. Bilging.] 1. (Naut.) To suffer a fracture in the bilge; to spring a leak by a fracture in the bilge.
Bilge Bilge, v. t. 1. (Naut.) To fracture the bilge of, or stave in the bottom of (a ship or other vessel).

bilgy.c: Bilgy Bil"gy (?), a. Having the smell of bilge water.

biliary.c: Biliary Bil"ia*ry (bĭl"yȧ*ry̆; 106), a. [L. bilis bile: cf. F. biliaire.] (Physiol.) Relating or belonging to bile; conveying bile; as, biliary acids; biliary ducts.

biliation.c: Biliation Bil`i*a"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The production and excretion of bile.

bilifuscin.c: Bilifuscin Bil`i*fus"cin (?), n. [L. bilis bile + fuscus dark.] (Physiol.) A brownish green pigment found in human gallstones and in old bile. It is a derivative of bilirubin.

bilimbing.c: Bilimbing Bilimbi { ‖Bi*lim"bi (?), ‖Bi*lim"bing (?), } n. [Malay.] The berries of two East Indian species of Averrhoa, of the Oxalideæ or Sorrel family. They are very acid, and highly esteemed when preserved or pickled. The juice is used as a remedy for skin diseases. [Written also blimbi and blimbing.]

biliment.c: Biliment Bil"i*ment (?), n. A woman's ornament; habiliment. [Obs.]

bilin.c: Bilin Bi"lin (?), n. [Cf. F. biline, from L. bilis bile.] (Physiol. Chem.) A name applied to the amorphous or crystalline mass obtained from bile by the action of alcohol and ether. It is composed of a mixture of the sodium salts of the bile acids.

bilinear.c: Bilinear Bi*lin"e*ar (?), a. (Math.) Of, pertaining to, or included by, two lines; as, bilinear coördinates.

bilingual.c: Bilingual Bi*lin"gual (?), a. [L. bilinguis; bis twice + lingua tongue, language.] Containing, or consisting of, two languages; expressed in two languages; as, a bilingual inscription; a bilingual dictionary. -- Bi*lin"gual*ly, adv.

bilingualism.c: Bilingualism Bi*lin"gual*ism (?), n. Quality of being bilingual.

bilinguist.c: Bilinguist Bi*lin"guist (?), n. One versed in two languages.

bilinguous.c: Bilinguous Bi*lin"guous (?), a. [L. bilinguis.] Having two tongues, or speaking two languages. [Obs.]

bilious.c: Bilious Bil"ious (bĭl"yŭs), a. [L. biliosus, fr. bilis bile.] 1. Of or pertaining to the bile.

biliousness.c: Biliousness Bil"ious*ness, n. The state of being bilious.

biliprasin.c: Biliprasin Bil`i*pra"sin (?), n. [L. bilis bile + prasinus green.] (Physiol.) A dark green pigment found in small quantity in human gallstones.

bilirubin.c: Bilirubin Bil`i*ru"bin (?), n. [L. bilis biel + ruber red.] (Physiol.) A reddish yellow pigment present in human bile, and in that from carnivorous and herbivorous animals; the normal biliary pigment.

biliteral.c: Biliteral Bi*lit"er*al (?), a. [L. bis twice + littera letter.] Consisting of two letters; as, a biliteral root of a Sanskrit verb. Sir W. Jones. -- n. A word, syllable, or root, consisting of two letters.

biliteralism.c: Biliteralism Bi*lit"er*al*ism (?), n. The property or state of being biliteral.

biliverdin.c: Biliverdin Bil`i*ver"din (?), n. [L. bilis bile + viridis green. Cf. Verdure.] (Physiol.) A green pigment present in the bile, formed from bilirubin by oxidation.

bilk.c: Bilk Bilk (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bilked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bilking.] [Origin unknown. Cf. Balk.] To frustrate or disappoint; to deceive or defraud, by nonfulfillment of engagement; to leave in the lurch; to give the slip to; as, to bilk a creditor. Thackeray.
Bilk Bilk, n. 1. A thwarting an adversary in cribbage by spoiling his score; a balk.

bill.c: Bill Bill (?), n. [OE. bile, bille, AS. bile beak of a bird, proboscis; cf. Ir. & Gael. bil, bile, mouth, lip, bird's bill. Cf. Bill a weapon.] A beak, as of a bird, or sometimes of a turtle or other animal. Milton.
Bill Bill, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Billed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Billing.] 1. To strike; to peck. [Obs.]
Bill Bill, n. The bell, or boom, of the bittern

Bill Bill, n. [OE. bil, AS. bill, bil; akin to OS. bil sword, OHG. bill pickax, G. bille. Cf. Bill bea?.] 1. A cutting instrument, with hook-shaped point, and fitted with a handle; -- used in pruning, etc.; a billhook. When short, called a hand bill, when long, a hedge bill.
Bill Bill (?), v. t. To work upon (as to dig, hoe, hack, or chop anything) with a bill.

Bill Bill, n. [OE. bill, bille, fr. LL. billa (or OF. bille), for L. bulla anything rounded, LL., seal, stamp, letter, edict, roll; cf. F. bille a ball, prob. fr. Ger.; cf. MHG. bickel, D. bikkel, dice. Cf. Bull papal edict, Billet a paper.]
Bill Bill, v. t. 1. To advertise by a bill or public notice.
Bill book Bill" book` (?). (Com.) A book in which a person keeps an account of his notes, bills, bills of exchange, etc., thus showing all that he issues and receives.
Bill broker Bill" bro`ker (?). One who negotiates the discount of bills.
Bill holder Bill" hold`er (bĭl" hōl`dẽr). 1. A person who holds a bill or acceptance.

billabong.c: Billabong Bil"la*bong` (?), n. [Native name.] In Australia, a blind channel leading out from a river; -- sometimes called an anabranch. This is the sense of the word as used in the Public Works Department; but the term has also been locally applied to mere back-waters forming stagnant pools and to certain water channels arising from a source.

billage.c: Billage Bil"lage (?), n. & v. t. & i. Same as Bilge.

billard.c: Billard Bil"lard (?), n. (Zool.) An English fish, allied to the cod; the coalfish. [Written also billet and billit.]

billbug.c: Billbug Billbeetle {Bill`bee"tle (?), or Bill"bug` } (?), n. (Zool.) A weevil or curculio of various species, as the corn weevil. See Curculio.

billboard.c: Billboard Bill"board` (?), n. 1. (Naut.) A piece of thick plank, armed with iron plates, and fixed on the bow or fore channels of a vessel, for the bill or fluke of the anchor to rest on. Totten.

billed.c: Billed Billed (?), a. Furnished with, or having, a bill, as a bird; -- used in composition; as, broad-billed.

billet.c: Billet Bil"let (?), n. [F. billet, dim. of an OF. bille bill. See Bill a writing.] 1. A small paper; a note; a short letter. “I got your melancholy billet.” Sterne.

Billet Bil"let, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Billeted; p. pr. & vb. n. Billeting.] [From Billet a ticket.] (Mil.) To direct, by a ticket or note, where to lodge. Hence: To quarter, or place in lodgings, as soldiers in private houses.
Billet Bil"let, n. [F. billette, bille, log; of unknown origin; a different word from bille ball. Cf. Billiards, Billot.] 1. A small stick of wood, as for firewood.

billetdoux.c: Billet-doux ‖Bil`let-doux" (bĭl`la*dōo"), n.; pl. Billets-doux (bĭl`la*dōoz"). [F. billet note + doux sweet, L. dulcis.] A love letter or note.

billethead.c: Billethead Bil"let*head` (bĭl"lĕt*hĕd), n. (Naut.) A round piece of timber at the bow or stern of a whaleboat, around which the harpoon line is run out when the whale darts off.

billfish.c: Billfish Bill"fish` (bĭl"fĭsh`), n. (Zool.) A name applied to several distinct fishes: (a) The garfish (Tylosurus longirostris, or Belone longirostris) and allied species. (b) The saury, a slender fish of the Atlantic coast (Scomberesox saurus). (c) The Tetrapturus albidus, a large oceanic species related to the swordfish; the spearfish. (d) The American fresh-water garpike (Lepidosteus osseus).

billhead.c: Billhead Bill"head` (bĭl"hĕd), n. A printed form, used by merchants in making out bills or rendering accounts.

billhook.c: Billhook Bill"hook` (?), n. [Bill + hook.] A thick, heavy knife with a hooked point, used in pruning hedges, etc. When it has a short handle, it is sometimes called a hand bill; when the handle is long, a hedge bill or scimiter.

billiard.c: Billiard Bil"liard (?), a. Of or pertaining to the game of billiards. “Smooth as is a billiard ball.” B. Jonson.

billiards.c: Billiards Bil"liards (?), n. [F. billiard billiards, OF. billart staff, cue form playing, fr. bille log. See Billet a stick.] A game played with ivory balls o a cloth-covered, rectangular table, bounded by elastic cushions. The player seeks to impel his ball with his cue so that it shall either strike (carom upon) two other balls, or drive another ball into one of the pockets with which the table sometimes is furnished.

billingsgate.c: Billingsgate Bil"lings*gate` (?), n. 1. A market near the Billings gate in London, celebrated for fish and foul language.

billion.c: Billion Bil"lion (?), n. [F. billion, arbitrarily formed fr. L. bis twice, in imitation of million a million. See Million.] According to the French and American method of numeration, a thousand millions, or 1,000,000,000; according to the English method, a million millions, or 1,000,000,000,000. See Numeration.

billman.c: Billman Bill"man (?), n.; pl. Billmen (?). One who uses, or is armed with, a bill or hooked ax. “A billman of the guard.” Savile.

billon.c: Billon ‖Bil`lon" (?), n. [F. Cf. Billet a stick.] An alloy of gold and silver with a large proportion of copper or other base metal, used in coinage.

billot.c: Billot Bil"lot (?), n. [F. billot, dim. of bille. See Billet a stick.] Bullion in the bar or mass.

billow.c: Billow Bil"low (?), n. [Cf. Icel. bylgja billow, Dan. bölge, Sw. bölja; akin to MHG. bulge billow, bag, and to E. bulge. See Bulge.] 1. A great wave or surge of the sea or other water, caused usually by violent wind.
Billow Bil"low, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Billowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Billowing.] To surge; to rise and roll in waves or surges; to undulate. “The billowing snow.” Prior.

billowy.c: Billowy Bil"low*y (?), a. Of or pertaining to billows; swelling or swollen into large waves; full of billows or surges; resembling billows.

billsticker.c: Billsticker Billposter { Bill"post`er (?), Bill"stick"er (?), } n. One whose occupation is to post handbills or posters in public places.

billy.c: Billy Bil"ly (?), n. 1. A club; esp., a policeman's club. Also called billy club
Billy goat Bil"ly goat` (?). A male goat. [Colloq.]

billycock.c: Billycock hat Billycock { Bil"ly*cock (?), n., or Bil"ly*cock hat` (?) }. [Perh. from bully + cock; that is, cocked like the hats of the bullies.] A round, low-crowned felt hat; a wideawake. “The undignified billycocks and pantaloons of the West.” B. H. Chamberlain.

billyboy.c: Billyboy Bil"ly*boy` (?), n. A flat-bottomed river barge or coasting vessel. [Eng.]

bilobate.c: Bilobate Bi*lo"bate (bi*lō"bat or bī"lo*bat), a. [Pref. bi- + lobate.] Divided into two lobes or segments.

bilocation.c: Bilocation Bi`lo*ca"tion (?), n. [Pref. bi- + location.] Double location; the state or power of being in two places at the same instant; -- a miraculous power attributed to some of the saints. Tylor.

bilocular.c: Bilocular Bi*loc"u*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + locular: cf. F. biloculaire.] Divided into two cells or compartments; as, a bilocular pericarp. Gray.

biltong.c: Biltong ‖Bil"tong (?), n. [S. African.] Lean meat cut into strips and sun-dried. H. R. Haggard.

bimaculate.c: Bimaculate Bi*mac"u*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + maculate, a.] Having, or marked with, two spots.

bimana.c: Bimana ‖Bim"a*na (?), n. pl. [NL. See Bimanous.] (Zool.) Animals having two hands; -- a term applied by Cuvier to man as a special order of Mammalia.

bimanous.c: Bimanous Bim"a*nous (?), a. [L. bis twice + manus hand.] (Zool.) Having two hands; two-handed.

bimarginate.c: Bimarginate Bi*mar"gin*ate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + marginate.] Having a double margin, as certain shells.

bimastism.c: Bimastism Bi*mas"tism (?), n. [Pref. bi- + Gr.? breast.] (Anat.) The condition of having two mammæ or teats.

bimedial.c: Bimedial Bi*me"di*al (?), a. [Pref. bi- + medial.] (Geom.) Applied to a line which is the sum of two lines commensurable only in power (as the side and diagonal of a square).

bimembral.c: Bimembral Bi*mem"bral (?), a. [L. bis twice + membrum member.] (Gram.) Having two members; as, a bimembral sentence. J. W. Gibbs.

bimensal.c: Bimensal Bi*men"sal (?), a. [Pref. bi- + mensal.] See Bimonthly, a. [Obs. or R.]

bimestrial.c: Bimestrial Bi*mes"tri*al (?), a. [L. bimestris; bis twice + mensis month.] Continuing two months. [R.]

bimetallic.c: Bimetallic Bi`me*tal"lic (?), a. [Pref. bi- + metallic: cf. F. bimétallique.] 1. Of or relating to, or using, a double metallic standard (as gold and silver) for a system of coins or currency. [archaic]

bimetallism.c: Bimetallism Bi*met"al*lism (?), n. [F. bimétalisme.] The legalized use of two metals (as gold and silver) in the currency of a country, at a fixed relative value; -- in opposition to monometallism.

bimetallist.c: Bimetallist Bi*met"al*list (?), n. An advocate of bimetallism.

bimolecular.c: bimolecular bi"mo*lec"u*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + molecular.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, involving, or formed from, two molecules; as, a bimolecular reaction (a reaction between two molecules).

bimonthly.c: bimonthly bi*month"ly (?), a. [Pref. bi- + monthly.] Occurring, done, or coming, once in two months; as, bimonthly visits; bimonthly publications. -- n. A bimonthly publication.
Bimonthly Bi*month"ly, adv. Once in two months.

bimuscular.c: Bimuscular Bi*mus"cu*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + muscular.] (Zool.) Having two adductor muscles, as a bivalve mollusk.

bin.c: Bin Bin (?), n. [OE. binne, AS. binn manager, crib; perh. akin to D. ben, benne, basket, and to L. benna a kind of carriage (a Gallic word), W. benn, men, wain, cart.] A box, frame, crib, or inclosed place, used as a receptacle for any commodity; as, a corn bin; a wine bin; a coal bin.
Bin Bin, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Binned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Binning.] To put into a bin; as, to bin wine.
Bin Bin. An old form of Be and Been. [Obs.]
Bin- Bin-. A euphonic form of the prefix Bi-.

binal.c: Binal Bi"nal (?), a. [See Binary.] Twofold; double. [R.] “Binal revenge, all this.” Ford.

binarseniate.c: Binarseniate Bin`ar*se"ni*ate (?), n. [Pref. bin- + arseniate.] (Chem.) A salt having two equivalents of arsenic acid to one of the base. Graham.

binary.c: Binary Bi"na*ry (?), a. [L. binarius, fr. bini two by two, two at a time, fr. root of bis twice; akin to E. two: cf. F. binaire.] Compounded or consisting of two things or parts; characterized by two (things).
Binary Bi"na*ry, n. That which is constituted of two figures, things, or parts; two; duality. Fotherby.

binate.c: Binate Bi"nate (?), a. [L. bini two and two.] (Bot.) Double; growing in pairs or couples. Gray.

binaural.c: Binaural Bin*au"ral (?), a. [Pref. bin- + aural.] Of or pertaining to, or used by, both ears.

binbashi.c: Binbashi ‖Bin*bash"i (?), n. [Turk., prop., chief of a thousand; bin thousand + bash head.] (Mil.) A major in the Turkish army.

bind.c: Bind Bind (?), v. t. [imp. Bound (?); p. p. Bound, formerly Bounden (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Binding.] [AS. bindan, perfect tense band, bundon, p. p. bunden; akin to D. & G. binden, Dan. binde, Sw. & Icel. binda, Goth. bindan, Skr. bandh (for bhandh) to bind, cf. Gr.? (for?) cable, and L. offendix. √90.] 1. To tie, or confine with a cord, band, ligature, chain, etc.; to fetter; to make fast; as, to bind grain in bundles; to bind a prisoner.
Bind Bind (?), v. i. 1. To tie; to confine by any ligature.
Bind Bind, n. 1. That which binds or ties.

binder.c: Binder Bind"er (?), n. 1. One who binds; as, a binder of sheaves; one whose trade is to bind; as, a binder of books.

bindery.c: Bindery Bind"er*y (?), n. A place where books, or other articles, are bound; a bookbinder's establishment.

bindheimite.c: Bindheimite Bind"heim*ite (?), n. [From Bindheim, a German who analyzed it.] (Min.) An amorphous antimonate of lead, produced from the alteration of other ores, as from jamesonite.

binding.c: Binding Bind"ing, n. 1. The act or process of one who, or that which, binds.
Binding post Bind"ing post`. (Elec.) A metallic post attached to electrical apparatus for convenience in making connections.
Binding screw Bind"ing screw`. A set screw used to bind parts together, esp. one for making a connection in an electrical circuit.

bindingly.c: Bindingly Bind"ing*ly, adv. So as to bind.

bindingness.c: Bindingness Bind"ing*ness, n. The condition or property of being binding; obligatory quality. Coleridge.

bindweed.c: Bindweed Bind"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant of the genus Convolvulus; as, greater bindweed (Convolvulus Sepium); lesser bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis); the white bindweed, the blue bindweed, the Syrian bindweed. The black bryony, or Tamus, is called black bindweed, and the Smilax aspera, rough bindweed.

bine.c: Bine Bine (?), n. [Bind, cf. Woodbine.] The winding or twining stem of a hop vine or other climbing plant.

binervate.c: Binervate Bi*nerv"ate (?), a. [L. bis twice + nervus sinew, nerve.] 1. (Bot.) Two-nerved; -- applied to leaves which have two longitudinal ribs or nerves.

bing.c: Bing Bing (?), n. [Cf. Icel. bingr, Sw. binge, G. beige, beuge. Cf. Prov. E. bink bench, and bench coal the uppermost stratum of coal.] A heap or pile; as, a bing of wood. “Potato bings.” Burns. “A bing of corn.” Surrey. [Obs. or Dial. Eng. & Scot.]

bink.c: Bink Bink (?), n. A bench. [North of Eng. & Scot.]

binnacle.c: Binnacle Bin"na*cle (?), n. [For bittacle, corrupted (perh. by influence of bin) fr. Pg. bitacola binnacle, fr. L. habitaculum dwelling place, fr. habitare to dwell. See Habit, and cf. Bittacle.] (Naut.) A case or box placed near the helmsman, containing the compass of a ship, and a light to show it at night. Totten.

binny.c: Binny Bin"ny (?), n. (Zool.) A large species of barbel (Barbus bynni), found in the Nile, and much esteemed for food.

binocle.c: Binocle Bin"o*cle (?), n. [F. binocle; L. bini two at a time + oculus eye.] (Opt.) A dioptric telescope, fitted with two tubes joining, so as to enable a person to view an object with both eyes at once; a double-barreled field glass or an opera glass.

binocular.c: Binocular Bin*oc"u*lar (?), a. [Cf. F. binoculaire. See Binocle.] 1. Having two eyes. “Most animals are binocular.” Derham.
Binocular Bin*oc"u*lar (?), n. A binocular glass, whether opera glass, telescope, or microscope.

binocularly.c: Binocularly Bin*oc"u*lar*ly, adv. In a binocular manner.

binomial.c: Binomial Bi*no"mi*al (?), n. [L. bis twice + nomen name: cf. F. binome, LL. binomius (or fr. bi- + Gr.? distribution?). Cf. Monomial.] (Alg.) An expression consisting of two terms connected by the sign plus (+) or minus (-); as, a + b, or 7 - 3.
Binomial Bi*no"mi*al, a. 1. Consisting of two terms; pertaining to binomials; as, a binomial root.

binominal.c: Binominal Bi*nom"i*nal (?), a. [See Binomial.] Of or pertaining to two names; binomial.

binotonous.c: Binotonous Bi*not"o*nous (?), a. [L. bini two at a time + tonus, fr. Gr.?, tone.] Consisting of two notes; as, a binotonous cry.

binoxalate.c: Binoxalate Bin*ox"a*late (?), n. [Pref. bin- + oxalate.] (Chem.) A salt having two equivalents of oxalic acid to one of the base; an acid oxalate.

binoxide.c: Binoxide Bin*ox"ide (?), n. [Pref. bin- + oxide.] (Chem.) Same as Dioxide.

binturong.c: Binturong ‖Bin"tu*rong (?), n. (Zool.) A small Asiatic civet of the genus Arctilis.

binucleate.c: Binucleate Binuclear { Bi*nu"cle*ar (?), Bi*nu"cle*ate (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + nuclear, nucleate.] (Biol.) Having two nuclei; as, binucleate cells.

binucleolate.c: Binucleolate Bi*nu"cle*o*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + nucleolus.] (Biol.) Having two nucleoli.

bioblast.c: Bioblast Bi"o*blast (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + -blast.] (Biol.) Same as Bioplast.

biocellate.c: Biocellate Bi*oc"el*late (?), a. [L. bis twice + ocellatus. See Ocellated.] (Zool.) Having two ocelli (eyelike spots); -- said of a wing, etc.

biochemistry.c: Biochemistry Bi`o*chem"is*try (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. chemistry.] (Biol.) The chemistry of living organisms; the chemistry of the processes incidental to, and characteristic of, life.

biodynamical.c: Biodynamical Biodynamic { Bi`o*dy*nam"ic (?), Bi`o*dy*nam"ic*al (?) }, a.} 1. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to biodynamics, or the doctrine of vital forces or energy.

biodynamics.c: Biodynamics Bi`o*dy*nam"ics (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. dynamics.] 1. (Biol.) The doctrine of vital forces or energy. [archaic]

biogeny.c: Biogeny Biogenesis { Bi`o*gen"e*sis (?), Bi*og"e*ny (?), } n. [Gr. bi`os life +?,?, birth.] (Biol.) (a) A doctrine that the genesis or production of living organisms can take place only through the agency of living germs or parents; -- called also biogeny; -- opposed to abiogenesis. (b) Life development generally.

biogenist.c: Biogenist Bi*og"e*nist (?), n. A believer in the theory of biogenesis.

biogeography.c: Biogeography Bi`o*ge*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. geography.] The branch of biology which deals with the geographical distribution of animals and plants. It includes both zoögeography and phytogeography. -- Bi`o*ge`o*graph"ic (#), a. -- Bi`o*ge`o*graph"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

biognosis.c: Biognosis ‖Bi`og*no"sis (?), n. [Gr.? life +? investigation.] (Biol.) The investigation of life.

biograph.c: Biograph Bi"o*graph (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + -graph.] 1. An animated picture machine for screen projection; a cinematograph. [obsolescent]

biographer.c: Biographer Bi*og"ra*pher (?), n. One who writes an account or history of the life of a particular person; a writer of lives, as Plutarch.

biographical.c: Biographical Biographic { Bi"o*graph"ic (?), Bi`o*graph"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to biography; containing biography. -- Bi`o*graph"ic*al*ly, adv.

biographize.c: Biographize Bi*og"ra*phize (?), v. t. To write a history of the life of. Southey.

biography.c: Biography Bi*og"ra*phy (?), n.; pl. Biographies (?). [Gr.?; bi`os life +? to write: cf. F. biographie. See Graphic.] 1. The written history of a person's life.

biological.c: Biological Biologic { Bi`o*log"ic (?), Bi`o*log"ic*al (?), } a. 1. Of or relating to biology. -- Bi`o*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

biologist.c: Biologist Bi*ol"o*gist (?), n. A student of biology; one versed in the science of biology.

biology.c: Biology Bi*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + -logy: cf. F. biologie.] The science of life; that branch of knowledge which treats of living matter as distinct from matter which is not living; the study of living tissue. It has to do with the origin, structure, development, function, and distribution of animals and plants.

biolysis.c: Biolysis ‖Bi*ol"y*sis (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life +? a dissolving.] (Biol.) The destruction of life.

biolytic.c: Biolytic Bi`o*lyt"ic (?), a. [Gr. bi`os life +? to destroy.] Relating to the destruction of life.

biomagnetism.c: Biomagnetism Bi`o*mag"net*ism (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. magnetism.] 1. Animal magnetism.

biometry.c: Biometry Bi*om"e*try (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + -metry.] Measurement of life; calculation of the probable duration of human life.

bion.c: Bion Bi"on (?), n. [Gr. biw^n living, p. pr. of bioy^n to live.] (Biol.) The physiological individual, characterized by definiteness and independence of function, in distinction from the morphological individual or morphon.

bionomy.c: Bionomy Bi*on"o*my (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + no`mos law.] Physiology. [R.] Dunglison.

biophore.c: Biophore Biophor { Bi"o*phor` Bi"o*phore` } (bī"o*fōr`), n. [Gr. bi`os life + fo`ros bearing, fr. fe`rein to bear.] (Biol.) One of the smaller vital units of a cell, the bearer of vitality and heredity. See Pangen, in Supplement.

biophotophone.c: Biophotophone Bi`o*pho"to*phone (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + photo + fwnh` sound, voice.] An instrument combining a cinematograph and a phonograph so that the moving figures on the screen are accompanied by the appropriate sounds; -- an archaic term replaced by movie projector. [archaic]

bioplasm.c: Bioplasm Bi"o*plasm (bī"o*plăz'm), n. [Gr. bi`os life + pla`sma form, mold, fr. pla`ssein to mold.] (Biol.) A name suggested by Dr. Beale for the germinal matter supposed to be essential to the functions of all living beings; the material through which every form of life manifests itself; unaltered protoplasm.

bioplasmic.c: Bioplasmic Bi`o*plas"mic (bī`o*plăz"mĭk), a. Pertaining to, or consisting of, bioplasm.

bioplast.c: Bioplast Bi"o*plast (-plăst), n. [Gr. bi`os life + pla`ssein to form.] (Biol.) A tiny mass of bioplasm, in itself a living unit and having formative power, as a living white blood corpuscle; bioblast.

biopsychical.c: Biopsychical Biopsychic { Bi`o*psy"chic (?), Bi`o*psy"chic*al (?) }, a.} [Gr. bi`os life + psychic, -cal.] Pertaining to psychical phenomena in their relation to the living organism or to the general phenomena of life.

biorgan.c: Biorgan Bi*or"gan (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. organ.] (Biol.) A physiological organ; a living organ; an organ endowed with function; -- distinguished from idorgan.

bioscope.c: Bioscope Bi"o*scope (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + -scope.] 1. A view of life; that which gives such a view.

biostatics.c: Biostatics Bi`o*stat"ics (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life +?. See Statics.] (Biol.) The physical phenomena of organized bodies, in opposition to their organic or vital phenomena.

biostatistics.c: Biostatistics Bi`o*sta*tis"tics (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life + E. statistics.] (Biol.) Vital statistics.

biotaxy.c: Biotaxy Bi"o*tax`y (?), n. [Gr. bi`os life +? arrangement.] (Biol.) The classification of living organisms according to their structural character; taxonomy.

biotic.c: Biotic Bi*ot"ic (?), a. [Gr. biwtiko`s pert. to life.] 1. (Biol.) Relating to life; as, the biotic principle.

biotite.c: Biotite Bi"o*tite (?), n. [From Biot, a French naturalist.] (Min.) Mica containing iron and magnesia, generally of a black or dark green color; -- a common constituent of crystalline rocks. See Mica.

bipalmate.c: Bipalmate Bi*pal"mate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + palmate.] (Bot.) Palmately branched, with the branches again palmated.

biparietal.c: Biparietal Bi`pa*ri"e*tal (?), a. [Pref. bi- + parietal.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the diameter of the cranium, from one parietal fossa to the other.

biparous.c: Biparous Bip"a*rous (?), a. [L. bis twice + parere to bring forth.] Bringing forth two at a birth.

bipartible.c: Bipartible Bi*part"i*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. bipartible. See Bipartite.] Capable of being divided into two parts.

bipartient.c: Bipartient Bi*par"tient (?), a. [L. bis twice + partiens, p. pr. of partire to divide.] Dividing into two parts. -- n. A number that divides another into two equal parts without a remainder.

bipartile.c: Bipartile Bi*par"tile (?), a. Divisible into two parts.

bipartite.c: Bipartite Bip"ar*tite (?), a. [L. bipartitus, p. p. of bipartire; bis twice + partire. See Partite.] 1. Being in two parts; having two correspondent parts, as a legal contract or writing, one for each party; shared by two; as, a bipartite treaty.

bipartition.c: Bipartition Bi`par*ti"tion (?), n. The act of dividing into two parts, or of making two correspondent parts, or the state of being so divided.

bipectinated.c: Bipectinated Bipectinate { Bi*pec"ti*nate (?), Bi*pec"ti*na`ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + pectinate.] (Biol.) Having two margins toothed like a comb.

biped.c: Biped Bi"ped (?), n. [L. bipes; bis twice + pes, pedis,?oot: cf. F. bipède.] A two-footed animal, as man.
Biped Bi"ped, a. Having two feet; two-footed.

bipedal.c: Bipedal Bip"e*dal (?), a. [L. bipedalis: cf. F. bipédal. See Biped, n.] 1. Having two feet; biped.

bipeltate.c: Bipeltate Bi*pel"tate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + peltate.] Having a shell or covering like a double shield.

bipennated.c: Bipennated Bipennate { Bi*pen"nate (?), Bi*pen"na*ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + pennate: cf. L. bipennis. Cf. Bipinnate.] Having two wings. “Bipennated insects.” Derham.

bipennis.c: Bipennis ‖Bi*pen"nis (?), n. [L.] An ax with an edge or blade on each side of the handle.

bipetalous.c: Bipetalous Bi*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. bi- + petalous.] (Bot.) Having two petals.

bipinnaria.c: Bipinnaria ‖Bi`pin*na"ri*a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. bis twice + pinna feather.] (Zool.) The larva of certain starfishes as developed in the free-swimming stage.

bipinnated.c: Bipinnated Bipinnate { Bi*pin"nate (?), Bi*pin"na*ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + pinnate; cf. F. bipinné. Cf. Bipennate.] Twice pinnate.

bipinnatifid.c: Bipinnatifid Bi`pin*nat"i*fid (?), a. [Pref. bi- + pinnatifid.] (Bot.) Doubly pinnatifid.

biplane.c: Biplane Bi"plane (?), n. [Pref. bi- + plane.] (Aëronautics) An aëroplane with two main supporting surfaces one above the other.
Biplane Bi"plane, a. (Aëronautics) Having, or consisting of, two superposed planes, aërocurves, or the like; of or pertaining to a biplane; as, a biplane rudder.

biplicate.c: Biplicate Bip"li*cate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + plicate.] Twice folded together. Henslow.

biplicity.c: Biplicity Bi*plic"i*ty (?), n. The state of being twice folded; reduplication. [R.] Bailey.

bipolar.c: Bipolar Bi*po"lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + polar. Cf. Dipolar.] Doubly polar; having two poles; as, a bipolar cell or corpuscle.

bipontine.c: Bipontine Bipont { Bi"pont (?), Bi*pont"ine } (?), a. (Bibliog.) Relating to books printed at Deuxponts, or Bipontium (Zweibrücken), in Bavaria.

biprism.c: Biprism Bi"prism (?), n. [Pref. bi- + prism.] 1. A prism whose refracting angle is very nearly 180 degrees.

bipunctate.c: Bipunctate Bi*punc"tate (?), a. [Pref. bi- + punctate.] Having two punctures, or spots.

bipupillate.c: Bipupillate Bi*pu"pil*late (?), a. [Pref. bi- + pupil (of the eye).] (Zool.) Having an eyelike spot on the wing, with two dots within it of a different color, as in some butterflies.

bipyramidal.c: Bipyramidal Bi`py*ram"i*dal (?), a. [Pref. bi- + pyramidal.] Consisting of two pyramids placed base to base; having a pyramid at each of the extremities of a prism, as in quartz crystals.

biquadrate.c: Biquadrate Bi*quad"rate (?), n. [Pref. bi- + quadrate.] (Math.) The fourth power, or the square of the square. Thus 4x4=16, the square of 4, and 16x16=256, the biquadrate of 4.

biquadratic.c: Biquadratic Bi`quad*rat"ic (?), a. [Pref. bi- + quadratic: cf. F. biquadratique.] (Math.) Of or pertaining to the biquadrate, or fourth power.
Biquadratic Bi`quad*rat"ic, n. (Math.) (a) A biquadrate. (b) A biquadratic equation.

biquintile.c: Biquintile Bi*quin"tile (?), n. [Pref. bi- + quintile: cf. F. biquintile.] (Astron.) An aspect of the planets when they are distant from each other by twice the fifth part of a great circle -- that is, twice 72 degrees.

biradiated.c: Biradiated Biradiate { Bi*ra"di*ate (?), Bi*ra"di*a`ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + radiate.] Having two rays; as, a biradiate fin.

biramous.c: Biramous Bi*ra"mous (?), a. [Pref. bi- + ramous.] (Biol.) Having, or consisting of, two branches.

birch.c: Birch Birch (bẽrch), n.; pl. Birches (-ĕz). [OE. birche, birk, AS. birce, beorc; akin to Icel. björk, Sw. björk, Dan. birk, D. berk, OHG. piricha, MHG. birche, birke, G. birke, Russ. bereza, Pol. brzoza, Serv. breza, Skr. bhūrja. √254. Cf. 1st Birk.] 1. A tree of several species, constituting the genus Betula; as, the white or common birch (Betula alba) (also called silver birch and lady birch); the dwarf birch (Betula glandulosa); the paper or canoe birch (Betula papyracea); the yellow birch (Betula lutea); the black or cherry birch (Betula lenta).
Birch Birch, a. Of or pertaining to the birch; birchen.
Birch Birch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Birched (bẽrcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Birching.] To whip with a birch rod or twig; to flog.

birchen.c: Birchen Birch"en (bẽrch"'n), a. Of or relating to birch.

bird.c: Bird Bird (bẽrd), n. [OE. brid, bred, bird, young bird, bird, AS. bridd young bird. √92.] 1. Orig., a chicken; the young of a fowl; a young eaglet; a nestling; and hence, a feathered flying animal (see 2).
Bird Bird (bẽrd), v. i. 1. To catch or shoot birds.
Bird cherry Bird" cher`ry (?). (Bot.) A shrub (Prunus Padus) found in Northern and Central Europe. It bears small black cherries.
Bird fancier Bird" fan`ci*er (?). 1. One who takes pleasure in rearing or collecting rare or curious birds.

Bird of paradise Bird" of par"a*dise (?). (Zool.) The name of several very beautiful birds of the genus Paradisea and allied genera, inhabiting New Guinea and the adjacent islands. The males have brilliant colors, elegant plumes, and often remarkable tail feathers.
Bird pepper Bird" pep`per (?). A species of capsicum (Capsicum baccatum), whose small, conical, coral-red fruit is among the most piquant of all red peppers.

birdbolt.c: Birdbolt Bird"bolt` (?), n. A short blunt arrow for killing birds without piercing them. Hence: Anything which smites without penetrating. Shak.

birdcage.c: Birdcage bird-cage Bird cage { Bird" cage", bird-cage, or Bird"cage` } (?), n. A cage for confining birds.

birdcall.c: Birdcall Bird"call` (?), n. 1. A sound made in imitation of the note or cry of a bird for the purpose of decoying the bird or its mate.

birdcatcher.c: Birdcatcher Bird"catch`er (?), n. One whose employment it is to catch birds; a fowler.

birdcatching.c: Birdcatching Bird"catch`ing, n. The art, act, or occupation or catching birds or wild fowls.

birdeyed.c: Bird-eyed Bird"-eyed` (?), a. Quick-sighted; catching a glance as one goes.

birdie.c: Birdie Bird"ie (?), n. A pretty or dear little bird; -- a pet name. Tennyson.

birdikin.c: Birdikin Bird"i*kin (?), n. A young bird. Thackeray.

birding.c: Birding Bird"ing, n. Birdcatching or fowling. Shak.

birdlet.c: Birdlet Bird"let, n. A little bird; a nestling.

birdlime.c: Birdlime Bird"lime` (?), n. [Bird + lime viscous substance.] An extremely adhesive viscid substance, usually made of the middle bark of the holly, by boiling, fermenting, and cleansing it. When a twig is smeared with this substance it will hold small birds which may light upon it. Hence: Anything which insnares.
Birdlime Bird"lime`, v. t. To smear with birdlime; to catch with birdlime; to insnare.

birdling.c: Birdling Bird"ling, n. A little bird; a nestling.

birdman.c: Birdman Bird"man (?), n. A fowler or birdcatcher.

birdsbeak.c: Bird's-beak Bird's"-beak` (?), n. (Arch.) A molding whose section is thought to resemble a beak.

birdseed.c: Birdseed Bird"seed` (?), n. Canary seed, hemp, millet or other small seeds used for feeding caged birds.

birdseye.c: Bird's-eye Bird's"-eye` (?), a. 1. Seen from above, as if by a flying bird; embraced at a glance; hence, general; not minute, or entering into details; as, a bird's-eye view.
Bird's-eye Bird's"-eye`, n. (Bot.) A plant with a small bright flower, as the Adonis or pheasant's eye, the mealy primrose (Primula farinosa), and species of Veronica, Geranium, etc.
Bird's-eye maple Bird's"-eye` ma"ple (?). See under Maple.

birdsfoot.c: Bird's-foot Bird's"-foot` (?), n. (Bot.) A papilionaceous plant, the Ornithopus, having a curved, cylindrical pod tipped with a short, clawlike point.

birdsmouth.c: Bird's-mouth Bird's-mouth` (?), n. (Arch.) An interior angle or notch cut across a piece of timber, for the reception of the edge of another, as that in a rafter to be laid on a plate; -- commonly called crow's-foot in the United States.

birdsnest.c: Bird's-nest Bird's nest { Bird's" nest`, or Bird's-nest } (?), n. 1. The nest in which a bird lays eggs and hatches her young.

birdsnesting.c: Bird's-nesting Bird's-nest`ing (bẽrdz"nĕst`ĭng), n. Hunting for, or taking, birds' nests or their contents.

birdwitted.c: Bird-witted Bird"-wit`ted (?), a. Flighty; passing rapidly from one subject to another; not having the faculty of attention. Bacon.

birdwoman.c: Birdwoman Bird"wom`an (?), n. An airwoman; an aviatress. [Colloq.]

birectangular.c: Birectangular Bi`rec*tan"gu*lar (?), a. [Pref. bi- + rectangular.] Containing or having two right angles; as, a birectangular spherical triangle.

bireme.c: Bireme Bi"reme (?), n. [L. biremis; bis twice + remus oar: cf. F. birème.] An ancient galley or vessel with two banks or tiers of oars.

birk.c: Birk Birk (?), n. [See Birch, n.] A birch tree. [Prov. Eng.] “The silver birk.” Tennyson.
Birk Birk, n. (Zool.) A small European minnow (Leuciscus phoxinus).

birken.c: Birken Birk"en (?), v. t. [From 1st Birk.] To whip with a birch or rod. [Obs.]
Birken Birk"en, a. Birchen; as, birken groves. Burns.

birkie.c: Birkie Bir"kie (?), n. A lively or mettlesome fellow. [Jocular, Scot.] Burns.

birl.c: Birl Birl (?), v. t. & i. To revolve or cause to revolve; to spin. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
Birl Birl (?), v. t. & i. [AS. byrlian. √92.] To pour (beer or wine); to ply with drink; to drink; to carouse. [Obs. or Dial.] Skelton.

birlaw.c: Birlaw Bir"law (?), n. [See By-law.] (Law) A law made by husbandmen respecting rural affairs; a rustic or local law or by-law. [Written also byrlaw, birlie, birley.]

birostrated.c: Birostrated Birostrate { Bi*ros`trate (?), Bi*ros"tra*ted (?), } a. [Pref. bi- + rostrate.] Having a double beak, or two processes resembling beaks.

birr.c: Birr Birr (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Birred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Birring.] [Cf. OE. bur, bir, wind, storm wind, fr. Icel. byrr wind. Perh. imitative.] To make, or move with, a whirring noise, as of wheels in motion.
Birr Birr, n. 1. A whirring sound, as of a spinning wheel.

birrus.c: Birrus Bir"rus (?), n. [LL., fr. L. birrus a kind of cloak. See Berretta.] A coarse kind of thick woolen cloth, worn by the poor in the Middle Ages; also, a woolen cap or hood worn over the shoulders or over the head.

birse.c: Birse Birse (?), n. A bristle or bristles. [Scot.]
