Block tin Block" tin` (?). See under Tin.

blockade.c: Blockade Block*ade" (?), n. [Cf. It. bloccata. See Block, v. t. ] 1. The shutting up of a place by troops or ships, with the purpose of preventing ingress or egress, or the reception of supplies; as, the blockade of the ports of an enemy.

Blockade Block*ade", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blockaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Blockading.] 1. To shut up, as a town or fortress, by investing it with troops or vessels or war for the purpose of preventing ingress or egress, or the introduction of supplies. See note under Blockade, n. “Blockaded the place by sea.” Gilpin.

blockage.c: Blockage Block"age (?), n. The act of blocking up; the state of being blocked up.

blockhead.c: Blockhead Block"head` (?), n. [Block + head.] A stupid fellow; a dolt; a person deficient in understanding.

blockheadism.c: Blockheadism Block"head*ism (?), n. That which characterizes a blockhead; stupidity. Carlyle.

blockhouse.c: Blockhouse Block"house` (?), n. [Block + house: cf. G. blockhaus.] 1. (Mil.) An edifice or structure of heavy timbers or logs for military defense, having its sides loopholed for musketry, and often an upper story projecting over the lower, or so placed upon it as to have its sides make an angle wit the sides of the lower story, thus enabling the defenders to fire downward, and in all directions; -- formerly much used in America and Germany.

blocking.c: Blocking Block"ing, n. 1. The act of obstructing, supporting, shaping, or stamping with a block or blocks.
Blocking course Block"ing course` (?). (Arch.) The finishing course of a wall showing above a cornice.

blockish.c: Blockish Block"ish, a. Like a block; deficient in understanding; stupid; dull. “Blockish Ajax.” Shak. -- Block"ish*ly, adv. -- Block"ish*ness, n.

blocklike.c: Blocklike Block"like` (?), a. Like a block; stupid.

bloedite.c: Bloedite Bloe"dite (?), n. [From the chemist Blöde.] (Min.) A hydrous sulphate of magnesium and sodium.

blolly.c: Blolly Blol"ly (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A shrub or small tree of southern Florida and the West Indies (Pisonia obtusata) with smooth oval leaves and a hard, 10-ribbed fruit. (b) The rubiaceous shrub Chicocca racemosa, of the same region.

blonket.c: Blonket Bloncket { Blonc"ket, Blon"ket } (?), a. [OF. blanquet whitish, dim. of blanc white. Cf. Blanket.] Gray; bluish gray. [Obs.]

blonde.c: Blonde Blond { Blond, Blonde } (?), a. [F., fair, light, of uncertain origin; cf. AS. blonden-feax gray-haired, old, prop. blended-haired, as a mixture of white and brown or black. See Blend, v. t. ] Of a fair color; light-colored; as, blond hair; a blond complexion.
Blonde Blonde (?), n. [F.] 1. A person of very fair complexion, with light hair and light blue eyes. [Written also blond.]

blond.c: Blond metal Blond" met`al (?). A variety of clay ironstone, in Staffordshire, England, used for making tools.

blondness.c: Blondness Blond"ness, n. The state of being blond. G. Eliot.

blood.c: Blood Blood (blŭd), n. [OE. blod, blood, AS. blōd; akin to D. bloed, OHG. bluot, G. blut, Goth. blōþ, Icel. blōð, Sw. & Dan. blod; prob. fr. the same root as E. blow to bloom. See Blow to bloom.] 1. The fluid which circulates in the principal vascular system of animals, carrying nourishment to all parts of the body, and bringing away waste products to be excreted. See under Arterial.
Blood Blood (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blooded; p. pr. & vb. n. Blooding.] 1. To bleed. [Obs.] Cowper.
Blood money Blood" mon`ey (?). 1. Money paid to the next of kin of a person who has been killed by another.
Blood vessel Blood" ves`sel (?). (Anat.) Any vessel or canal in which blood circulates in an animal, as an artery or vein.

bloodbird.c: Bloodbird Blood"bird` (blŭd"bẽrd`), n. (Zool.) An Australian honeysucker (Myzomela sanguineolata); -- so called from the bright red color of the male bird.

bloodboltered.c: Blood-boltered Blood"-bol`tered (?), a. [Blood + Prov. E. bolter to mat in tufts. Cf. Balter.] Having the hair matted with clotted blood. [Obs. & R.]

blooded.c: Blooded Blood"ed, a. Having pure blood, or a large admixture or pure blood; of approved breed; of the best stock.

bloodflower.c: Bloodflower Blood"flow`er (?), n. [From the color of the flower.] (Bot.) A genus of bulbous plants, natives of Southern Africa, named Hæmanthus, of the Amaryllis family. The juice of Hæmanthus toxicarius is used by the Hottentots to poison their arrows.

bloodguilty.c: Bloodguilty Blood"guilt`y (?), a. Guilty of murder or bloodshed. “A bloodguilty life.” Fairfax. -- Blood"guilt`i*ness (?), n. -- Blood"guilt`less, a.

bloodhound.c: Bloodhound Blood"hound` (blŭd"hound`), n. A breed of large and powerful dogs, with long, smooth, and pendulous ears, and remarkable for acuteness of smell. It is employed to recover game or prey which has escaped wounded from a hunter, and for tracking criminals. Formerly it was used for pursuing runaway slaves. Other varieties of dog are often used for the same purpose and go by the same name. The Cuban bloodhound is said to be a variety of the mastiff.

bloodily.c: Bloodily Blood"i*ly (?), adv. In a bloody manner; cruelly; with a disposition to shed blood.

bloodiness.c: Bloodiness Blood"i*ness, n. 1. The state of being bloody.

bloodless.c: Bloodless Blood"less, a. [AS. blōdleás.] 1. Destitute of blood, or apparently so; as, bloodless cheeks; lifeless; dead.

bloodlet.c: Bloodlet Blood"let` (blŭd"lĕt`), v. t. [AS. blōdlǣtan; blōd blood + lǣatan to let.] bleed; to let blood. Arbuthnot.

bloodletter.c: Bloodletter Blood"let`ter (?), n. One who, or that which, lets blood; a phlebotomist.

bloodletting.c: Bloodletting Blood"let`ting, n. (Med.) The act or process of letting blood or bleeding, as by opening a vein or artery, or by cupping or leeches; -- esp. applied to venesection.

bloodroot.c: Bloodroot Blood"root` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant (Sanguinaria Canadensis), with a red root and red sap, and bearing a pretty, white flower in early spring; -- called also puccoon, redroot, bloodwort, tetterwort, turmeric, and Indian paint. It has acrid emetic properties, and the rootstock is used as a stimulant expectorant. See Sanguinaria.

bloodshed.c: Bloodshed Blood"shed` (?), n. [Blood + shed] The shedding or spilling of blood; slaughter; the act of shedding human blood, or taking life, as in war, riot, or murder.

bloodshedder.c: Bloodshedder Blood"shed`der (?), n. One who sheds blood; a manslayer; a murderer.

bloodshot.c: Bloodshot Blood"shot` (?), a. [Blood + shot, p. p. of shoot to variegate.] Red and inflamed; suffused with blood, or having the vessels turgid with blood, as when the conjunctiva is inflamed or irritated.

bloodstick.c: Bloodstick Blood"stick" (?), n. (Far.) A piece of hard wood loaded at one end with lead, and used to strike the fleam into the vein. Youatt.

bloodstone.c: Bloodstone Blood"stone` (?), n. (Min.) (a) A green siliceous stone sprinkled with red jasper, as if with blood; hence the name; -- called also heliotrope. (b) Hematite, an ore of iron yielding a blood red powder or “streak.”

bloodstroke.c: Bloodstroke Blood"stroke` (?), n. [Cf. F. coup de sang.] Loss of sensation and motion from hemorrhage or congestion in the brain. Dunglison.

bloodsucker.c: Bloodsucker Blood"suck`er (?), n. 1. (Zool.) Any animal that sucks blood; esp., the leech (Hirudo medicinalis), and related species.

bloodthirsty.c: Bloodthirsty Blood"thirst`y (?), a. Eager to shed blood; cruel; sanguinary; murderous; having a bloodlust. -- Blood"thirst`i*ness (?), n.

bloodwit.c: Bloodwit Bloodwite { Blood"wite` (?), Blood"wit` (?), } n. [AS. blōwīte; blōd blood, + wīte wite, fine.] (Anc. Law) A fine or amercement paid as part of a settlement for the shedding of blood; also, a riot wherein blood was spilled.

bloodwood.c: Bloodwood Blood"wood (?), n. (Bot.) A tree having the wood or the sap of the color of blood.

bloodwort.c: Bloodwort Blood"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant, Rumex sanguineus, or bloody-veined dock. The name is applied also to bloodroot (Sanguinaria Canadensis), and to an extensive order of plants (Hæmodoraceæ), the roots of many species of which contain a red coloring matter useful in dyeing.

bloody.c: Bloody Blood"y (?), a. [AS. blōdig.] 1. Containing or resembling blood; of the nature of blood; as, bloody excretions; bloody sweat.
Bloody Blood"y, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bloodied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bloodying.] To stain with blood. Overbury.
Bloody flux Blood"y flux` (?). The dysentery, a disease in which the flux or discharge from the bowels has a mixture of blood. Arbuthnot.
Bloody hand Blood"y hand` (?). 1. A hand stained with the blood of a deer, which, in the old forest laws of England, was sufficient evidence of a man's trespass in the forest against venison. Jacob.
Bloody sweat Blood"y sweat` (?). A sweat accompanied by a discharge of blood; a disease, called sweating sickness, formerly prevalent in England and other countries.

bloodyminded.c: Bloody-minded Blood"y-mind"ed (?), a. Having a cruel, ferocious disposition; bloodthirsty. Dryden.

bloom.c: Bloom Bloom (?), n. [OE. blome, fr. Icel. bl?m, bl?mi; akin to Sw. blom, Goth. bl?ma, OS. bl?mo, D. bloem, OHG. bluomo, bluoma, G. blume; fr. the same root as AS. bl?wan to blow, blossom. See Blow to bloom, and cf. Blossom.] 1. A blossom; the flower of a plant; an expanded bud; flowers, collectively.
Bloom Bloom, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bloomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blooming.] 1. To produce or yield blossoms; to blossom; to flower or be in flower.
Bloom Bloom, v. t. 1. To cause to blossom; to make flourish. [R.]

Bloom Bloom, n. [AS. bl?ma a mass or lump, īsenes bl?ma a lump or wedge of iron.] (Metal.) (a) A mass of wrought iron from the Catalan forge or from the puddling furnace, deprived of its dross, and shaped usually in the form of an oblong block by shingling. (b) A large bar of steel formed directly from an ingot by hammering or rolling, being a preliminary shape for further working.

bloomer.c: Bloomer Bloom"er (?), n. [From Mrs. Bloomer, an American, who sought to introduce this style of dress.] 1. A costume for women, consisting of a short dress, with loose trousers gathered round ankles, and (commonly) a broad-brimmed hat.

bloomery.c: Bloomery Bloom"er*y (?), n. (Manuf.) A furnace and forge in which wrought iron in the form of blooms is made directly from the ore, or (more rarely) from cast iron.

blooming.c: Blooming Bloom"ing, n. (Metal.) The process of making blooms from the ore or from cast iron.
Blooming Bloom"ing, a. 1. Opening in blossoms; flowering.

bloomingly.c: Bloomingly Bloom"ing*ly, adv. In a blooming manner.

bloomless.c: Bloomless Bloom"less, a. Without bloom or flowers. Shelley.

bloomy.c: Bloomy Bloom"y (?), a. 1. Full of bloom; flowery; flourishing with the vigor of youth; as, a bloomy spray.

blooth.c: Blooth Blooth (?), n. Bloom; a blossoming. [Prov. Eng.]

blore.c: Blore Blore (?), n. [Perh. a variant of blare, v. i.; or cf. Gael. & Ir. blor a loud noise.] The act of blowing; a roaring wind; a blast. [Obs.]

blossom.c: Blossom Blos"som (blŏs"sŭm), n. [OE. blosme, blostme, AS. blōsma, blōstma, blossom; akin to D. bloesem, L. fios, and E. flower; from the root of E. blow to blossom. See Blow to blossom, and cf. Bloom a blossom.] 1. The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages; florescence; bloom; the flowers of a plant, collectively; as, the blossoms and fruit of a tree; an apple tree in blossom.
Blossom Blos"som, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blossomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blossoming.] [AS. bl?stmian. See Blossom, n.] 1. To put forth blossoms or flowers; to bloom; to blow; to flower.

blossomy.c: Blossomy Blos"som*y (?), a. Full of blossoms; flowery.

blot.c: Blot Blot (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blotted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blotting.] [Cf. Dan. plette. See 3d Blot.]
Blot Blot, v. i. To take a blot; as, this paper blots easily.
Blot Blot, n. [Cf. Icel. blettr, Dan. plet.] 1. A spot or stain, as of ink on paper; a blur. “Inky blots and rotten parchment bonds.” Shak.

Blot Blot, n. [Cf. Dan. blot bare, naked, Sw. blott, d. bloot, G. bloss, and perh. E. bloat.] 1. (Backgammon) (a) An exposure of a single man to be taken up. (b) A single man left on a point, exposed to be taken up.

blotch.c: Blotch Blotch (?), n. [Cf. OE. blacche in blacchepot blacking pot, akin to black, as bleach is akin to bleak. See Black, a., or cf. Blot a spot.] 1. A blot or spot, as of color or of ink; especially a large or irregular spot. Also Fig.; as, a moral blotch.

blotched.c: Blotched Blotched (?), a. Marked or covered with blotches.

blote.c: Blote Blote (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bloted; p. pr. & vb. n. Bloting.] [Cf. Sw. blöt-fisk soaked fish, fr. blöta to soak. See 1st Bloat.] To cure, as herrings, by salting and smoking them; to bloat. [Obs.]

blotter.c: Blotter Blot"ter (blŏt"tẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, blots; esp. a device for absorbing superfluous ink.

blottesque.c: Blottesque Blot*tesque" (blŏt*tĕsk"), a. (Painting) Characterized by blots or heavy touches; coarsely depicted; wanting in delineation. Ruskin.

blotting.c: Blotting paper Blot"ting pa`per (pā`pẽr). A kind of thick, bibulous, unsized paper, used to absorb superfluous ink from a freshly written manuscript, and thus prevent blots.

blouse.c: Blouse Blouse (blouz; F. blōoz), n. [F. blouse. Of unknown origin.] A light, loose over-garment, like a smock frock, worn especially by workingmen in France; also, a loose coat of any material, as the undress uniform coat of the United States army.

blow.c: Blow Blow (blō), v. i. [imp. Blew (blū); p. p. Blown (blōn); p. pr. & vb. n. Blowing.] [OE. blowen, AS. blōwan to blossom; akin to OS. blōjan, D. bloeijen, OHG. pluojan, MHG. blüejen, G. blühen, L. florere to flourish, OIr. blath blossom. Cf. Blow to puff, Flourish.] To flower; to blossom; to bloom.
Blow Blow, v. t. To cause to blossom; to put forth (blossoms or flowers).
Blow Blow, n. (Bot.) A blossom; a flower; also, a state of blossoming; a mass of blossoms. “Such a blow of tulips.” Tatler.
Blow Blow, n. [OE. blaw, blowe; cf. OHG. bliuwan, pliuwan, to beat, G. bläuen, Goth. bliggwan.] 1. A forcible stroke with the hand, fist, or some instrument, as a rod, a club, an ax, or a sword.

Blow Blow, v. i. [imp. Blew (blū); p. p. Blown (blōn); p. pr. & vb. n. Blowing.] [OE. blawen, blowen, AS. blāwan to blow, as wind; akin to OHG. plājan, G. blähen, to blow up, swell, L. flare to blow, Gr. 'ekflai`nein to spout out, and to E. bladder, blast, inflate, etc., and perh. blow to bloom.] 1. To produce a current of air; to move, as air, esp. to move rapidly or with power; as, the wind blows.
Blow Blow, v. t. 1. To force a current of air upon with the mouth, or by other means; as, to blow the fire.
Blow Blow (?), n. 1. A blowing, esp., a violent blowing of the wind; a gale; as, a heavy blow came on, and the ship put back to port.
Blow valve Blow" valve` (?). (Mach.) See Snifting valve.

blowball.c: Blowball Blow"ball` (?), n. The downy seed head of a dandelion, which children delight to blow away. B. Jonson.

blowess.c: Blowess Blowen { Blow"en (?), Blow"ess (?), } n. A prostitute; a courtesan; a strumpet. [Low] Smart.

blower.c: Blower Blow"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, blows.

blowfly.c: Blowfly Blow"fly` (?), n. (Zool.) Any species of fly of the genus Musca that deposits its eggs or young larvæ (called flyblows and maggots) upon meat or other animal products.

blowgun.c: Blowgun Blow"gun` (?), n. A tube, as of cane or reed, sometimes twelve feet long, through which an arrow (sometimes poisoned) or other projectile may be impelled by the force of the breath. It is a weapon much used by certain Indians of America and the West Indies; -- called also blowpipe, and blowtube. See Sumpitan.

blowhole.c: Blowhole Blow"hole` (?), n. 1. A cavern in a cliff, at the water level, opening to the air at its farther extremity, so that the waters rush in with each surge and rise in a lofty jet from the extremity.

blown.c: Blown Blown (?), p. p. & a. 1. Swollen; inflated; distended; puffed up, as cattle when gorged with green food which develops gas.
Blown Blown, p. p. & a. Opened; in blossom or having blossomed, as a flower. Shak.

blowoff.c: Blow-off Blow"-off` (?), n. 1. A blowing off steam, water, etc.; -- Also, adj. as, a blow-off cock or pipe.

blowout.c: Blow-out Blow"-out` (?), n. The cleaning of the flues of a boiler from scale, etc., by a blast of steam.

blowpipe.c: Blowpipe Blow"pipe` (?), n. 1. A tube for directing a jet of air into a fire or into the flame of a lamp or candle, so as to concentrate the heat on some object.

blowth.c: Blowth Blowth (?), n. [From Blow to blossom: cf. Growth.] A blossoming; a bloom. [Obs. or Archaic] “In the blowth and bud.” Sir W. Raleigh.

blowy.c: Blowy Blow"y (?), a. Windy; as, blowy weather; a blowy upland.

blowze.c: Blowze Blowze (?), n. [Prob. from the same root as blush.] A ruddy, fat-faced woman; a wench. [Obs.] Shak.

blowzed.c: Blowzed Blowzed (?), a. Having high color from exposure to the weather; ruddy-faced; blowzy; disordered.

blowzy.c: Blowzy Blowz"y (?), a. Coarse and ruddy-faced; fat and ruddy; high colored; frowzy.

blub.c: Blub Blub (?), v. t. & i. [Cf. Bleb, Blob.] To swell; to puff out, as with weeping. [Obs.]

blubber.c: Blubber Blub"ber, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blubbered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blubbering.] To weep noisily, or so as to disfigure the face; to cry in a childish manner.
Blubber Blub"ber, v. t. 1. To swell or disfigure (the face) with weeping; to wet with tears.

blubbered.c: Blubbered Blub"bered (?), p. p. & a. Swollen; turgid; as, a blubbered lip. Spenser.

blubbering.c: Blubbering Blub"ber*ing, n. The act of weeping noisily.

bluchers.c: bluchers blucher blu"cher, blu"chers (blū"kẽr), n. A kind of half boot, or high shoe, with laces over the tongue; -- named from the Prussian general Blücher. Thackeray.

bludgeon.c: Bludgeon Bludg"eon (?), n. [Cf. Ir. blocan a little block, Gael. plocan a mallet, W. plocyn, dim. of ploc block; or perh. connected with E. blow a stroke. Cf. Block, Blow a stroke.] A short stick, with one end loaded, or thicker and heavier that the other, used as an offensive weapon.

blue.c: Blue Blue (blū), a. [Compar. Bluer (blū"ẽr); superl. Bluest.] [OE. bla, blo, blew, blue, livid, black, fr. Icel.blār livid; akin to Dan. blaa blue, Sw. blå, D. blauw, OHG. blāo, G. blau; but influenced in form by F. bleu, from OHG. blāo.] 1. Having the color of the clear sky, or a hue resembling it, whether lighter or darker; as, the deep, blue sea; as blue as a sapphire; blue violets. “The blue firmament.” Milton.

Blue Blue (blū), n. 1. One of the seven colors into which the rays of light divide themselves, when refracted through a glass prism; the color of the clear sky, or a color resembling that, whether lighter or darker; a pigment having such color. Sometimes, poetically, the sky; as, to fly off into the blue.
Blue Blue, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bluing.] To make blue; to dye of a blue color; to make blue by heating, as metals, etc.
Blue blood Blue blood (blū"blŭd`), n. 1. a member of the nobility or aristocracy, or a person of high social status.
Blue book Blue" book` (?). 1. A parliamentary publication, so called from its blue paper covers. [Eng.]
Blue grass Blue" grass` (?). (Bot.) A species of grass (Poa compressa) with bluish green stems, valuable in thin gravelly soils; wire grass.

Blue Hen State Blue Hen State. The State of Delaware; -- a popular sobriquet. It is said, though the story lacks proof, to have taken its origin from the insistence of a Delaware Revolutionary captain, named Caldwell, that no cock could be truly game unless the mother was a blue hen, whence Blue Hen's Chickens came to be a nickname for the people of Delaware.
Blue jay Blue" jay` (?). (Zool.) The common jay of the United States (Cyanocitta, or Cyanura, cristata). The predominant color is bright blue.

blue jeans blue" jeans` (?), n. pl. a tight-fitting trousers made of blue denim or a similar fabric, designed originally to serve as inexpensive durable workclothes, and often having metal rivets for reinforcement. They have become very popular as casual wear for all age groups, and more expensive and more carefully styled and tailored versions called designer jeanshave also become popular among girls and women.

blueback.c: Blueback Blue"back` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A trout (Salmo oquassa) inhabiting some of the lakes of Maine. (b) A salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka) of the Columbia River and northward. (c) An American river herring (Clupea æstivalis), closely allied to the alewife.

bluebeard.c: Bluebeard Blue"beard (?), n. The hero of a mediæval French nursery legend, who, leaving home, enjoined his young wife not to open a certain room in his castle. She entered it, and found the murdered bodies of his former wives. -- Also used adjectively of a subject which it is forbidden to investigate.

bluebell.c: Bluebell Blue"bell` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A plant of the genus Campanula, especially the Campanula rotundifolia, which bears blue bell-shaped flowers; the harebell. (b) A plant of the genus Scilla (Scilla nutans).

blueberry.c: Blueberry Blue"berry (?), n. [Cf. Blaeberry.] (Bot.) The berry of several species of Vaccinium, an ericaceous genus, differing from the American huckleberries in containing numerous minute seeds instead of ten nutlets. The commonest species are Vaccinium Pennsylvanicum and Vaccinium vacillans. Vaccinium corymbosum is the tall blueberry.

bluebill.c: Bluebill Blue"bill` (?), n. (Zool.) A duck of the genus Fuligula. Two American species (Fuligula marila and Fuligula affinis) are common. See Scaup duck.

bluebird.c: Bluebird Blue"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) A small song bird (Sialia sialis), very common in the United States, and, in the north, one of the earliest to arrive in spring. The male is blue, with the breast reddish. It is related to the European robin.

bluebonnet.c: Blue-bonnet Blue bonnet { Blue" bon`net or Blue"-bon`net } (?), n. 1. A broad, flat Scottish cap of blue woolen, or one wearing such cap; a Scotchman.

bluebottle.c: blue-bottle Bluebottle Blue"bot`tle, blue-bottle (?), n. 1. (Bot.) an annual Eurasian plant (Centaurea cyanus) which grows in grain fields; -- called also bachelor's button. It receives its name from its blue bottle-shaped flowers. Varieties cultivated in North America have showy heads of blue or purple or pink or white flowers

bluebreast.c: Bluebreast Blue"breast` (?), n. (Zool.) A small European bird; the blue-throated warbler.

bluecap.c: Bluecap Blue"cap` (?), n. 1. (Zool.) (a) The bluepoll. (b) The blue bonnet or blue titmouse.

bluecoat.c: Bluecoat Blue"coat` (?), n. One dressed in blue, as a soldier, a sailor, a beadle, etc.

blueeye.c: Blue-eye Blue"-eye` (?), n. (Zool.) The blue-cheeked honeysucker of Australia.

blueeyed.c: Blue-eyed grass Blue-eyed grass (?) (Bot.) a grasslike plant (Sisyrinchium anceps), with small flowers of a delicate blue color.

bluefin.c: Bluefin Blue"fin` (?), n. (Zool.) A species of whitefish (Coregonus nigripinnis) found in Lake Michigan.

bluefish.c: Bluefish Blue"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) 1. A large voracious fish (Pomatomus saitatrix), of the family Carangidæ, valued as a food fish, and widely distributed on the American coast. On the New Jersey and Rhode Island coast it is called the horse mackerel, in Virginia saltwater tailor, or skipjack.

bluegown.c: Bluegown Blue"gown` (?), n. One of a class of paupers or pensioners, or licensed beggars, in Scotland, to whim annually on the king's birthday were distributed certain alms, including a blue gown; a beadsman.

bluegrass.c: Blue-grass State Blue-grass State. The Sate of Kentucky; -- a nickname alluding to the blue-grass region, where fine horses are bred.

bluejohn.c: Blue-john Blue"-john` (?), n. A name given to fluor spar in Derbyshire, where it is used for ornamental purposes.

bluely.c: Bluely Blue"ly, adv. With a blue color. Swift.

blueness.c: Blueness Blue"ness, n. The quality of being blue; a blue color. Boyle.

bluenoser.c: Bluenoser Bluenose Blue"nose` (?), n. A nickname for a Nova Scotian; also, a Nova Scotian ship (called also Blue"nos`er (?)); a Nova Scotian potato, etc.

bluepoll.c: Bluepoll Blue"poll` (?), n. [Blue + poll head.] (Zool.) A kind of salmon (Salmo Cambricus) found in Wales.

blueskylaw.c: Blue-skylaw Blue"-sky"law`. A law enacted to provide for the regulation and supervision of investment companies in order to protect the public against companies that do not intend to do a fair and honest business and that offer investments that do not promise a fair return; -- so called because the promises made by some investment companies are as boundless or alluring as the blue sky, or, perhaps, because designed to clear away the clouds and fogs from the simple investor's horizon. [Colloq.]

bluestocking.c: Bluestocking Blue"stock`ing (?), n. 1. A literary lady; a female pedant. [Colloq.]

bluestockingism.c: Bluestockingism Blue"stock`ing*ism (?), n. The character or manner of a bluestocking; female pedantry. [Colloq.]

bluethroat.c: Bluethroat Blue"throat` (?), n. (Zool.) A singing bird of northern Europe and Asia (Cyanecula Suecica), related to the nightingales; -- called also blue-throated robin and blue-throated warbler.

bluets.c: Bluets Blu"ets (?), n. [F. bluet, bleuet, dim. of bleu blue. See Blue, a.] (Bot.) A name given to several different species of plants having blue flowers, as the Houstonia cœrulea, the Centaurea cyanus or bluebottle, and the Vaccinium angustifolium.

blueveined.c: Blue-veined Blue"-veined` (?), a. Having blue veins or blue streaks.

bluewing.c: Bluewing Blue"wing` (?), n. (Zool.) The blue-winged teal. See Teal.

bluey.c: Bluey Blue"y (?), n. [From Blue, a.] [Australasia] 1. A bushman's blanket; -- named from its color.

bluff.c: Bluff Bluff (?), a. [Cf. OD. blaf flat, broad, blaffaert one with a broad face, also, a boaster; or G. verblüffen to confuse, LG. bluffen to frighten; to unknown origin.] 1. Having a broad, flattened front; as, the bluff bows of a ship. “Bluff visages.” Irving.
Bluff Bluff, n. 1. A high, steep bank, as by a river or the sea, or beside a ravine or plain; a cliff with a broad face.

Bluff Bluff, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bluffed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bluffing.] 1. (Poker) To deter (an opponent) from taking the risk of betting on his hand of cards, as the bluffer does by betting heavily on his own hand although it may be of less value. [U. S.]
Bluff Bluff, v. i. To act as in the game of bluff.

bluffbowed.c: Bluff-bowed Bluff"-bowed` (?), a. (Naut.) Built with the stem nearly straight up and down.

bluffheaded.c: Bluff-headed Bluff"-head`ed (?), a. (Naut.) Built with the stem nearly straight up and down.

bluffness.c: Bluffness Bluff"ness, n. The quality or state of being bluff.

bluffy.c: Bluffy Bluff"y (?), a. 1. Having bluffs, or bold, steep banks.

bluing.c: Bluing Blu"ing (?), n. 1. The act of rendering blue; as, the bluing of steel. Tomlinson.

bluish.c: Bluish Blu"ish (?), a. Somewhat blue; as, bluish veins. “Bluish mists.” Dryden. -- Blu"ish*ly, adv. -- Blu"ish*ness, n.

blunder.c: Blunder Blun"der (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blundered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blundering.] [OE. blunderen, blondren, to stir, confuse, blunder; perh. allied to blend to mix, to confound by mixture.] 1. To make a gross error or mistake; as, to blunder in writing or preparing a medical prescription. Swift.
Blunder Blun"der, v. t. 1. To cause to blunder. [Obs.] “To blunder an adversary.” Ditton.

blunderbuss.c: Blunderbuss Blun"der*buss (?), n. [Either fr. blunder + D. bus tube, box, akin to G. büchse box, gun, E. box; or corrupted fr. D. donderbus (literally) thunder box, gun, musket.] 1. A short gun or firearm, with a large bore, capable of holding a number of balls, and intended to do execution without exact aim.

blunderer.c: Blunderer Blun"der*er (?), n. One who is apt to blunder.

blunderhead.c: Blunderhead Blun"der*head` (?), n. [Blunder + head.] A stupid, blundering fellow.

blunderingly.c: Blunderingly Blun"der*ing*ly, adv. In a blundering manner.

blunge.c: Blunge Blunge (?), v. t. To amalgamate and blend; to beat up or mix in water, as clay.

blunger.c: Blunger Blun"ger (?), n. [Corrupted from plunger.] A wooden blade with a cross handle, used for mi?ing the clay in potteries; a plunger. Tomlinson.

blunging.c: Blunging Blun"ging (?), n. The process of mixing clay in potteries with a blunger. Tomlinson.

blunt.c: Blunt Blunt (blŭnt), a. [Cf. Prov. G. bludde a dull or blunt knife, Dan. blunde to sleep, Sw. & Icel. blunda; or perh. akin to E. blind.] 1. Having a thick edge or point, as an instrument; dull; not sharp.
Blunt Blunt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blunted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blunting.] 1. To dull the edge or point of, by making it thicker; to make blunt. Shak.

bluntish.c: Bluntish Blunt"ish, a. Somewhat blunt. -- Blunt"ish*ness, n.

bluntly.c: Bluntly Blunt"ly, adv. In a blunt manner; coarsely; plainly; abruptly; without delicacy, or the usual forms of civility.

bluntness.c: Bluntness Blunt"ness, n. 1. Want of edge or point; dullness; obtuseness; lack of sharpness.

blur.c: Blur Blur (blûr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blurred (blûrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Blurring.] [Prob. of same origin as blear. See Blear.] 1. To render obscure by making the form or outline of confused and uncertain, as by soiling; to smear; to make indistinct and confused; as, to blur manuscript by handling it while damp; to blur the impression of a woodcut by an excess of ink.
Blur Blur (blûr), n. 1. That which obscures without effacing; a stain; a blot, as upon paper or other substance.

blurry.c: Blurry Blur"ry (blûr"ry̆), a. Full of blurs; blurred.

blurt.c: Blurt Blurt (blûrt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blurted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blurting.] [Cf. Blare.] To utter suddenly and unadvisedly; to divulge inconsiderately; to ejaculate; -- commonly with out.

blush.c: Blush Blush (blŭsh) v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blushed (blŭsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Blushing.] [OE. bluschen to shine, look, turn red, AS. blyscan to glow; akin to blysa a torch, āblȳsian to blush, D. blozen, Dan. blusse to blaze, blush.]
Blush Blush, v. t. 1. To suffuse with a blush; to redden; to make roseate. [Obs.]
Blush Blush, n. 1. A suffusion of the cheeks or face with red, as from a sense of shame, confusion, or modesty.

blushet.c: Blushet Blush"et (?), n. A modest girl. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

blushing.c: Blushing Blush"ing, a. Showing blushes; rosy red; having a warm and delicate color like some roses and other flowers; blooming; ruddy; roseate.
Blushing Blush"ing, n. The act of turning red; the appearance of a reddish color or flush upon the cheeks.

blushingly.c: Blushingly Blush"ing*ly, adv. In a blushing manner; with a blush or blushes; as, to answer or confess blushingly.

blushless.c: Blushless Blush"less, a. Free from blushes; incapable of blushing; shameless; impudent.

blushy.c: Blushy Blush"y (?), a. Like a blush; having the color of a blush; rosy. [R.] “A blushy color.” Harvey.

bluster.c: Bluster Blus"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blustered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Blustering.] [Allied to blast.]
Bluster Blus"ter, v. t. To utter, or do, with noisy violence; to force by blustering; to bully.
Bluster Blus"ter, n. 1. Fitful noise and violence, as of a storm; violent winds; boisterousness.

blusterer.c: Blusterer Blus"ter*er (?), n. One who, or that which, blusters; a noisy swaggerer.

blustering.c: Blustering Blus"ter*ing, a. 1. Exhibiting noisy violence, as the wind; stormy; tumultuous.

blusteringly.c: Blusteringly Blus"ter*ing*ly, adv. In a blustering manner.

blusterous.c: Blusterous Blus"ter*ous (?), a. Inclined to bluster; given to blustering; blustering. Motley.

bo.c: Bo Bo (?), interj. [Cf. W. bw, an interj. of threatening or frightening; n., terror, fear, dread.] An exclamation used to startle or frighten. [Spelt also boh and boo.]

Bo tree Bo" tree` (?). (Bot.) The peepul tree; esp., the very ancient tree standing at Anurajahpoora in Ceylon, grown from a slip of the tree under which Gautama is said to have received the heavenly light and so to have become Buddha.

boa.c: Boa Bo"a (bō"ȧ), n.; pl. Boas. [L. boa a kind of water serpent. Perh. fr. bos an ox.] 1. (Zool.) A genus of large American serpents, including the boa constrictor, the emperor boa of Mexico (Boa imperator), and the chevalier boa of Peru (Boa eques).
Boa constrictor Bo"a con*strict"or (?). [NL. See Boa, and Constrictor.] (Zool.) A large and powerful serpent of tropical America, sometimes twenty or thirty feet long. See Illustration in Appendix.

boanerges.c: Boanerges ‖Bo`a*ner"ges (?). [Gr.?, fr. Heb. bnē hargem sons of thunder. -- an appellation given by Christ to two of his disciples (James and John). See Mark iii. 17.] Any declamatory and vociferous preacher or orator.

boar.c: Boar Boar (bōr), n. [OE. bar, bor, bore, AS. bār; akin to OHG. pēr, MHG. bēr, G. bär, boar (but not bär bear), and perh. Russ. borov' boar.] (Zool.) The uncastrated male of swine; specifically, the wild hog.

board.c: Board Board (bōrd), n. [OE. bord, AS. bord board, shipboard; akin to bred plank, Icel. borð board, side of a ship, Goth. fōtu-baurd footstool, D. bord board, G. brett, bort. See def. 8. √92.] 1. A piece of timber sawed thin, and of considerable length and breadth as compared with the thickness, -- used for building, etc.
Board Board, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Boarding.] 1. To cover with boards or boarding; as, to board a house. “The boarded hovel.” Cowper.
Board Board (bōrd), v. i. To obtain meals, or meals and lodgings, statedly for compensation; as, he boards at the hotel.
Board Board, v. t. [F. aborder. See Abord, v. t.] To approach; to accost; to address; hence, to woo. [Obs.]

boardable.c: Boardable Board"a*ble (?), a. That can be boarded, as a ship.

boarder.c: Boarder Board"er (?), n. 1. One who has food statedly at another's table, or meals and lodgings in his house, for pay, or compensation of any kind.

boarding.c: Boarding Board"ing, n. 1. (Naut.) The act of entering a ship, whether with a hostile or a friendly purpose.

boarfish.c: Boarfish Boar"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A Mediterranean fish (Capros aper), of the family Caproidæ; -- so called from the resemblance of the extended lips to a hog's snout. (b) An Australian percoid fish (Histiopterus recurvirostris), valued as a food fish.

boast.c: Boast Boast (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boasted; p. pr. & vb. n. Boasting.] [OE. bosten, boosten, v., bost, boost, n., noise, boasting; cf. G. bausen, bauschen, to swell, pusten, Dan. puste, Sw. pusta, to blow, Sw. pösa to swell; or W. bostio to boast, bost boast, Gael. bosd. But these last may be from English.] 1. To vaunt one's self; to brag; to say or tell things which are intended to give others a high opinion of one's self or of things belonging to one's self; as, to boast of one's exploits courage, descent, wealth.
Boast Boast, v. t. 1. To display in ostentatious language; to speak of with pride, vanity, or exultation, with a view to self-commendation; to extol.
Boast Boast, v. t. [Of uncertain etymology.] 1. (Masonry) To dress, as a stone, with a broad chisel. Weale.
Boast Boast, n. 1. Act of boasting; vaunting or bragging.

boaster.c: Boaster Boast"er (?), n. One who boasts; a braggart.
Boaster Boast"er, n. A stone mason's broad-faced chisel.

boastful.c: Boastful Boast"ful (?), a. Given to, or full of, boasting; inclined to boast; vaunting; vainglorious; self-praising. -- Boast"ful*ly, adv. -- Boast"ful*ness, n.

boasting.c: Boasting Boast"ing, n. The act of glorying or vaunting; vainglorious speaking; ostentatious display.

boastingly.c: Boastingly Boast"ing*ly, adv. Boastfully; with boasting. “He boastingly tells you.” Burke.

boastless.c: Boastless Boast"less, a. Without boasting or ostentation.

boat.c: Boat Boat (bōt), n. [OE. boot, bat, AS. bāt; akin to Icel. bātr, Sw. båt, Dan. baad, D. & G. boot. Cf. Bateau.]
Boat Boat (bōt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boated; p. pr. & vb. n. Boating.] 1. To transport in a boat; as, to boat goods.
Boat Boat, v. i. To go or row in a boat.

Boat bug Boat" bug` (?). (Zool.) An aquatic hemipterous insect of the genus Notonecta; -- so called from swimming on its back, which gives it the appearance of a little boat. Called also boat fly, boat insect, boatman, and water boatman.

Boat shell Boat" shell` (?). (Zool.) (a) A marine gastropod of the genus Crepidula. The species are numerous. It is so named from its form and interior deck. (b) A marine univalve shell of the genus Cymba.

boatable.c: Boatable Boat"a*ble (?), a. 1. Such as can be transported in a boat.

boatage.c: Boatage Boat"age (?), n. Conveyance by boat; also, a charge for such conveyance.

boatbill.c: Boatbill Boat"bill` (?), n. (Zool.) 1. A wading bird (Cancroma cochlearia) of the tropical parts of South America. Its bill is somewhat like a boat with the keel uppermost.

boatful.c: Boatful Boat"ful (?), n.; pl. Boatfuls. The quantity or amount that fills a boat.

boathouse.c: Boathouse Boat"house` (?), n. A house for sheltering boats.

boating.c: Boating Boat"ing, n. 1. The act or practice of rowing or sailing, esp. as an amusement; carriage in boats.

boation.c: Boation Bo*a"tion (?), n. [L. boatus, fr. boare to roar.] A crying out; a roaring; a bellowing; reverberation. [Obs.]

boatman.c: Boatman Boat"man (?), n.; pl. Boatmen (?). 1. A man who manages a boat; a rower of a boat.

boatmanship.c: Boatmanship Boat"man*ship, n. The art of managing a boat.

boatswain.c: Boatswain Boat"swain (?), n. [Boat + swain.] 1. (Naut.) An officer who has charge of the boats, sails, rigging, colors, anchors, cables, cordage, etc., of a ship, and who also summons the crew, and performs other duties.

boattail.c: Boat-tail Boat"-tail` (?), n. (Zool.) A large grackle or blackbird (Quiscalus major), found in the Southern United States.

boatwoman.c: Boatwoman Boat"wom`an (?), n.; pl. Boatwomen (?). A woman who manages a boat.

bob.c: Bob Bob (bŏb), n. [An onomatopoetic word, expressing quick, jerky motion; OE. bob bunch, bobben to strike, mock, deceive. Cf. Prov. Eng. bob, n., a ball, an engine beam, bunch, blast, trick, taunt, scoff; as, a v., to dance, to courtesy, to disappoint, OF. bober to mock.] 1. Anything that hangs so as to play loosely, or with a short abrupt motion, as at the end of a string; a pendant; as, the bob at the end of a kite's tail.

Bob Bob (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bobbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bobbing.] [OE. bobben. See Bob, n.] 1. To cause to move in a short, jerking manner; to move (a thing) with a bob. “He bobbed his head.” W. Irving.
Bob Bob, v. i. 1. To have a short, jerking motion; to play to and fro, or up and down; to play loosely against anything. “Bobbing and courtesying.” Thackeray.
Bob wig Bob" wig` (?). A short wig with bobs or short curls; -- called also bobtail wig. Spectator.

bobance.c: Bobance Bo*bance" (?), n. [OF. bobance, F. bombance, boasting, pageantry, fr. L. bombus a humming, buzzing.] A boasting. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bobber.c: Bobber Bob"ber (?), n. One who, or that which, bobs.

bobbery.c: Bobbery Bob"ber*y (?), n. [Prob. an Anglo-Indian form of Hindi bāp re O thou father! (a very disrespectful address).] A squabble; a tumult; a commotion; a noisy disturbance; as, to raise a bobbery. [Low] Halliwell.

bobbin.c: Bobbin Bob"bin (?), n. [F. bobine; of uncertain origin; cf. L. bombus a humming, from the noise it makes, or Ir. & Gael. baban tassel, or E. bob.] 1. A small pin, or cylinder, formerly of bone, now most commonly of wood, used in the making of pillow lace. Each thread is wound on a separate bobbin which hangs down holding the thread at a slight tension.

bobbinet.c: Bobbinet Bob`bi*net" (?), n. [Bobbin + net.] A kind of cotton lace which is wrought by machines, and not by hand. [Sometimes written bobbin net.]

bobbinwork.c: Bobbinwork Bob"bin*work` (?), n. Work woven with bobbins.

bobbish.c: Bobbish Bob"bish (?), a. Hearty; in good spirits. [Low, Eng.] Dickens.

bobby.c: Bobby Bob"by (?), n. A nickname for a British policeman; -- from Sir Robert Peel, who remodeled the police force. See Peeler. [Slang, Eng.] Dickens.

bobcherry.c: Bob-cherry Bob"-cher`ry (?), n. A play among children, in which a cherry, hung so as to bob against the mouth, is to be caught with the teeth.

bobfly.c: Bobfly Bob"fly` (?), n. (Fishing) The fly at the end of the leader; an end fly.

bobolink.c: Bobolink Bob"o*link` (?), n. (Zool.) An American singing bird (Dolichonyx oryzivorus). The male is black and white; the female is brown; -- called also, ricebird, reedbird, and Boblincoln.

bobsleigh.c: Bobsleigh Bobsled { Bob"sled` (?), Bob"sleigh` } (?), n. 1. A short sled, mostly used as one of a pair connected by a reach or coupling; also, the compound sled so formed. [U. S.]

bobstay.c: Bobstay Bob"stay` (?), n. [Bob + stay.] (Naut.) A rope or chain to confine the bowsprit of a ship downward to the stem or cutwater; -- usually in the pl.

bobtail.c: Bobtail Bob"tail` (?), n. [Bob + tail.] An animal (as a horse or dog) with a short tail.

bobtailed.c: Bobtailed Bob"tailed` (?), a. Having the tail cut short, or naturally short; curtailed; as, a bobtailed horse or dog; a bobtailed coat.

bobwhite.c: Bobwhite Bob"white` (?), n. (Zool.) The common quail of North America (Colinus, or Ortyx, Virginianus); -- so called from its note.

bocal.c: Bocal Bo"cal (?), n. [F.] A cylindrical glass vessel, with a large and short neck.

bocardo.c: Bocardo Bo*car"do (?), n. [A mnemonic word.] 1. (Logic) A form of syllogism of which the first and third propositions are particular negatives, and the middle term a universal affirmative.

bocasine.c: Bocasine Boc"a*sine (?), n. [F. bocassin, boucassin.] A sort of fine buckram.

bocca.c: Bocca ‖Boc"ca (?), n. [It., mouth.] The round hole in the furnace of a glass manufactory through which the fused glass is taken out. Craig.

boce.c: Boce Boce (bōs), n. [L. box, bocis, Gr. bo`ax, bw^x.] (Zool.) A European fish (Box vulgaris), having a compressed body and bright colors; -- called also box, and bogue.

bock.c: Bock beer Bock" beer` (?). [G. bockbier; bock a buck + bier beer; -- said to be so named from its tendency to cause the drinker to caper like a goat.] A strong beer, originally made in Bavaria. [Also written buck beer.]

bockelet.c: Bockelet Bock"e*let (?), n. (Zool.) A kind of long-winged hawk; -- called also bockerel, and bockeret. [Obs.]

bockey.c: Bockey Bock"ey (?), n. [D. bokaal.] A bowl or vessel made from a gourd. [Local, New York] Bartlett.

bocking.c: Bocking Bock"ing, n. A coarse woolen fabric, used for floor cloths, to cover carpets, etc.; -- so called from the town of Bocking, in England, where it was first made.

bockland.c: Bockland Bookland { Book"land` (?), Bock"land` } (?), n. [AS. bōcland; bōc book + land land.] (O. Eng. Law) Charter land held by deed under certain rents and free services, which differed in nothing from free socage lands. This species of tenure has given rise to the modern freeholds.

bode.c: Bode Bode (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boded; p. pr. & vb. n. Boding.] [OE. bodien, AS. bodian to announce, tell from bod command; akin to Icel. bo?a to announce, Sw. båda to announce, portend. √89. See Bid.] To indicate by signs, as future events; to be the omen of; to portend to presage; to foreshow.
Bode Bode, v. i. To foreshow something; to augur.
Bode Bode, n. 1. An omen; a foreshadowing. [Obs.]
Bode Bode, n. [AS. boda; akin to OFries. boda, AS. bodo, OHG. boto. See Bode, v. t.] A messenger; a herald. Robertson.
Bode Bode, n. [See Abide.] A stop; a halting; delay. [Obs.]
Bode Bode, imp. & p. p. from Bide. Abode.
Bode Bode, p. p. of Bid. Bid or bidden. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bodement.c: Bodement Bode"ment (?), n. An omen; a prognostic. [Obs.]

bodge.c: Bodge Bodge (?), n. A botch; a patch. [Dial.] Whitlock.
Bodge Bodge (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bodged (?).] To botch; to mend clumsily; to patch. [Obs. or Dial.]

bodhisattwa.c: Bodhisattwa Bodhisattva Bodhisat { Bo"dhi*sat (?), ‖Bo`dhi*satt"va, ‖Bo`dhi*satt"wa (?) }, n. [Skr. bōdhisattva (perh. through Pali bōdhisattō); fr. bōdhi knowledge, enlightenment + sattva being, essence.] (Buddhism) One who has reached the highest degree of saintship, so that in his next incarnation he will be a Buddha, or savior of the world. -- Bo"dhi*sat`ship, n.

bodian.c: Bodian Bo"di*an (?), n. (Zool.) A large food fish (Diagramma lineatum), native of the East Indies.

bodice.c: Bodice Bod"ice (?), n. [This is properly the plural of body, Oe. bodise a pair of bodies, equiv. to a bodice. Cf. Corset, and see Body.] 1. A kind of under waist stiffened with whalebone, etc., worn esp. by women; a corset; stays.

bodiced.c: Bodiced Bod"iced (?), a. Wearing a bodice. Thackeray.

bodied.c: Bodied Bod"ied (?), a. Having a body; -- usually in composition; as, able-bodied.

bodily.c: Bodily Bod"i*ly (?), a. 1. Having a body or material form; physical; corporeal; consisting of matter.
Bodily Bod"i*ly, adv. 1. Corporeally; in bodily form; united with a body or matter; in the body.

boding.c: Boding Bod"ing (bōd"ĭng), a. Foreshowing; presaging; ominous. -- Bod"ing*ly, adv.
Boding Bod"ing, n. A prognostic; an omen; a foreboding.

bodkin.c: Bodkin Bod"kin (bŏd"kĭn), n. [OE. boydekyn dagger; of uncertain origin; cf. W. bidog hanger, short sword, Ir. bideog, Gael. biodag.] 1. A dagger. [Obs.]

bodle.c: Bodle Bo"dle (?), n. A small Scotch coin worth about one sixth of an English penny. Sir W. Scott.

bodleian.c: Bodleian Bod"lei*an, a. Of or pertaining to Sir Thomas Bodley, or to the celebrated library at Oxford, founded by him in the sixteenth century.

bodock.c: Bodock Bo*dock" (?), n. [Corrupt. fr. bois d'arc.] The Osage orange. [Southwestern U.S.]

bodrage.c: Bodrage Bod"rage (?), n. [Prob. of Celtic origin: cf. Bordrage.] A raid. [Obs.]

bod.c: Bod veal Bod veal. Veal too immature to be suitable for food.

body.c: Body Bod"y (?), n.; pl. Bodies (?). [OE. bodi, AS. bodig; akin to OHG. botah. √257. Cf. Bodice.]
Body Bod"y (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bodied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bodying.] To furnish with, or as with, a body; to produce in definite shape; to embody.

bodyguard.c: Bodyguard Bod"y*guard` (?), n. 1. A guard or group of guards to protect or defend the person; a lifeguard.

boeotian.c: Boeotian Bœ*o"tian (be*ō"shain), a. [L. Boeotia, Gr. boiwti`a, noted for its moist, thick atmosphere, and the dullness and stupidity of its inhabitants.] Of or pertaining to Bœotia. -- n. A native of Bœotia; also, one who is dull and ignorant.

boer.c: Boer ‖Boer (?), n. [D., a farmer. See Boor.] A colonist or farmer in South Africa of Dutch descent.

boes.c: Boes Bo"es (?), 3d sing. pr. of Behove. Behoves or behooves. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bog.c: bog bog (bŏg), n. [Ir. & Gael. bog soft, tender, moist: cf. Ir. bogach bog, moor, marsh, Gael. bogan quagmire.]
Bog Bog, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bogged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bogging.] To sink, as into a bog; to submerge in a bog; to cause to sink and stick, as in mud and mire.

bogberry.c: Bogberry Bog"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) The small cranberry (Vaccinium oxycoccus), which grows in boggy places.

bogey.c: Bogey Bo"gey (?), n.; pl. Bogeys (#). [Also bogie and bogy, plural bogies.] 1. A goblin; a bugbear.
Bogey Bo"gey (bō"gē), n.; pl. bogeys (bō"gēz), 1. A goblin; a bugbear.

bogeyman.c: Bogeyman Bo"gey*man (?), n.; pl. Bogeymen (#). A goblin; a bugbear; a bogey{1}. This is the form used by parents to frighten children; as, if you don't eat your vegetables, the bogeyman will get you.

Bogeyman Boogeyman {Boog"ey*man (bŏog"ē*măn), Bo"gey*man } (?), n. Something frightful, as a specter; anything imaginary that causes needless fright; something used to excite needless fear; also, something really dangerous, or an imaginary monster, used to frighten children, etc. “Go to sleep or the Boogeyman will get you.”

boggle.c: Boggle Bog"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Boggling (?).] [ See Bogle, n.] 1. To stop or hesitate as if suddenly frightened, or in doubt, or impeded by unforeseen difficulties; to take alarm; to exhibit hesitancy and indecision.
Boggle Bog"gle, v. t. To embarrass with difficulties; to make a bungle or botch of. [Local, U. S.]

boggy.c: Boggy Bog"gy (?), a. Consisting of, or containing, a bog or bogs; of the nature of a bog; swampy; as, boggy land.

bogie.c: Bogie Bo"gie (?), n. [A dialectic word. N. of Eng. & Scot.] A four-wheeled truck, having a certain amount of play around a vertical axis, used to support in part a locomotive on a railway track.
Bogie engine Bo"gie en"gine. (Railroads) A switching engine the running gear and driving gear of which are on a bogie, or truck.

bogle.c: Bogle Bo"gle (?), n. [Scot. and North Eng. bogle, bogill, bugill, specter; as a verb, to terrify, fr. W. bwgwl threatening, fear, bwg, bwgan, specter, hobgoblin. Cf. Bug.] A goblin; a specter; a frightful phantom; a bogy; a bugbear. [Written also boggle.]

bogsucker.c: Bogsucker Bog"suck`er (?), n. (Zool.) The American woodcock; -- so called from its feeding among the bogs.

bogtrotter.c: Bogtrotter Bog"trot`ter (?), n. One who lives in a boggy country; -- applied in derision to the lowest class of Irish. Halliwell.

bogue.c: Bogue Bogue (?), v. i. (Naut.) To fall off from the wind; to edge away to leeward; -- said only of inferior craft.
Bogue Bogue (?), n. (Zool.) The boce; -- called also bogue bream. See Boce.

bogus.c: Bogus Bo"gus (?), a. [Etymol. uncertain.] Spurious; fictitious; sham; -- a cant term originally applied to counterfeit coin, and hence denoting anything counterfeit. [Colloq. U. S.]
Bogus Bo"gus, n. A liquor made of rum and molasses. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

bogwood.c: Bogwood Bog"wood` (?), n. The wood of trees, esp. of oaks, dug up from peat bogs. It is of a shining black or ebony color, and is largely used for making ornaments.

bogy.c: Bogy Bo"gy (?), n.; pl. Bogies (?). [See Bogle.] A specter; a hobgoblin; a bugbear. “Death's heads and bogies.” J. H. Newman. [Written also bogey.]

bohea.c: Bohea Bo*hea" (?), n. [From Wu-i, pronounced by the Chinese bu-i, the name of the hills where this kind of tea is grown.] Bohea tea, an inferior kind of black tea. See under Tea.

bohemia.c: Bohemia Bo*he"mi*a (?), n. 1. A country of central Europe.

bohemian.c: Bohemian Bo*he"mi*an (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to Bohemia, or to the language of its ancient inhabitants or their descendants. See Bohemian, n., 2.
Bohemian Bo*he"mi*an (?), n. 1. A native of Bohemia.

bohemianism.c: Bohemianism Bo*he"mi*an*ism (?), n. The characteristic conduct or methods of a Bohemian. [Modern]

boil.c: Boil Boil (boil), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boiled (boild); p. pr. & vb. n. Boiling.] [OE. boilen, OF. boilir, builir, F. bouillir, fr. L. bullire to be in a bubbling motion, from bulla bubble; akin to Gr.?, Lith. bumbuls. Cf. Bull an edict, Budge, v., and Ebullition.] 1. To be agitated, or tumultuously moved, as a liquid by the generation and rising of bubbles of steam (or vapor), or of currents produced by heating it to the boiling point; to be in a state of ebullition; as, the water boils.
Boil Boil, v. t. 1. To heat to the boiling point, or so as to cause ebullition; as, to boil water.
Boil Boil, n. Act or state of boiling. [Colloq.]

Boil Boil, n. [Influenced by boil, v. See Beal, Bile.] A hard, painful, inflamed tumor, which, on suppuration, discharges pus, mixed with blood, and discloses a small fibrous mass of dead tissue, called the core.

boiled.c: Boiled Boiled (?), a. Dressed or cooked by boiling; subjected to the action of a boiling liquid; as, boiled meat; a boiled dinner; boiled clothes.

boiler.c: Boiler Boil"er, n. A sunken reef; esp., a coral reef on which the sea breaks heavily.

boilery.c: Boilery Boil"er*y (boil"ẽr*y̆), n. [Cf. F. bouillerie.] A place and apparatus for boiling, as for evaporating brine in salt making.

boiling.c: Boiling Boil"ing, a. Heated to the point of bubbling; heaving with bubbles; in tumultuous agitation, as boiling liquid; surging; seething; swelling with heat, ardor, or passion.
Boiling Boil"ing, n. 1. The act of ebullition or of tumultuous agitation.

boilingly.c: Boilingly Boil"ing*ly, adv. With boiling or ebullition.

bois.c: Bois d'arc ‖Bois" d'arc" (?). [F., bow wood. So called because used for bows by the Western Indians.] (Bot.) The Osage orange (Maclura aurantiaca).
Bois durci ‖Bois" dur`ci" (?). [F., hardened wood.] A hard, highly polishable composition, made of fine sawdust from hard wood (as rosewood) mixed with blood, and pressed.

boist.c: Boist Boist (?), n. [OF. boiste, F. boîte, from the same root as E. box.] A box. [Obs.]

boisterous.c: Boisterous Bois"ter*ous (?), a. [OE. boistous; of uncertain origin; cf. W. bwyst wild, savage, wildness, ferocity, bwystus ferocious.] 1. Rough or rude; unbending; unyielding; strong; powerful. [Obs.] “Boisterous sword.” “Boisterous hand.” Shak.

boisterously.c: Boisterously Bois"ter*ous*ly, adv. In a boisterous manner.

boisterousness.c: Boisterousness Bois"ter*ous*ness, n. The state or quality of being boisterous; turbulence; disorder; tumultuousness.

boistous.c: Boistous Bois"tous (?), a. Rough or rude; coarse; strong; violent; boisterous; noisy. [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Bois"tous*ly, adv. -- Bois"tous*ness, n. [Obs.] Chaucer.

bojanus.c: Bojanus organ Bo*ja"nus or"gan (?). [From Bojanus, the discoverer.] (Zool.) A glandular organ of bivalve mollusca, serving in part as a kidney.

boke.c: Boke Boke, v. t. & i. To poke; to thrust. [Obs. or Dial.]

bolar.c: Bolar Bo"lar (?), a. [See Bole clay.] Of or pertaining to bole or clay; partaking of the nature and qualities of bole; clayey.

bolas.c: Bolas ‖Bo"las (?), n. sing. & pl. [Sp.] A kind of missile weapon consisting of one, two, or more balls of stone, iron, or other material, attached to the ends of a leather cord; -- used by the Gauchos of South America, and others, for hurling at and entangling an animal.

bold.c: Bold Bold (bōld), a. [OE. bald, bold, AS. bald, beald; akin to Icel. ballr, OHG. bald, MHG. balt, D. boud, Goth. balþei boldness, It. baldo. In Ger. there remains only bald, adv. soon. Cf. Bawd, n.] 1. Forward to meet danger; venturesome; daring; not timorous or shrinking from risk; brave; courageous.
Bold eagle Bold eagle (?), (Zool.) an Australian eagle (Aquila audax), which destroys lambs and even the kangaroo. -- To make bold, to take liberties or the liberty; to venture.
Bold Bold (?), v. t. To make bold or daring. [Obs.] Shak.
Bold Bold, v. i. To be or become bold. [Obs.]

bolden.c: Bolden Bold"en (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boldened (?). ] To make bold; to encourage; to embolden.

boldfaced.c: Bold-faced Bold"-faced` (?), a. 1. Somewhat impudent; lacking modesty; as, a bold-faced woman.

boldly.c: Boldly Bold"ly, adv. [AS. bealdlīce.] In a bold manner.

boldness.c: Boldness Bold"ness, n. The state or quality of being bold.

boldu.c: Boldu Boldo { ‖Bol"do (?), ‖Bol"du (?), } n. (Bot.) A fragrant evergreen shrub of Chili (Peumus Boldus). The bark is used in tanning, the wood for making charcoal, the leaves in medicine, and the drupes are eaten.

bole.c: Bole Bole (?), n. [OE. bole, fr. Icel. bolr; akin to Sw. bål, Dan. bul, trunk, stem of a tree, G. bohle a thick plank or board; cf. LG. boll round. Cf. Bulge.] The trunk or stem of a tree, or that which is like it.
Bole Bole, n. [Etym. doubtful.] An aperture, with a wooden shutter, in the wall of a house, for giving, occasionally, air or light; also, a small closet. [Scot.]
Bole Bole, n. A measure. See Boll, n., 2. Mortimer.

Bole Bole, n. [Gr.? a clod or lump of earth: cf. F. bol, and also L. bolus morsel. Cf. Bolus.] 1. Any one of several varieties of friable earthy clay, usually colored more or less strongly red by oxide of iron, and used to color and adulterate various substances. It was formerly used in medicine. It is composed essentially of hydrous silicates of alumina, or more rarely of magnesia. See Clay, and Terra alba.

bolection.c: Bolection Bo*lec"tion (?), n. (Arch.) A projecting molding round a panel. Same as Bilection. Gwilt.

bolero.c: Bolero ‖Bo*le"ro (?), n. [Sp.] (Mus.) 1. A Spanish dance, or the lively music which accompanies it.

boletic.c: Boletic Bo*let"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, the Boletus.

boletus.c: Boletus ‖Bo*le"tus (?), n. [L. boletus, Gr.?.] (Bot.) A genus of fungi having the under side of the pileus or cap composed of a multitude of fine separate tubes. A few are edible, and others very poisonous.

bolye.c: Bolye Boley { Bo"ley, Bo"lye } (?), n. Same as Booly.

bolide.c: Bolide Bo"lide (?), n. [F. See Bolis.] A kind of meteor; a bolis.

bolis.c: Bolis ‖Bo"lis, n. [L., fr. Gr.? missile, arrow, fr.? to throw.] A meteor or brilliant shooting star, followed by a train of light or sparks; esp. one which explodes.

bolivian.c: Bolivian Bo*liv"i*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Bolivia. -- n. A native of Bolivia.

boll.c: Boll Boll (?), n. [OE. bolle boll, bowl, AS. bolla. See Bowl a vessel.] 1. The pod or capsule of a plant, as of flax or cotton; a pericarp of a globular form.
Boll Boll, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bolled (?).] To form a boll or seed vessel; to go to seed.

bollandists.c: Bollandists Bol"land*ists (?), n. pl. The Jesuit editors of the “Acta Sanctorum”, or Lives of the Saints; -- named from John Bolland, who began the work.

bollard.c: Bollard Bol"lard (?), n. [Cf. Bole the stem of a tree, and Pollard.] An upright wooden or iron post in a boat or on a dock, used in veering or fastening ropes.

bollen.c: Bollen Boln { Boln (?), Boll"en (?), } a. Swollen; puffed out.

bolling.c: Bolling Boll"ing (?), n. [Cf. Bole stem of a tree, and Poll, v. t.] A tree from which the branches have been cut; a pollard.

bollworm.c: Bollworm Boll"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) The larva of a moth (Heliothis armigera) which devours the bolls or unripe pods of the cotton plant, often doing great damage to the crops. Heliothis zea?? = cotton bollworm, corn earworm, tomato fuitworm?? -->

boln.c: Boln Boln (?), v. i. [OE. bolnen, bollen; cf. Dan. bulne. Cf. Bulge.] To swell; to puff. Holland.

bolo.c: Bolo ‖Bo"lo (?), n. [Sp.] A kind of large knife resembling a machete. [Phil. Islands]

bologna.c: Bologna Bo*lo"gna (?), n. 1. A city of Italy which has given its name to various objects.

bolognese.c: Bolognese Bo*lo`gnese" (?), a. Of or pertaining to Bologna. -- n. A native of Bologna.

bolometer.c: Bolometer Bo*lom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? a stroke, ray + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring minute quantities of radiant heat, especially in different parts of the spectrum; -- called also actinic balance, thermic balance. S. P. Langley.

bolsa.c: Bolsa ‖Bol"sa (?), n. [Sp., lit., purse. See Bourse.] An exchange for the transaction of business. [Sp. Amer. & Phil. Islands]

bolster.c: Bolster Bol"ster (bōl"stẽr; 110), n. [AS. bolster; akin to Icel. bōlstr, Sw. & Dan. bolster, OHG. bolstar, polstar, G. polster; from the same root as E. bole stem, bowl hollow vessel. Cf. Bulge, Poltroon.] 1. A long pillow or cushion, used to support the head of a person lying on a bed; -- generally laid under the pillows.
Bolster Bol"ster, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bolstered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Bolstering.] 1. To support with a bolster or pillow. S. Sharp.

bolt.c: Bolt Bolt (?), n. [AS. bolt; akin to Icel. bolti, Dan. bolt, D. bout, OHG. bolz, G. bolz, bolzen; of uncertain origin.] 1. A shaft or missile intended to be shot from a crossbow or catapult, esp. a short, stout, blunt-headed arrow; a quarrel; an arrow, or that which resembles an arrow; a dart.
Bolt Bolt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bolted; p. pr. & vb. n. Bolting.] 1. To shoot; to discharge or drive forth.
Bolt Bolt (bōlt; 110), v. i. 1. To start forth like a bolt or arrow; to spring abruptly; to come or go suddenly; to dart; as, to bolt out of the room.
Bolt Bolt, adv. In the manner of a bolt; suddenly; straight; unbendingly.
Bolt Bolt, n. [From Bolt, v. i.] 1. A sudden spring or start; a sudden spring aside; as, the horse made a bolt.

Bolt Bolt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bolted; p. pr. & vb. n. Bolting.] [OE. bolten, boulten, OF. buleter, F. bluter, fr. Ll. buletare, buratare, cf. F. bure coarse woolen stuff; fr. L. burrus red. See Borrel, and cf. Bultel.]
Bolt Bolt, n. A sieve, esp. a long fine sieve used in milling for bolting flour and meal; a bolter. B. Jonson.

bolter.c: Bolter Bolt"er (?), n. One who bolts; esp.: (a) A horse which starts suddenly aside. (b) A man who breaks away from his party.
Bolter Bolt"er, n. 1. One who sifts flour or meal.
Bolter Bolt"er, n. A kind of fishing line. See Boulter.

bolthead.c: Bolthead Bolt"head` (?), n. 1. (Chem.) A long, straight-necked, glass vessel for chemical distillations; -- called also a matrass or receiver.

bolting.c: Bolting Bolt"ing, n. A darting away; a starting off or aside.
Bolting Bolt"ing, n. 1. A sifting, as of flour or meal.

boltonite.c: Boltonite Bol"ton*ite (?), n. (Min.) A granular mineral of a grayish or yellowish color, found in Bolton, Massachusetts. It is a silicate of magnesium, belonging to the chrysolite family.

boltrope.c: Boltrope Bolt"rope` (?), n. (Naut.) A rope stitched to the edges of a sail to strengthen the sail.

boltsprit.c: Boltsprit Bolt"sprit` (?), n. [A corruption of bowsprit.] (Naut.) See Bowsprit.

bolty.c: Bolty Bol"ty (?), n. (Zool.) An edible fish of the Nile (genus Chromis). [Written also bulti.]

bolus.c: Bolus Bo"lus (?), n.; pl. Boluses (?). [L. bolus bit, morsel; cf. G.? lump of earth. See Bole, n., clay.] A rounded mass of anything, esp. a large pill.

bom.c: Bom Bom (?), n. (Zool.) A large American serpent, so called from the sound it makes.

bomb.c: Bomb Bomb (?), n. [F. bombe bombshell, fr. L. bombus a humming or buzzing noise, Gr.?.]
Bomb Bomb, v. t. To bombard. [Obs.] Prior.
Bomb Bomb, v. i. [Cf. Boom.] To sound; to boom; to make a humming or buzzing sound. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

bombard.c: Bombard Bom"bard (?), n. [F. bombarde, LL. bombarda, fr. L. bombus + -ard. Cf. Bumper, and see Bomb.] 1. (Gun.) A piece of heavy ordnance formerly used for throwing stones and other ponderous missiles. It was the earliest kind of cannon.
Bombard Bom"bard (?), n. [OE. bombarde, fr. F. bombarde.] (Mus.) See Bombardo. [Obs.]
Bombard Bom*bard" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bombarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bombarding.] To attack with bombards or with artillery; especially, to throw shells, hot shot, etc., at or into.

bombardier.c: Bombardier Bom`bar*dier" (?), n. [F. bombardier.] (Mil.) (a) One who used or managed a bombard; an artilleryman; a gunner. [Archaic] (b) A noncommissioned officer in the British artillery.

bombardman.c: Bombardman Bom"bard*man (?), n. One who carried liquor or beer in a can or bombard. [Obs.]

bombardment.c: Bombardment Bom*bard"ment (?), n. [F. bombardement.] An attack upon a fortress or fortified town, with shells, hot shot, rockets, etc.; the act of throwing bombs and shot into a town or fortified place.

bombardon.c: Bombardon Bombardo { ‖Bom*bar"do (?), Bom*bar"don (?), } n. [It. bombardo.] (Mus.) Originally, a deep-toned instrument of the oboe or bassoon family; thence, a bass reed stop on the organ. The name bombardon is now given to a brass instrument, the lowest of the saxhorns, in tone resembling the ophicleide. Grove.

bombast.c: Bombast Bom"bast (bŏm"bȧst or bŭm"bȧst; 277), n. [OF. bombace cotton, LL. bombax cotton, bombasium a doublet of cotton; hence, padding, wadding, fustian. See Bombazine.] 1. Originally, cotton, or cotton wool. [Obs.]
Bombast Bom"bast, a. High-sounding; inflated; big without meaning; magniloquent; bombastic.
Bombast Bom*bast" (bŏm*bȧst" or bŭm*bȧst"), v. t. To swell or fill out; to pad; to inflate. [Obs.]

bombastical.c: Bombastical Bombastic { Bom*bas"tic (bŏm*bȧs"tĭk or bŭm*bȧs"tĭk), Bom*bas"tic*al } (?), a. Characterized by bombast; high-sounding; inflated. -- Bom*bas"tic*al*ly, adv.

bombastry.c: Bombastry Bom"bast*ry (?), n. Swelling words without much meaning; bombastic language; fustian.

bombax.c: Bombax ‖Bom"bax (?), n. [LL., cotton. See Bombast, n.] (Bot.) A genus of trees, called also the silkcotton tree; also, a tree of the genus Bombax.

bombazet.c: Bombazet Bombazette { Bom`ba*zet" Bom`ba*zette" } (?), n. [Cf. Bombazine.] A sort of thin woolen cloth. It is of various colors, and may be plain or twilled.

bombazine.c: Bombazine Bom`ba*zine" (?), n. [F. bombasin, LL. bombacinium, bambacinium, L. bombycinus silken, bombycinum a silk or cotton texture, fr. bombyx silk, silkworm, Gr.?. Cf. Bombast, Bombycinous.] A twilled fabric for dresses, of which the warp is silk, and the weft worsted. Black bombazine has been much used for mourning garments. [Sometimes spelt bombasin, and bombasine.] Tomlinson.

bombic.c: Bombic Bom"bic (?), a. [L. bombyx silk, silkworm: cf. F. bombique.] Pertaining to, or obtained from, the silkworm; as, bombic acid.

bombilate.c: Bombilate Bom"bi*late (?), v. i. [LL. bombilare, for L. bombitare. See Bomb, n.] To hum; to buzz. [R.]

bombilation.c: Bombilation Bom`bi*la"tion (?), n. A humming sound; a booming.

bombinate.c: Bombinate Bom"bi*nate (?), v. i. To hum; to boom.

bombination.c: Bombination Bom`bi*na"tion (?), n. A humming or buzzing.

bombolo.c: Bombolo Bom"bo*lo (?), n.; pl. Bomboloes (?). [Cf. It bombola a pitcher.] A thin spheroidal glass retort or flask, used in the sublimation of camphor. [Written also bumbelo, and bumbolo.]

bombproof.c: Bombproof Bomb"proof` (?), a. Secure against the explosive force of bombs. -- n. A structure which heavy shot and shell will not penetrate.

bombshell.c: Bombshell Bomb"shell` (?), n. 1. A bomb. See Bomb, n.

bombycid.c: Bombycid Bom*by"cid (?), a. (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the genus Bombyx, or the family Bombycidæ.

bombycinous.c: Bombycinous Bom*byc"i*nous (bŏm*bĭs"ĭ*nŭs), a. [L. bombycinus. See Bombazine.] 1. Silken; made of silk. [Obs.] Coles.

bombylious.c: Bombylious Bom*byl"i*ous (bŏm*bĭl"ĭ*ŭs), a. [L. bombylius a bumblebee, Gr. bombylio`s.] Buzzing, like a bumblebee; as, the bombylious noise of the horse fly. [Obs.] Derham.

bombyx.c: Bombyx ‖Bom"byx (bŏm"bĭks), n. [L., silkworm. See Bombazine.] (Zool.) A genus of moths, which includes the silkworm moth. See Silkworm.

bon.c: Bon ‖Bon (?), a. [F., fr. L. bonus.] Good; valid as security for something.
Bon Silene ‖Bon" Si`lène" (bôN" se`lan"). [F.] (Bot.) A very fragrant tea rose with petals of various shades of pink.
Bon ton ‖Bon" ton" (bôN" tôN"). [F., good tone, manner.] The height of the fashion; fashionable society.
Bon vivant ‖Bon` vi`vant" (bôN` ve`väN"); pl. Bons vivants (-väN"z). [F. bon good + vivant, p. pr. of vivre to live.] A good fellow; a jovial companion; a free liver.

bonaccord.c: Bon-accord Bon-ac*cord" (?), n. Good will; good fellowship; agreement. [Scot.]

bonaci.c: Bonaci ‖Bo`na*ci" (?), n. [Amer. Sp. bonasí, prob. from native name.] (Zool.) (a) A large grouper (Mycteroperca bonaci) of Florida and the West Indies, valuable as a food fish; -- called also aguaji and, in Florida, black grouper. (b) Also, any one of several other similar fishes.

bona.c: Bona fide ‖Bo"na fi"de (?). [L.] In or with good faith; without fraud or deceit; real or really; actual or actually; genuine or genuinely; as, you must proceed bona fide; a bona fide purchaser or transaction.
Bona fides ‖Bo"na fi"des (bō"nȧ fī"dēz). [L.] Good faith; honesty; freedom from fraud or deception.
Bona roba ‖Bo"na ro"ba (?). [It., prop. “good stuff.”] A showy wanton; a courtesan. Shak

bonair.c: Bonair Bo*nair" (?), a. [OE., also bonere, OF. bonnaire, Cotgr., abbrev. of debonnaire. See Debonair.] Gentle; courteous; complaisant; yielding. [Obs.]

bonanza.c: Bonanza Bo*nan"za (?), n. [Sp., prop. calm., fair weather, prosperity, fr. L. bonus good.] In mining, a rich mine or vein of silver or gold; hence, anything which is a mine of wealth or yields a large income. [Colloq. U. S.]

bonapartean.c: Bonapartean Bo`na*part"e*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Napoleon Bonaparte or his family.

bonapartism.c: Bonapartism Bo"na*part`ism (?), n. The policy of Bonaparte or of the Bonapartes.

bonapartist.c: Bonapartist Bo"na*part`ist, n. One attached to the policy or family of Bonaparte, or of the Bonapartes.

bonassus.c: Bonassus Bonasus { Bo*na"sus (?), Bo*nas"sus } (?), n. [L. bonasus, Gr.?,?.] (Zool.) The aurochs or European bison. See Aurochs.

bonbon.c: Bonbon ‖Bon"bon` (?), n. [F. bonbon, fr. bon bon very good, a superlative by reduplication, fr. bon good.] Sugar confectionery; a sugarplum; hence, any dainty.

bonbonniere.c: Bonbonniere ‖Bon`bon`nière" (?), n.; pl. -nières (#). [F.] A small fancy box or dish for bonbons.

bonce.c: Bonce Bonce (?), n. [Etymol. unknown.] A boy's game played with large marbles.

bonchretien.c: Bonchretien ‖Bon`chré`tien" (?), n. [F., good Christian.] A name given to several kinds of pears. See Bartlett.

boncilate.c: Boncilate Bon"ci*late (?), n. [Empirical trade name.] A substance composed of ground bone, mineral matters, etc., hardened by pressure, and used for making billiard balls, boxes, etc.

bond.c: Bond Bond (bŏnd), n. [The same word as band. Cf. Band, Bend.] 1. That which binds, ties, fastens, or confines, or by which anything is fastened or bound, as a cord, chain, etc.; a band; a ligament; a shackle or a manacle.

Bond Bond (bŏnd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bonded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bonding.] 1. To place under the conditions of a bond; to mortgage; to secure the payment of the duties on (goods or merchandise) by giving a bond.

Bond Bond, n. [OE. bond, bonde, peasant, serf, AS. bonda, bunda, husband, bouseholder, from Icel. bōndi husbandman, for būandi, fr. būa to dwell. See Boor, Husband.] A vassal or serf; a slave. [Obs. or Archaic]
Bond Bond, a. In a state of servitude or slavery; captive.
Bond servant bond-servant bond-servant, Bond" serv`ant (sẽrv`aint). A slave; one who is bound to service without wages.
Bond service Bond" serv`ice (sẽrv`ĭs). The condition of a bond servant; service without wages; slavery.

bondage.c: Bondage Bond"age (-aj), n. [LL. bondagium. See Bond, a.]

bondager.c: Bondager Bond"a*ger (-a*jẽr), n. A field worker, esp. a woman who works in the field. [Scot.]

bondar.c: Bondar ‖Bon"dar (bŏn"där), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A small quadruped of Bengal (Paradoxurus bondar), allied to the genet; -- called also musk cat.

bonded.c: Bonded Bond"ed (bŏnd"ĕd), a. Placed under, or covered by, a bond, as for the payment of duties, or for conformity to certain regulations.

bonder.c: Bonder Bond"er (bŏnd"ẽr), n. 1. One who places goods under bond or in a bonded warehouse.
Bonder Bond"er, n. [Norwegian bonde.] A freeholder on a small scale. [Norway] Emerson.

bondholder.c: Bondholder Bond"hold`er (-hōld`ẽr), n. A person who holds the bonds of a public or private corporation for the payment of money at a certain time.

bondmaid.c: Bondmaid Bond"maid` (-mād`), n. [Bond, a. or n. + maid.] A female slave, or one bound to service without wages, as distinguished from a hired servant.

bondman.c: Bondman Bond"man (-main), n.; pl. Bondmen (-mein). [Bond,a.orn.+ man.] 1. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages. “To enfranchise bondmen.” Macaulay.

bondslave.c: Bondslave Bond"slave` (-slāv`), n. A person in a state of slavery; one whose person and liberty are subjected to the authority of a master.

bondsman.c: Bondsman Bonds"man (?), n.; pl. Bondsmen. [Bond, a. or n. + man.] 1. A slave; a villain; a serf; a bondman.

bondstone.c: Bondstone Bond"stone` (bŏnd"stōn`), n. [Bond,n.+ stone.] (Masonry) A stone running through a wall from one face to another, to bind it together; a binding stone.

bonduc.c: Bonduc ‖Bon"duc (bŏn"dŭk), n. [F. bonduc, fr. Ar. bunduq hazel nut, filbert nut.] (Bot.) See Nicker tree.

bondwoman.c: Bondwoman Bond"wom`an (bŏnd"wŏom`ain), n.; pl. Bondwomen (-wĭm`ein). [Bond,a.orn.+ woman.] A woman who is a slave, or in bondage.

bone.c: Bone Bone (bōn; 110), n. [OE. bon, ban, AS. bān; akin to Icel. bein, Sw. ben, Dan. & D. been, G. bein bone, leg; cf. Icel. beinn straight.] 1. (Anat.) The hard, calcified tissue of the skeleton of vertebrate animals, consisting very largely of calcium carbonate, calcium phosphate, and gelatine; as, blood and bone.
Bone Bone (bōn), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boned (bōnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Boning.] 1. To withdraw bones from the flesh of, as in cookery. “To bone a turkey.” Soyer.

Bone Bone, v. t. [F. bornoyer to look at with one eye, to sight, fr. borgne one-eyed.] To sight along an object or set of objects, to see if it or they be level or in line, as in carpentry, masonry, and surveying. Knight.

boneache.c: Boneache Bone"ache` (-āk`), n. Pain in the bones. Shak.

boneblack.c: Boneblack Bone"black` (?), n. See Bone black, under Bone, n.

boned.c: Boned Boned (bōnd), a. 1. Having (such) bones; -- used in composition; as, big-boned; strong-boned.

boneless.c: Boneless Bone"less, a. Without bones. “Boneless gums.” Shak.

boneset.c: Boneset Bone"set` (-sĕt`), n. (Bot.) A medicinal plant, the thoroughwort (Eupatorium perfoliatum). Its properties are diaphoretic and tonic.

bonesetter.c: Bonesetter Bone"set*ter (-sĕt*tẽr), n. One who sets broken or dislocated bones; -- commonly applied to one, not a regular surgeon, who makes an occupation of setting bones. -- Bone"set*ting, n.

bonetta.c: Bonetta Bo*net"ta (bo*nĕt"tȧ), n. See Bonito. Sir T. Herbert.

bonfire.c: Bonfire Bon"fire` (?), n. [OE. bonefire, banefire, orig. a fire of bones; bone + fire; but cf. also Prov. E. bun a dry stalk.] A large fire built in the open air, as an expression of public joy and exultation, or for amusement.

bongo.c: Bongo Bon"go (?), n. Either of two large antelopes (Boöcercus eurycercus of West Africa, and Boöcercus isaaci of East Africa) of a reddish or chestnut-brown color with narrow white stripes on the body. Their flesh is especially esteemed as food.

Bongo Bon"go (bŏṉ"gō), n. Either of two large antelopes (Boöcercus eurycercus of West Africa, and Boöcercus isaaci of East Africa) of a reddish or chestnut-brown color with narrow white stripes on the body. Their flesh is especially esteemed as food.

bongrace.c: Bongrace Bon"grace` (bŏn"grās`), n. [F. bon good + grâce grace, charm.] A projecting bonnet or shade to protect the complexion; also, a wide-brimmed hat. [Obs.]

bonhommie.c: Bonhommie Bonhomie ‖Bon`ho*mie", ‖Bon`hom*mie" (bŏn`ŏ*mē"), n. [F.] Good nature; pleasant and easy manner.

boniface.c: Boniface Bon"i*face (?), n. [From the sleek, jolly landlord in Farquhar's comedy of “The Beaux' Stratagem.”] An innkeeper.

boniform.c: Boniform Bon"i*form (?), a. [L. bonus good + -form.] Sensitive or responsive to moral excellence. Dr. H. More.

bonify.c: Bonify Bon"i*fy (?), v. t. [L. bonus good + -fy: cf. F. bonifier.] To convert into, or make, good.

boniness.c: Boniness Bon"i*ness (?), n. The condition or quality of being bony.

boning.c: Boning Bon"ing, n. [Senses 1 and 2 fr. 1st Bone, sense 3 fr. 3d Bone.] 1. The clearing of bones from fish or meat.

bonitary.c: Bonitary Bon"i*ta*ry (?), a. Beneficial, as opposed to statutory or civil; as, bonitary dominion of land.

bonito.c: Bonito Bo*ni"to (bo*nē"to), n.; pl. Bonitoes (-toz). [Sp. & Pg. bonito, fr. Ar. bainīt and bainīth.] [Often incorrectly written bonita.] (Zool.) 1. A large tropical fish (Orcynus pelamys) allied to the tunny. It is about three feet long, blue above, with four brown stripes on the sides. It is sometimes found on the American coast.

bonmot.c: Bonmot ‖Bon"mot` (bôN"mo`), n.; pl. Bonsmots (-moz`). [ F. bon good + mot word.] A witty repartee; a jest.

bonnaz.c: Bonnaz Bon"naz (?), n. A kind of embroidery made with a complicated sewing machine, said to have been originally invented by a Frenchman of the name of Bonnaz. The work is done either in freehand or by following a perforated design.

bonne.c: Bonne ‖Bonne (bŏn), n. [F., prop. good woman.] A female servant charged with the care of a young child.
Bonne bouche ‖Bonne" bouche" (bŏn' bŏosh`); pl. Bonnes bouches (bŏn' bŏosh`). [F. bon, fem. bonne, good + bouche mouth.] A delicious morsel or mouthful; a tidbit.

bonnet.c: Bonnet Bon"net (bŏn"nĕt), n. [OE. bonet, OF. bonet, bonete. F. bonnet fr. LL. bonneta, bonetum; orig. the name of a stuff, and of unknown origin.] 1. A headdress for men and boys; a cap. [Obs.] Milton. Shak.
Bonnet Bon"net, v. i. To take off the bonnet or cap as a mark of respect; to uncover. [Obs.] Shak.
Bonnet rouge ‖Bon`net" rouge" (?). [F.] The red cap adopted by the extremists in the French Revolution, which became a sign of patriotism at that epoch; hence, a revolutionist; a Red Republican.

bonneted.c: Bonneted Bon"net*ed, a. 1. Wearing a bonnet. “Bonneted and shawled.” Howitt.

bonnethead.c: bonnethead bonnet head bonnet head, bonnethead n. (Zool.), small harmless hammerhead shark (Sphyrna tiburio) of the southern United States and West Indies, having a spade-shaped head; abundant in bays and estuaries.

bonnibel.c: Bonnibel Bon"ni*bel (bŏn"nĭ*bĕl), n. [F. bonne et belle, good and beautiful. Cf. Bellibone.] A handsome girl. [Obs.]

bonnilass.c: Bonnilass Bon"ni*lass` (bŏn"ny̆*lȧs`), n. [Bonny + lass.] A “bonny lass”; a beautiful girl. [Obs.] Spenser.

bonniness.c: Bonniness Bon"ni*ness, n. The quality of being bonny; gayety; handsomeness. [R.]

bonny.c: Bonny Bon"ny (-ny̆), a. [Spelled bonnie by the Scotch.] [OE. boni, prob. fr. F. bon, fem. bonne, good, fr. L. bonus good. See Bounty, and cf. Bonus, Boon.] 1. Handsome; beautiful; pretty; attractively lively and graceful.
Bonny Bon"ny, n. (Mining) A round and compact bed of ore, or a distinct bed, not communicating with a vein.

bonnyclabber.c: Bonnyclabber Bon"ny*clab`ber (-klăb`bẽr), n. [Ir. bainne, baine, milk + clabar mud, mire.] Coagulated sour milk; loppered milk; curdled milk; -- sometimes called simply clabber. B. Jonson.

bonspiel.c: Bonspiel Bon"spiel (bŏn"spēl), n. [Scot.; of uncertain origin.] A curling match between clubs. [Scot.]

bontebok.c: Bontebok ‖Bon"te*bok (bŏn"te*bŏk), n. [D. bont a sort of skin or fur, prop. variegated + bok buck.] (Zool.) The pied antelope of South Africa (Alcelaphus pygarga). Its face and rump are white. Called also nunni.

bonus.c: Bonus Bo"nus (bō"nŭs), n.; pl. Bonuses (-ĕz). [L. bonus good. Cf. Bonny.] 1. (Law) A premium given for a loan, or for a charter or other privilege granted to a company; as the bank paid a bonus for its charter. Bouvier.

bony.c: Bony Bon"y (bō"ny̆), a. 1. Consisting of bone, or of bones; full of bones; pertaining to bones.

bonze.c: Bonze Bon"ze (bŏn"ze; 277), n. [Pg. bonzo, fr. Japan. bōzu a Buddhist priest: cf. F. bonze.] A Buddhist or Fohist priest, monk, or nun.

booby.c: Booby Boo"by (bōo"by̆), n.; pl. Boobies (-bĭz). [Sp. bobo dunce, idiot; cf. L. balbus stammering, E. barbarous.]
Booby Boo"by (bōo"by̆), a. Having the characteristics of a booby; stupid.

boodh.c: Boodh Boodh (bōod), n. Same as Buddha. Malcom.

boodle.c: Boodle Boo"dle (bōo"d`l), n. [Origin uncertain.] 1. The whole collection or lot; caboodle. [Low, U. S.] Bartlett.

boohoo.c: Boohoo Boo`hoo" (bōo`hōo"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boohooed (bōo`hōod"); p. pr. & vb. n. Boohooing.] [An imitative word.] To bawl; to cry loudly. [Low] Bartlett.
Boohoo Boo"hoo` (bōo"hōo`), n. (Zool.) The sailfish; -- called also woohoo.

book.c: Book Book (bŏok), n. [OE. book, bok, AS. bōc; akin to Goth. bōka a letter, in pl. book, writing, Icel. bōk, Sw. bok, Dan. bog, OS. bōk, D. boek, OHG. puoh, G. buch; and fr. AS. bōc, bēce, beech; because the ancient Saxons and Germans in general wrote runes on pieces of beechen board. Cf. Beech.] 1. A collection of sheets of paper, or similar material, blank, written, or printed, bound together; commonly, many folded and bound sheets containing continuous printing or writing.
Book Book, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Booked (bŏokt); p. pr. & vb. n. Booking.] 1. To enter, write, or register in a book or list.
Book muslin Book" mus`lin (?). 1. A kind of muslin used for the covers of books.

bookbinder.c: Bookbinder Book"bind`er (bŏok"bīnd`ẽr), n. One whose occupation is to bind books.
